projects.title: Up & Out
projects.tagline: Up & Out turns an elevator ride into an interactive story. Enter world-model-powered floors, meet unique characters, blur the lines between reality and fiction.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Inspired by the “UP AND OUT” chapter in Roald Dahl’s Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, we asked: what if every elevator button opened a world you could influence?

What it does

Up & Out turns your phone into a glass elevator. Each stop opens onto a world-model-generated floor, where you use your camera to complete real-world quests and change what happens next.

How we built it

Reactor H3 generates the animated encounters, while ElevenLabs voices the characters. Node.js and Express manage the journey and rewards. Codex supported development, Higgsfield helped create visual assets and VEED was used to edit test and demo footage.

Challenges we ran into

Choosing and scoping the idea, unreliable Wi-Fi and working within provider credit limits.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We authored 28 distinct rooms and connected their generated stories to visitors’ real-world actions.

What we learned

We learned how to prompt time-sensitive interactive video and combine the sponsor tools into one live experience.

projects.title: Golem
projects.tagline: Give it an image. Get a world with rules. One photo becomes a validated glide game rendered live by a world model, then you speak a rule and the same world plays differently.
projects.description:
Give it an image. Get a world with rules.

Hand Golem a photo, a doodle, or a webcam frame. A multimodal model reads it and writes a short first-person glide game: a title, a world, three rings and a goal. A deterministic runtime plays that game while a world model renders it live, in the style of your image. When you win, you say one sentence out loud ("double the turn rate") and the same world replays under the new rule. You leave with a downloadable Game Cartridge: your image on the left, the generated world on the right, the path you flew in between.

Inspiration

World models can now render a coherent place from one image and let you steer through it. A place is not a game, though. A game needs exact state: where you are, which gate is next, how much time is left, whether you won. LingBot World 2 gives you a video track and camera commands. It has no colliders, no map, no idea what a checkpoint is.

We wanted one image to become two things at once: an explicit, validated game program, and the live visual identity of a video-model world. And we wanted the beat most AI game generators skip: change one rule, and the world you were just in plays differently without being regenerated.

How it works

image or camera frame
  → normalized to 1664×960 WebP, SHA-256 seed id
  → in parallel: upload to LingBot World 2  +  POST to game compiler
  → Kimi K3 (Modal Shared Endpoint) returns a strict-JSON GameSpec
  → schema → references → bounds → route order → headless pilot → prompt budget
  → at most ONE repair call, then a known-valid fallback
  → live world starts; deterministic 60 Hz Glide loop starts
  → rings, HUD, timer, win drawn from deterministic state over the video
  → win → speak a rule → bounded turn-rate patch, validated, applied transactionally
  → same Reactor session replays under the new rule
  → 1600×1000 Game Cartridge rendered locally, downloadable as PNG

The model designs the game; code plays it. Kimi K3, on a Modal Shared Endpoint, authors a title, a world prompt with two to four concrete landmarks, five proxy entities (start, three checkpoints, goal) and four Glide multipliers. It cannot invent technical identity: the validator injects the reference image id and RNG seed. Its output is treated as
unknown
, parsed with Zod twice (a strict
json_schema
at the provider, generated from the same Zod definition, then again locally), and only a branded
ValidatedGameSpec
reaches the runtime.

Validation fails closed and still ships a game. Schema, unique ids, resolved references, finite numbers inside the calibrated envelope, checkpoints monotonic in forward
z
, a headless pilot that completes the course inside the time limit, and a composed LingBot prompt under 2,000 characters. A failed candidate gets one repair turn with structured issues attached (at most 16, 160 characters each); if that fails too, a known-valid fallback loads. Nothing unvalidated ever initialises the runtime.

Gameplay is deterministic even though the world is generative. A fixed-step (1/60 s) Glide core owns pose, speed, checkpoint order, timer, respawn and win. Gate crossings use segment–sphere intersection so a fast frame cannot tunnel through a ring; the same 1,800 inputs produce byte-identical state every run. The LingBot stream fills the viewport and the rings,
0/3
counter and timer are drawn over it from runtime state alone. Turn and pitch map to
set_look_horizontal
and
set_look_vertical
, and every latched Reactor control is released on blur, hidden tab, win, error and unmount.

The patch keeps the world. After the original win, Chrome speech recognition auto-submits its final transcript. A second, text-only model call returns a strict patch that can do exactly one thing: multiply Glide turn rate by a bounded factor. The runtime multiplier and Reactor
set_rotation_speed_deg
update together, the seed, world, entities and live session stay put, and the patched replay starts on its own.
Type instead
is always one click away.

The patched win captures a live frame and composes a 1600×1000 cartridge in the browser: original seed, generated world, title,
GLIDE
, completion time, path trace,
TURN RATE ×2
, and the caption the model wrote. No final model call, nothing persisted, essential text mirrored in semantic DOM.

What we measured

Compiler, image to GameSpec, on three materially different seeds: 8.5 s / 5.1 s / 6.3 s. All three validated on the first try; no repair needed.

Spoken patch: 1.8 s / 1.8 s / 1.3 s. "Double the turn rate" gave ×2, "make it turn way slower and smoother" gave ×0.5.

Make playable to first live frame: 9.8 s and 11.2 s with pool capacity, 50 s once when auto-retry had to wait for a slot.

Input to overlay: 8 ms. Command to next
chunk_complete
: 1.0–2.0 s, each mapped action confirmed in the chunk's
active_action
.

A 2 s held turn at
rotation_speed_deg 6
swung the world about 90°, so we recalibrated runtime yaw to 0.78 rad/s to match the stream.

20
node:test
cases and a Playwright fake-world flow run with zero paid calls; an opt-in
REAL_REACTOR=1
spec records live sessions.

Challenges

The world lags the rules. LingBot responds one to two chunks (1–2 s) after a command. No prompt fixes that, so the architecture absorbs it: the overlay is the collision truth and the stream is appearance only.

Reactor's shared pool intermittently returned HTTP 429 "no available capacity" (2 of 4 attempts on one run). The SDK gives up after three fast retries, so we replaced those with a slow reconnect every 8 s and kept the refusals in the evidence folder.

One bug fit in one line. Reactor returns
expires_at
in epoch seconds; we read it as milliseconds, so every request re-minted a token and later session calls 403'd. Multiply by 1000.

Calibration was empirical. Base speed, yaw rate, ring radii, spacing and course duration were tuned against the real stream and live in one
GLIDE_CALIBRATION
constant.

And we cut scope hard. "Anything becomes any game" is not achievable on a hosted video world model in one day. "Any image becomes a validated glide game with its own world, and you can change its rules" is, so that is what we built. Glide is the only mechanic; no generated JavaScript, no physics engine, no Three.js.

What we learned

Don't run model-written code on the critical path. A declarative, bounded, twice-parsed spec still counts as the model writing the game program; the program just has no authority outside the game.

Model events are the source of truth for a live session. Sending a command means nothing until the model acknowledges it.

A headless pilot is the best validator we have. If code cannot finish the course, a judge cannot either.

Truthful progress beats fake progress. The four staging rows (Reading the seed / Writing the rules / Testing the game / Warming the world) show real states, including "repaired" and "fallback".

What's next

Camera-pose translation for boost feedback, a second mechanic (Grapple) once its spatial grounding is trustworthy, and a shareable cartridge gallery.

projects.title: TourMemory
projects.tagline: Turn travel photos into memories you can step inside: a local-first photo journal with spatial views and AI-generated worlds you can explore.
projects.description:
Paste the following into the project story field. Adjust the first-person wording if needed to match your team.

Inspiration
A photograph captures a view, but revisiting a place means remembering more than what fit inside the frame. There’s the path you walked, the details you noticed, and the little things that never made it into a caption.

Memory explores a simple question: what if your photo album gave you a way to step back inside a moment?

We wanted to connect world models to something personal: the places people already care about.

What it does
Memory turns five to ten photographs into a personal photo journey. You can arrange the stops, add recollections, and return to your favorite moments.

Three optional AI features let you explore further:

Spatial photos: Modal runs Depth Anything V2 to estimate relative depth, which Three.js uses to give a photograph a subtle sense of perspective as you move.
Landscape scenes: Runware generates a wider scene using a source photograph and up to two additional references. Generated images stay separate from the saved source photos.
Live walks: Reactor’s LingBot World 2 uses one selected photograph to start an AI-generated world. You can move with WASD, look around with arrow keys, pause, and save a generated frame.
The journal is local-first. Saved photo copies and notes live in your browser, with export and import for portability. Cloud actions require an access code and explicit consent to send photos to the selected provider.
ow we built it
We built the application with Next.js, React, and TypeScript, using IndexedDB for local persistence.

The browser prepares resized photo copies and removes embedded metadata. Server-side API routes validate requests with Zod, normalize provider-bound images with Sharp, and keep provider credentials out of the client.

A Python worker on Modal runs Depth Anything V2 on an L4 GPU. The resulting depth maps drive the Three.js spatial viewer.

Runware’s FLUX.2 Pro integration creates optional landscape scenes. Reactor’s LingBot World 2 SDK handles interactive world generation and streams the result into the browser.

We used Vitest and Playwright to test data contracts, local journal workflows, consent boundaries, and provider failure handling.

Challenges we faced
One important challenge was distinguishing a photograph from an AI interpretation. Estimated depth is not a measured 3D reconstruction, and a generated walk cannot guarantee what actually exists beyond the frame. We kept those distinctions visible and preserved source photos separately from generated scenes.

Real-time controls also needed careful handling. Movement commands persist until stopped, so releasing a key, switching tabs, pausing, or ending a session must clear the input.

Cloud processing introduced another challenge: a request can fail after other work has already succeeded. Spatial preparation saves completed photos as it goes, allowing the user to retry unfinished stops without losing progress.

Accomplishments that we’re proud of
We connected a personal photo journal to three distinct AI workflows while keeping the journal useful without cloud processing.

We also made preservation part of the experience: source photos remain separate, generated content is labeled, and memories can be exported instead of being tied to one browser forever.

What we learned
World models need clear boundaries around what they generate. A convincing scene can feel like a memory even when its details are invented.

We also learned that session management, consent, and recovery deserve as much attention as the generation itself. They determine whether someone can comfortably use the feature with photos that matter to them.

What’s next for Memory
We want to improve scene continuity, make longer photo journeys easier to organize, and offer a clearer comparison between the source photograph and its generated interpretation.

The goal is to make revisiting a memory more expressive while keeping the original record intact.

projects.title: RoomShift AI
projects.tagline: Turn any room photo into your next interior: remove furniture, discover real products, place them with AI, and generate a realistic preview and video in minutes.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Buying furniture online is easy, but imagining how it will actually look in your own room is much harder. We wanted to bridge the gap between online furniture shopping and interior visualisation by letting users redesign their real space before making a purchase.

The idea behind RoomShift AI is simple: start with a photo of your current room, remove what you no longer want, find real furniture online, and use AI to visualise what the room could become.

What it does

RoomShift AI turns a room photo into an interactive AI-powered redesign experience.

Users can:

Upload a photo of their own room.

Select and remove unwanted furniture.

Search for real furniture products from online shopping results.

Select a product and describe where they want it placed.

Generate an AI preview showing that product inside their room.

Turn the redesigned room into a short AI-generated video.

This creates an end-to-end journey from
"this is my room now" → "this is what I could buy" → "this is what my room could look like."

How we built it

We built RoomShift AI as a browser-based application with a Python backend and an HTML/JavaScript frontend.

The system connects several AI and search components into one workflow:

Runware
is used for selected-object removal and room clearing.

Google's image model through Runware
generates the redesigned room using both the original room and selected furniture as visual references.

SerpApi Google Shopping
provides real furniture search results.

Reactor Helios
converts the final redesigned room into a short generated video.

Rather than building each feature as an isolated demo, we connected them into a single user workflow where outputs from one stage become inputs to the next.

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges was preserving the original room while making targeted changes. Generative image models can unintentionally modify walls, lighting, windows, flooring, or other furniture when the goal is to change only one object.

Furniture placement was another challenge. A product image from a shopping result does not contain complete information about its real-world scale, orientation, or how it should interact with the geometry of the room.

We also had to integrate multiple external services with different APIs, image formats, response structures, generation times, and failure modes while keeping the experience simple for the user.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're particularly proud that RoomShift AI became an end-to-end working prototype rather than just an image-generation demo.

A user can start with their own room photograph, remove existing furniture, discover a real product, place it into their room using natural-language instructions, and finally generate a video of the redesigned space.

We also built the application so users can upload their own images rather than being restricted to a predefined demonstration room.

What we learned

We learned that building a useful generative AI product is not just about choosing a powerful model. A large part of the challenge is connecting models, external data, user interaction, and generation steps into a reliable workflow.

We also saw the limitations of current image generation when precise spatial relationships, product identity, scale, and preservation of the original environment all matter simultaneously.

Most importantly, we learned how multiple AI capabilities can be orchestrated to turn a simple user request into a complete interactive experience.

What's next for RoomShift AI

The next step is to make RoomShift AI more spatially aware.

We would like to add room and furniture dimensions so generated designs reflect whether a product can actually fit in the available space. We also want to improve product-appearance preservation, support more furniture categories, and allow users to compare several alternative designs.

Ultimately, RoomShift AI could evolve from an AI visualisation prototype into a bridge between
furniture discovery, spatial planning, and online shopping
.

projects.title: GPT-H3
projects.tagline: We freeze the H3 video model and combine its physical understanding from video input with a 250M parameter action model.
projects.description:
A video model does more than recognize what is in a frame. To predict what comes next, it must build internal representations of how a scene changes over time. Those states can encode motion, viewpoint changes, object dynamics, and the effects of actions. A camera moving forward, rotating, or closing in on an object is not far from a robot doing the same thing with cameras mounted on its body.

This project tests whether those internal dynamics can be reused for control.

We freeze the MiniMax H3 video model and use it as a temporal visual feature extractor. The inputs are a task instruction plus synchronized external and wrist-camera observations from LIBERO. A separate roughly 255M parameter Transformer reads six selected H3 layers and predicts 34 consecutive 7D robot actions.

The policy alternates cross-attention and self-attention blocks. Causal video attention, historical cross-attention cutoffs, and isolated action-query groups prevent future observations from leaking into predictions.

Current training uses LIBERO-Spatial with 450 demonstrations for training and 50 for validation.

projects.title: Skopos
projects.tagline: Skopos is a live world model of a real physical environment. It maps the space, searches it for the combinations that hold up, and lets agents deploy and optimise against a Monte Carlo baseline.
projects.description:
Inspiration

We had been working on adversarial stress-testing of autonomous systems under distributional shift - the question of how a policy behaves when the world stops matching the distribution it was trained on. That work lives in simulators for space robotics, where the gap between the modelled environment and the real one is obvious and everybody admits it.

Then we started noticing the same question wearing different clothes.

Every home robot demo is filmed in the room it was trained in. Bright light, clean floor, furniture exactly where the engineers left it. But the robot does not fail in the lab. It fails in the ten-thousandth home, on a Tuesday, in the dark - on a surface its depth sensor cannot resolve, in a room that has been rearranged since the scan.

The industry has two answers to "will this robot work in this environment?" Ship it and find out, which is slow and expensive and discovers the worst failures in production. Or build a metric-accurate digital twin, which needs ground truth, a physics engine, and a rendering budget nobody can justify per household.

Both answers share the same mistake. They treat the scanned environment as the environment. But a scan is one photograph of a space that will have changed by the time the robot arrives. The question is not "does this work in this room?" It is:

Does this work in every plausible version of this room?

That is a statistical question. And it turns out you can answer it , live —, if you stop trying to answer it with pixels.

What it does

Skopos is a live world model of a real physical environment.

It maps the space, holds it as a structured, continuously updatable model rather than a frozen capture, and then does the thing a static twin cannot: it explores the space of plausible variations of that environment, surfaces the combinations that hold up and the ones that break, and gives deploying agents a measured Monte Carlo baseline to optimise against.

Concretely, the loop is:

Map. Perception collapses the environment into a scene graph: objects, positions, extents, and material flags such as reflective and low-contrast, plus room-level lighting and clutter. This is the live model, and it is a few hundred bytes of structured text.
Perturb. A perturbation 𝜃
θ is a continuous sample: per-object drift 
(𝑑𝑥, 𝑑𝑦), presence flips, a lighting value, and a Poisson count of unmodelled clutter. There is no enumerated list of "scenarios" - there is a distribution.
Score. Every sampled configuration is evaluated against a task, in microseconds, on the graph rather than on rendered frames.
Search. A cross-entropy method refits the sampler toward its own worst outcomes, finding rare-but-plausible failure modes rather than absurd ones.
Deploy. Agents choose a strategy per configuration and optimise against the Monte Carlo baseline the campaign established.

The output is a readiness estimate with an honest uncertainty interval, a ranked attribution of which object in the environment is responsible for the failures, and a set of configurations worth a human's attention.

And the whole thing runs live. You can drag an object across the map and watch the estimate re-measure.

How we built it:
The statistical core
Readiness is a Monte Carlo estimate of a failure probability under an environment prior

Twenty thousand samples give a standard error on the order of 
1/𝑛 , which is why the number on screen converges rather than jumps. You are watching an estimator settle.

Re-weighting instead of re-sampling:

Different environments have different priors - how much things drift, how often something is missing, how bright it usually is. Estimating each one separately costs a full campaign each, and that kills "live."

So Skopos samples once from a defensive mixture proposal and reweighs. The proposal mixes every target prior plus one deliberately over-dispersed component.

Refusing to lie:

Importance weights can collapse onto a handful of samples, at which point the estimate is noise wearing a number's clothes. So every re-weighted estimate carries its effective sample size, so the search finds failures that could actually happen rather than pathological ones. Five iterations, four hundred samples each, refitting the proposal to its own worst decile and blending toward the fit so convergence is visible across iterations.

It works, and the way it works is the nicest result in the project: it was never told what makes an environment dangerous, and it discovers darkness. The proposal's mean lighting collapses from 
0.68 to 0.06 and the failure rate climbs from 46% to 90+%.

Agent strategy selection:

Strategy choice here is genuinely one-step — pick an approach, observe the outcome, no state transition — so a contextual bandit is the honest model rather than a full RL policy pretending to be one. LinUCB over four arms:
Each tick draws a fresh perturbed environment from the same proposal the campaign uses, so the agent adapts to exactly the distribution the readiness number is measured over. The entire model is five numbers per arm — and they are drawn on screen, exploration bonus rendered separately from the mean, because a model small enough to display should be displayed.

The build: engine.py is stdlib-only and is the fixed dependency nothing else is allowed to modify. bandit.py is pure-Python LinUCB. privacy.py holds the ledger and a startup assertion. app.py is FastAPI with a single WebSocket. The front end is vanilla JavaScript with no build step and no external requests — every chart drawn on a raw  from engine output. recorder.py makes any run reproducible from a seed and replayable with nothing on the network. selftest.py checks every claim in the README, including grepping the codebase to enforce that nothing is trained.

No API keys, no npm, no network required to run it.

Privacy, as an architectural property

Frames become a scene graph in memory and are then dropped. Only structured text crosses the network. The UI shows the exact payload live alongside counters for frames processed, frames discarded, frames written to disk, and a permanent pixels transmitted: 0.

There is exactly one escape hatch, it defaults off, and when it is on the startup log shouts and the panel turns red. If a provider is ever configured to upload reference imagery, the privacy banner downgrades itself to REDUCED BY CONFIGURATION and states how many images left the device.

This fell out of the architecture rather than being bolted onto it. Scoring on the graph instead of on frames is what makes the privacy claim cheap to keep.

Challenges we ran into:

Making "live" and "statistically honest" compatible. These pull in opposite directions. Live means sub-second response; honest means enough samples for the confidence interval to mean something. Re-weighting rather than re-sampling was the resolution, but it introduced its own failure mode — weight collapse - which then needed the ESS gate. Every performance shortcut bought a new way to be wrong, and each one had to be closed explicitly.

Deciding when not to show a number. This was harder than any of the maths. The instinct when a verdict is unreliable is to show it with a caveat. But a caveated number is still a number, and people act on numbers. Replacing the headline verdict with a hatched panel felt like removing a feature. It is the feature.

Keeping the surrogate honest about being a surrogate. The scoring function is hand-written. There was constant pressure to present it as more than that. We settled on making every coefficient a named constant, writing the limitations into the README before anyone asked, and stamping mock renders with the words MOCK RENDER inside the image itself so a screenshot cannot misrepresent them.

projects.title: VIbeParty
projects.tagline: Video Imagination be Pary
projects.description:
Inspiration

We adapted familiar party games into shared AI video experiences:

Our game

Inspired by

Word by Word

Consequences

Prompt Royale

Quiplash by Jackbox Games

Reverse Prompt

Telephone

What it does

VibeParty brings friends together through three browser games, hosted on a laptop with players joining from their phones:

Word by Word:
Secret contributions build one evolving video scene.

Prompt Royale:
Players write prompts for a shared topic, watch anonymous clips, and vote for their favorite.

Reverse Prompt:
Players pass an idea through videos and descriptions, then guess the original prompt.

How we built it

React, TypeScript, and Vite power the frontend, with Python and FastAPI on the backend. The demo uses one local server, in-memory rooms, HTTP polling, and FFmpeg to prepare saved video clips.

Model

Role

Reactor FastH3

Video generation for Word by Word and Reverse Prompt

Reactor Helios

Video generation for Prompt Royale

all-MiniLM-L6-v2

Local similarity scoring for Reverse Prompt through Sentence Transformers

Challenges we ran into

Building the portal and all three games in parallel made integration and thorough testing challenging. We coordinated coding agent sessions in real time to work in parallel and used computer use to play through the games as a human tester would.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Reimagined traditional party games using generative AI to turn players' ideas into shared video experiences.

Integrated a shared portal and all three games into a runnable local demo.

Added labelled fixture rounds, replay, and navigation between games.

What we learned

We learned how to work with video generation models and build more efficiently by coordinating coding agents in parallel.

What's next for VIbeParty

Deploy VibeParty online.

Run more evaluations of video generation quality, speed, reliability, and cost.

Explore increasing support from four to eight players.

Add more games to VibeParty.

projects.title: WorldGym
projects.tagline: A test rig for real-time world models: it drives Reactor's models like a player and scores whether the world is still there when you come back. It isn't.
projects.description:
WorldGym tests whether a real-time world model's world is still there when you come back. It drives Reactor's three navigable world models (LingBot World 2, LingBot v1, HappyOyster) with scripted moves and scores the frames from 0 to 1.

Results:
https://worldgym-900.pages.dev
. The front page opens with the per-model table, and the frames behind each score are below it.

Demo video (2 min):
https://worldgym-900.pages.dev/dashboard/exhibits/worldgym-demo.mp4

Drive a model live:
https://worldgym-900.pages.dev/webxr/
. Passcode: worldgym-2073. Click Connect & start, then use W A S D to move and the arrow keys to look. Motion lags 2–3 seconds. If it says "no available capacity", Reactor is busy: wait 10 seconds and click again.

How to read the scores: "Standing still" (0.80–0.95) is the baseline. "Walk forward and back" and "Turn away and back" measure whether you return to the same view, and every model scores 0.1–0.3.

Caveats: LingBot World 2 and v1 had 2–3 runs each. HappyOyster had one run per test and streams at 11–20 fps against about 45 for LingBot, so its holds last longer in real time.

Code (public):
https://github.com/hashkanna/worldgym
. One command runs the suite on any Reactor model: scripts/run_probes.py.

Inspiration

World models went real-time: you can walk around a world generated from a single photo. People judge them by eye, for a few seconds. If you want to use one as a simulator — for robots, driving or reinforcement learning — the question that matters is different: when you act in the world and come back, is it the same world?

What it does

WorldGym wraps any Reactor world model as a Gym-style environment —
reset(photo, prompt, seed)
,
step(action)
— and runs probes that have a known right answer:

Controls respond:
does each of six actions move the scene the right way, and how late?

Standing still:
how much does the world drift when you do nothing?

Walk forward and back / Turn away and back:
does the view return to where you started?

Prompt swap:
does a new prompt restyle the scene while keeping its layout?

Every score runs from 0 to 1 and ships with the frames behind it: a findings page, a scorecard across runs and models, and a live viewer where you drive the model yourself.

0.67 (4 of 6; the wall blocks forward)

0.95

0.22

0.30

no prompt control

2

LingBot's controls are right every time but land 2–3 seconds late; HappyOyster's work wherever nothing blocks them.

HappyOyster, which promises permanent worlds, holds best and stops at the wall where LingBot walks through the screen — but turning away and back still lands somewhere new. It streams 11–20 fps to our harness (LingBot about 45), so its holds last longer in real time; one run per test.

Standing still holds. Walk away and back, or turn away and back, and you land in a re-imagined room: walking into the wall TV takes you through the screen into another office, and walking back never brings the slide back.

A new prompt does nothing while you stand still; once you move, the prompt beats the photo.

How we built it

A Python harness on the Reactor Python SDK:
WorldEnv
(async reset / step / pose), per-model action mappings, the probes, and classical computer-vision metrics — SSIM, RANSAC-verified ORB feature matches, Farneback optical flow.

19 offline tests against a procedural fake world with drift and hallucination knobs, so each probe is shown to catch a broken world before it touches a live model.

A findings page, scorecard and browser viewer (three.js + Reactor JS SDK) on Cloudflare Pages, with a Pages Function that mints short-lived session tokens behind a passcode.

Headless Chrome (Playwright) to record drives and capture frames and stream stats.

Challenges we ran into

Command lag.
Actions show up 2–3 seconds late, so our first walk test stopped measuring before the return finished. Every hold and settle is now 192 frames (about 4 seconds).

set_camera_pose
is a bias, not a rig.
Our "360° turn" turned a fraction of a circle, so we replaced it with turning away and back using the same command, which needs no calibration.

A test that passed because nothing happened.
The first prompt swap scored well because the picture never changed. The probe now measures idle drift first and flags the swap when it changes the picture no more than drift does.

Capacity.
At a busy hackathon, sessions often come back "no available capacity"; the harness and the viewer retry.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Every number is backed by frames you can look at, and each probe flags when its premise didn't happen instead of scoring it.

One command runs the same suite on a different Reactor world model.

What we learned

Today's real-time world models are controllable but not persistent: the world you return to is re-imagined.

Standing still is the baseline to read every other score against.

What's next

More seeds and photos for error bars, and new Reactor world models as they ship.

Closure scores as an RL reward and as a regression test for model releases.

DINOv2 similarity (already wired in
modal_app.py
) as a lenient companion to SSIM and ORB.

projects.title: Ember Command
projects.tagline: Turn fire into simulation, turn pressure into readiness.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Firefighter training has a gap in the middle. You can read a textbook on size-up, and you can do a live burn in a training tower, but the live burn costs thousands of dollars, needs a crew and a safety officer, and most departments get a handful per year. The thing you actually need to rehearse - standing in front of a building that is getting worse every second and picking one action out of five - is the part you get the fewest repetitions of.

Every digital tool we looked at solves this with a branching tree. Someone writes twelve scenarios, films or renders them, and the trainee walks through paths that were decided months ago. Trainees learn the tree, not the fire.

Real-time world models change what's possible here. If the building can be generated as you watch it, the scenario doesn't have to be written in advance, and it doesn't have to stop while you think.

What it does

Ember Command drops you in front of a burning structure and gives you five options and thirty seconds.

A Simulation Manager (Claude) writes the opening scene as a prompt. Gemini Nano Banana Pro renders it as a still, and that still anchors a live world model session on Reactor, so the first frame you see is the scene the story actually called for rather than whatever the video model felt like producing. From there the video never stops. Pick "force the front door" and the stream morphs into the door giving way and the smoke changing colour. Pick nothing and the timer runs out, and that's an input too: the Simulation Manager pushes the fire forward without you.

You set the length up front, in minutes, and the Simulation Manager paces the scenario to fit - a five-minute run is one deteriorating room, a twenty-minute run has a rescue, a water supply problem, and a decision about whether to keep crews inside.

Quick-decision mode is a toggle. On, you're graded on speed as well as judgement. Off, you can take as long as you want and only the calls themselves count. We split these deliberately. A probationary firefighter learning the decision space and a veteran drilling reaction time need different clocks.

The whole run is timestamped: every option that was on the table, which one you took, and how long you sat there. At the end that transcript goes back to the Simulation Manager for a debrief that can say things like "you ventilated before confirming the seat of the fire, three times, all in the first four minutes."

How we built it

The system is three models with a state machine in the middle.

Claude runs as the Simulation Manager. It holds the scenario state as structured text - fire location and stage, victim status, crew position, water supply, elapsed time - and it owns the story. Each turn it emits two things: five options for the trainee, and a short prompt describing what the world should look like now.

Gemini Nano Banana Pro generates the establishing image once, at session start.

Reactor hosts the world model. We use Visko Orbis Stable, which takes the Nano Banana still as an image-anchored opening and then accepts a new prompt per chunk that morphs the scene without cutting. Its bounded memory is the reason a fifteen-minute session stays the same building; earlier tests with clip-based generation gave us a new front door every time the prompt changed. The Reactor SDK handles the WebRTC session, and the frontend just plays the stream and renders the option buttons over it.

The history log is the part we care most about. Every turn appends a record with the timestamp, the world state at that moment, the five options offered, the option chosen, and the decision latency in milliseconds. The evaluation prompt at the end reads that log, not the video.

Challenges we ran into

The video will happily show a fire that behaves nothing like a fire. Orbis steers generation toward plausible motion, but no video model reasons about Ember Command conditions or flow paths. Early on our evaluation was implicitly grading the trainee against what the stream rendered, which meant a good decision could get marked down because the model decided the smoke should clear. We rebuilt it so the Simulation Manager's text state is authoritative and the video is a visual layer over it. If they disagree, the state wins and the next prompt corrects the picture.

Prompt drift was the other big one. Firefighting vocabulary and video-model vocabulary don't overlap. "Vertical ventilation" produces nothing useful. We ended up with a translation layer: the Simulation Manager emits an operational event, and a small prompt template turns it into visual language the model can render - smoke colour, where flame is showing, what the crew is doing on screen.

Timing the morph against the clock took longer than expected. Prompt changes land on the next chunk, so there's a beat between the trainee committing and the world reacting. Too short and the choice feels ignored; too long and the thirty seconds feel unfair. We pin the option buttons to the chunk boundary now so the beat is consistent instead of random.

Cost discipline, too. Reactor bills by the second for as long as the session is held. An open tab burns money. We added an idle cutoff after the first time we left a session running through lunch.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The no-decision path. Timing out isn't a skipped turn, it generates a worse situation, and you watch it get worse. As far as we know nothing else in training software does this, and it only works because the underlying model is a live stream rather than a clip generator. Indecision having a visible cost is the single most useful thing in the build.

The debrief also turned out better than we expected. Because the log holds the options that weren't taken, Claude can talk about the decision space and not just the outcome - what a trainee passed over, repeatedly, without noticing.

What we learned

World models are a rendering target, not a simulator. We spent the first day treating Orbis like a physics engine and the rest of the hackathon undoing that. The useful mental model: the world model is the screen, your state machine is the game.

Also, image-anchored openings matter more than we assumed. Starting from a Nano Banana still instead of a text prompt gave us control over the scenario that text alone never did, and it made scenario authoring reproducible - same still, same starting conditions, comparable runs across trainees.

And thirty seconds is a long time. We assumed it would feel brutal. Watching people use it, most decisions land around eight seconds, and the ones that run to twenty are the interesting ones.

What's next for Ember Command

Real firefighters, then real feedback. Nothing here has been validated against NFPA guidance or reviewed by an instructor, and until that happens this is a prototype, not a training tool. We want a fire service training officer to tear apart the scoring rubric.

Beyond that: multi-crew sessions where two trainees run interior and exterior on the same scene and see each other's consequences; Helios as an alternate backend for its rewind buffer, so the debrief can replay a decision point and show the branch you didn't take; and scenario packs for specific structure types - high-rise, wildland interface, vehicle fire - with the Simulation Manager constrained to the tactics that apply.

projects.title: Loop House
projects.tagline: A building that resets every 60 seconds, generated live by a world model no assets, no level, no map. Find the key and you get out. The house resets. You don't.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Time loop stories only work because of one thing: the world resets and the person doesn't. Groundhog Day, Outer Wilds, Edge of Tomorrow — the entire feeling comes from being the only one who remembers.

That's also, almost exactly, the thing a world model can do and a video model can't. A video model decides everything up front and hands you a clip. A world model generates a place that keeps running and keeps coming back. So the story structure and the technology turned out to be the same shape, and I wanted to build the thing that sat at the intersection.

What it does

You wake up in a building. It resets every 60 seconds. Somewhere in it there is a key — find it and you get out.

The building isn't built. There's no level, no 3D model, no assets, no map. It's generated live by a world model as you move through it, and it regenerates from the same anchor frame each loop, so it comes back as recognisably the same place. Nothing in the world knows you've been there before.

You're the only thing carrying memory across the reset. The house resets. You don't.

How we built it

The core architectural decision was to split ownership:

The world model owns the world. Reactor generates the building, the rooms and the atmosphere, and responds to movement input in real time. [CHECK: name the model you ended up using]
My code owns what's true. A small state machine outside the model tracks position, loop number, seconds remaining and whether the key has been found.

That split is the reason it runs at all. World models generate scenes; they don't reliably track discrete objects, so asking the model to remember where the key is would have been a coin flip in front of a judge. Keeping game state in application code and letting the model do what it's actually good at made the whole thing demoable.

Persistence across the reset is handled with a fixed anchor frame — each loop seeds from the same image, which is what makes the building recognisable cycle after cycle rather than a new building every time.

Built on Next.js and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. The Reactor key stays server-side; a route handler mints a short-lived session token and the browser connects with that.

Challenges we ran into

Persistence was the load-bearing unknown. The entire concept rests on the building coming back as the same building. That isn't something a world model gives you for free, and if it hadn't worked the idea would have had to change shape completely. The anchor frame approach is what made it hold.

World models aren't game engines, and the first instinct — let the model handle the house and the objects in it — is the wrong one. Rebuilding around the state-machine split cost time but was the difference between a demo and a gamble.

Latency and streaming. World models bill and stream per session-second while a GPU is held, so performance tuning is a live constraint, not a polish task. [CHECK: mention what you actually did — resolution drop, session cleanup, model choice]

Building solo against a hard 17:30 cutoff meant cutting continuously. Several ideas that would have made it richer — [CHECK: loop-to-loop decay? talking avatars? sound?] — were scoped out in favour of making one complete loop work reliably.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Shipping a playable, deployed build solo in a single day, in a category where most teams had three or four people.

More than that: getting to a concept where the model is genuinely load-bearing. The test I kept applying was "could this have been pre-rendered?" — and a time loop can't be, because the whole point is a place that persists through a reset while you keep the memory. The story isn't decorated with a world model. It doesn't exist without one.

What we learned

The big one: don't ask the model to hold state. Let it generate the world, and keep the truth in your own code. That's not a workaround, it's the right architecture for this class of model, and I'd start there on anything I build next.

Also that the constraint is a design tool. Once I accepted that the model wouldn't remember anything between loops, that limitation became the premise — the house forgets, you don't. The most interesting part of the story came directly from the thing the technology couldn't do.

What's next for Loop House

Loops that diverge. Right now the reset returns you to the same conditions. The version I want has the building shift each cycle — decaying, changing light, doors that were locked standing open — so the dread compounds and the loop count becomes something you feel rather than read.

A voice in the house. A previous occupant, rendered with VEED Fabric, who appears each loop and says something different — helpful at first, tired of explaining by loop four, and by loop seven telling you she's been here longer than you have. The loop counter becomes a character arc.

More building. More rooms, more reasons to go into them, and a key that's genuinely hard to find rather than findable by exhaustion.

Mobile. The premise works even better on a phone — being trapped somewhere you hold in your hand.

projects.title: Emergent Wave Phenomenon from JEPA World Models
projects.tagline: We train a JEPA model on examples of wave dynamics in a reaction diffusion model. We show that even without training on spiral wave dynamics, the model learns to predict this behaviour.
projects.description:
Inspiration

We wanted to see whether we could get a JEPA world model to learn underlying physical laws, such that it could generalise to show a physical phenomenon not in its training data.

What it does

We trained a JEPA model to predict a latent next frame which is then decoded into pixel data, from numerical simulations of Barkley's reaction-diffusion model.

How we built it

Trained a JEPA model on wave dynamics - excluding the spiral dynamics we hope it will learn autonomously. The JEPA model is trained to predict latents, encouraging the model to learn the underlying dynamics of the system rather than the surface behaviour.

Challenges we ran into

Time was incredibly tight, especially as we were training the full JEPA model from scratch

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're proud that the model seemed to be able to generalise.

What we learned

We learned how to work quickly under time pressure. Additionally, neither of us had any previous experience with JEPA models, and it was interesting to get some hands-on experience with them.

What's next for Emergent Wave Phenomenon from JEPA World Models

Investigating whether we can train larger models on more data / longer rollouts.

projects.title: Atlas
projects.tagline: Newspapers have for centuries recorded the biggest events in human history. Right now, they are discarded, not read. This software uses reactor to bring up life, to teach historical events.
projects.description:
Introduction

Newspapers are unusual in how they have throughout modern history recorded daily events and stories that otherwise would have faded into oblivion never to be known by anyone. Well, despite that, newspaper readership has declined considerably over the years and the stories despite being recorded never get read. Atlas bridges this gap by transforming it into an interactive medium with Reactor that increases the instructional value of these records and turns them into extremely valuable and captivating learning materials.

Inspiration

A historical event is three things: a place, a time, and a set of things that were true at that place and time. Every format we use to teach one throws away the first. A paragraph describes a place. A photograph gives you one frame of a place. A documentary walks you along a camera operator's path through a place. None of them let you look left.

For most of the history of media that was a hardware fact rather than a choice. Building a walkable 1969 lunar surface, or the Bornholmer Strasse crossing on the night of 9 November 1989, meant an art team, several months, and a budget only a film studio could carry. So the past stayed flat, and we all agreed to call reading about a place the same thing as knowing it.

Meanwhile the formats that carry history have been quietly losing the room.

Signal

Number

Source

People who still reach news in print, down from around half in 2013

10%

Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2025

People who say they sometimes or often avoid the news, a record high

40%

Reuters Institute, DNR 2025

18 to 24 year olds who avoid the news, up from 30% in 2017

42%

Reuters Institute, DNR 2025

People who trust most news most of the time, flat for three years

40%

Reuters Institute, DNR 2025

US adults getting news from social and video, now ahead of TV at 50%

54%

Reuters Institute, DNR 2025

Share of all web traffic that is automated rather than human

51%

Imperva, 2025 Bad Bot Report

US eighth graders scoring below NAEP Basic in US history

40%

NAEP, 2022

Read together, those numbers say something blunter than any one of them says alone. Nine in ten people have stopped touching print. Four in ten steer around the news on purpose, and among 18 to 24 year olds it is more than four in ten, up twelve points in eight years. Trust has not moved in three years. Attention has migrated to short video and social feeds, where more than half of the traffic is now machines talking to machines. And in the classroom, 40% of American eighth graders cannot reliably pull a simple idea out of a primary source.

Every fix the industry has tried swaps one passive format for another. Longer video. Shorter video. Vertical video. Newsletters. None of it worked, because the problem was never the resolution of the picture. It was that nothing ever asked the reader to do anything.

The one intervention with a consistent, replicated effect size is participation. Freeman and colleagues pooled
225 studies in PNAS
and found that students in traditional lectures were
1.5 times more likely to fail
than students in active learning sections, with examination performance up
0.47 standard deviations
. Making somebody do something is the only lever in education research that keeps working across two hundred replications.

Two things changed at once this year. Real time world models made the cost of a place collapse from studio months to cents per second. And the archives finished digitising: the
British Newspaper Archive
has passed 100 million pages, the Library of Congress's
Chronicling America
holds more than 23 million, and essentially nobody outside a research library opens either.

So the raw material is sitting there, fully sourced and fully licensed, and the technology to stand inside it finally exists. That is the whole reason Atlas exists. Not a better article about the Berlin Wall. Ninety seconds standing at the checkpoint on the night the gate opened, with the source for every detail one keypress away.

What it does

Atlas is a newspaper you can walk into.

Each article in the archive carries an archival photograph and a structured scene brief written against sources. Atlas compiles that brief into a layered prompt, refuses to serve it if any part of the prompt cannot be traced back to a citation, mints a short lived scoped token, and hands the browser a plan it can drive. The reader clicks the play control on the photograph and walks around inside it in first person.

Ten events ship in the archive today: Apollo 11, the night the Berlin Wall opened, the eve of D-Day at Greenham Common, the March on Washington, the midnight of Partition, the Armistice at Compiegne, the San Francisco relief camps of 1906, the Triangle fire mourning march, the Bandung Conference, and the Windrush arrival at Tilbury.

Control

Does

W

S

walk forward and back

A

D

strafe, or turn on a model with no lateral axis

mouse, or drag

look, with pointer lock where the browser grants it

two finger trackpad

look, without holding a button

arrow keys

look, without a mouse at all

space
/
C

jump / crouch

1
to
9

hold a sourced event from the article

Esc

leave the world

The reading surface has no navigation at all. There is a wordmark, a list of events in the left margin, and a paper in the middle of the screen that only ever moves up and down. Whatever the list lands on is already open, so there is no confirm step and no panel to dismiss. Where a real scan of the original front page exists, it sits inside the same vertical scroll as the story, full width, credited to the library that holds it. On a phone the margin list becomes one horizontal row above the same single column of paper, and inside a world thumb pads replace the keyboard, chosen by
(pointer: coarse)
rather than by screen width, because a narrow browser window on a laptop is not a phone.

The part we care about most is what the world is
not
allowed to do:

Every world is anchored on a
real archival photograph
, cropped to the model's native 1664x960 frame, with its licence and credit preserved and shown in the interface.

Prompts are
compiled from structured briefs
, never hand written, with landmarks pinned by explicit count and camera behaviour bound to reader input.

A
fidelity linter
blocks absence phrasing, camera direction that has escaped the camera layer, over budget prompts, and any hold key event that cannot cite a source. The test suite fails if the shipped archive produces so much as a warning.

Sensitive events carry a
content note
naming what the world deliberately does not stage. The Triangle fire world is the mourning march ten days later. The D-Day world is the airfield the evening before.

Seeds are fixed
, so the same article renders the same world every time, which means a teacher or a judge can check us.

The reader is told in the article itself that the world is a
reconstruction and not footage
.

How we built it

Atlas is a pnpm workspace of seven packages and two apps, written in TypeScript 6, with zod contracts at every boundary so a malformed article fails at the edge instead of halfway down the pipe.

content/articles/*.json     sourced article, archival photo, scene brief
  -> @atlas/schema          parse and validate against the contract
  -> @atlas/scene           compile the layered prompt, lint it for fidelity
  -> @atlas/archive         index the archive, withhold anything unservable
  -> @atlas/world           pick the model, mint a scoped JWT, build the plan
  -> browser
  -> @atlas/runtime         connect, stage, map input to model commands
  -> Reactor                LingBot World 2, WebRTC video at 1664x960

Package

Responsibility

@atlas/schema

zod contracts for articles, scene briefs, sessions and control state

@atlas/scene

compiles a brief into layered prompts, composes them, lints them for fidelity

@atlas/archive

loads and validates the local JSON archive, withholds unservable articles

@atlas/world

Reacto

projects.title: Cities in the Past World Model
projects.tagline: We find real photos of that city from that era, seed a Reactor world model with the best one, and stream a navigable world you explore with WASD
projects.description:
Inspiration

Historical photographs show us what a city looked like, but leave us wondering what was just outside the frame. What would it feel like to turn the corner, walk down the street, or explore the neighborhood?

We built Cities in the Past World Model around that curiosity: turning archival photographs from something you look at into a starting point for somewhere you can explore.

What it does

Choose a city and a decade, and the app searches for historical photographs to anchor an interactive, AI-generated world. You can explore the resulting
 scene using WASD and mouse-look controls.

The experience brings together:

• Archival photo discovery, ranking, and image preparation.
   • Decade-specific prompts that guide the generated environment.
   • Photo credits and licensing information.
   • Re-seeding controls to restart exploration from another selected photograph.

When suitable photographs are unavailable, the app reports that limitation rather than forcing a result.

This is an AI-generated interpretation grounded in historical imagery, not an exact reconstruction of the streets or events of the past.

How we built it

We built a full-stack Next.js and TypeScript application, keeping the interface and backend orchestration in one codebase.

The pipeline geocodes the selected city, searches Wikimedia Commons, Europeana, and Flickr Commons, and ranks candidate photographs for relevance and
 suitability. Google Custom Search provides a fallback when archive coverage is limited.

Selected images are prepared with sharp, normalized to a landscape format, and stored in Vercel Blob. Upstash Redis provides caching and rate limiting.

A decade-specific prompt and the prepared photograph then seed a Reactor world-model session. We implemented a shared adapter interface for LingBot World 2
 and Happy Oyster Adventure, allowing model-specific behavior without tying the interface to one engine.

We also designed an optional Modal / Real-ESRGAN restoration path, with a CPU-only fallback. Browser access uses short-lived, model-scoped tokens; API keys
 stay on the server.

Challenges we ran into

Finding the right photograph was harder than finding any photograph. A search result might match the city and decade but show a document, a close-up, or a
 viewpoint unsuitable for exploration. Image quality, composition, provenance, and licensing all mattered.

Interactive generation required careful session management. Movement controls, streamed video, reconnects, re-seeding, and cleanup had to work together—
 especially because live sessions are metered.

Different models behaved differently. Image requirements, control vocabularies, and startup behavior needed model-specific handling. Mock tests helped us
 develop safely, but live testing remained essential.

We also had to account for generated-world drift: starting from a real photograph does not guarantee that everything generated beyond it remains
 historically or spatially accurate.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

• Achieving a live LingBot smoke test with advancing video and working WASD input.
   • Connecting archival sourcing, image preparation, prompt composition, and interactive exploration in one application.
   • Establishing a visually reviewed Amsterdam, 1960s reference set.
   • Building unit and browser regression coverage for controls, navigation, credits, cancellation, and session behavior.
   • Keeping source attribution, honest limitations, and model flexibility central to the design.

What we learned

A convincing historical experience starts before generation. Choosing a useful camera perspective, checking dates and licenses, and preparing the image
 carefully are core product decisions—not just preprocessing.

We also learned to distinguish software correctness from model quality. A passing integration test cannot tell us whether a generated street feels coherent
 or historically plausible. Automated testing and visual review serve different purposes, and both are necessary.

What's next for Cities in the Past World Model

Our immediate priorities are completing Happy Oyster live-video validation, finishing model calibration, and expanding the reviewed city-and-decade
 collection.

Next, we want to improve spatial consistency through historical maps and GIS alignment, and investigate persistent, revisitable environments using 3D
 reconstruction techniques such as Gaussian splatting.

We also envision location-aware historical narration that adds context to exploration while clearly distinguishing documented facts from generated content.

The goal is to make urban history more accessible and engaging—without losing sight of the evidence that makes it meaningful.

projects.title: Afterimage
projects.tagline: AFTERIMAGE is a time-loop boss game powered by Happy Oyster. Explore a live AI world, test actions, retain evidence across resets, and uncover hidden rules to win.
projects.description:
Inspiration

World models can generate interactive environments, but they may forget details over time. We turned that limitation into a time-loop game mechanic.

What it does

Afterimage is a boss game where players experiment, fail, reset, and retain evidence. Winning requires discovering the boss’s hidden causal rules.

How we built it

Happy Oyster on Reactor generates the playable world. A TypeScript state machine manages deterministic rules, while an evidence board preserves discoveries across loops.

Challenges we ran into

Generated visuals are not always consistent or deterministic. We separated visual generation from game logic and added fixed IDs and fallback states.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We made world-model uncertainty part of the gameplay and created an experience that remains understandable and playable across generated timelines.

What we learned

World models work best when combined with structured state, clear controls, and mechanics that embrace uncertainty rather than hiding it.

What's next for Afterimage

We plan to add automatic object tracking, more bosses, multiplayer investigation, and adaptive rules that respond to player behaviour.

projects.title: Ajar
projects.tagline: Build your brand a world
projects.description:
Inspirati# Ajar — Make your brand a world.

Inspiration

Brands spend six figures on pop-ups that reach a few thousand people, in one city, for three weeks — and can't measure any of it. Meanwhile every poster, shelf and product page they already pay for is a dead end. We asked: what if the poster wasn't the end of the ad, but the door? Real-time world models finally make that possible from photography the brand already owns.

What it does

Ajar turns any placement into a
Door
. Scan a QR on a Coach poster and you step into Coach's London: pick your neighbourhood, your chapter, your bag, your name — then walk a live-generated street to the Coach store, see yourself wearing the look in a live mirror, and leave with a 9-second personalised film. Everything behind the door is observed — who came in, where they went, what they reached for. That's
Footfall
: the first honest attribution layer for brand advertising.

How we built it

Reactor
lingbot-world-2
— image-anchored navigable world; the street you walk through, steered live by your chosen chapter.

Reactor
x2
— reference-guided live video; the in-store try-on mirror.

Reactor
ltx2
— selfie + script → lip-synced film with audio in one pass.

Modal
— FastAPI backend, session state in
modal.Dict
, background generation jobs.

Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind
on Vercel — phone flow at
/play
, projector dashboard at
/dash
.

Anchor stills and look boards pre-generated so the live path has something to fall back on.

Built in five hours by three people plus coding agents.

Challenges we ran into

Presence is fragile.
Stutter kills the illusion faster than low resolution — we tiered the experience: pre-rendered path for browsing, live generation reserved for those who engage.

Brand safety vs. generation.
Legal will never approve unbounded output. We anchored on approved photography, ran the camera on a fixed path, and built a fallback to reviewed footage on drift.

Permissions choreography.
Camera, gyro and audio each need a gesture at exactly the right moment on mobile, or the flow dies before the world loads.

Cost per session
is the whole business — every design decision had to survive that number.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

A working end-to-end door: physical poster → QR → personalised, walkable world → try-on → film, on a phone, in under 90 seconds.

Three Reactor models composed into one continuous experience, not three demos.

A business case that argues on one ratio — cost per minute of voluntary attention — and concedes honestly where video still wins.

What we learned

Insertion beats destination. Nobody visits a virtual store; everybody is already standing in front of a poster.

World models are ready for bounded, brand-owned imagery — the constraint is the feature, not the limitation.

The pilot is the product: one brand, one world, three success criteria, a control, and a renewal clause.

What's next for Ajar

Footfall dashboard
as a real product: session-level behaviour, variant performance, reservation chain.

Ajar Studio
: one anchor image → every localised and seasonal variant, no re-shoot.

Lock down true cost per engaged session with Reactor, then run a six-week pilot with one brand on placements already live.

Steer every deal from campaign to always-on — a world that stays open.

projects.title: HazardDetection
projects.tagline: A simulator which exposes hazards before consequences happen.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Numerous injuries happen to toddlers and elderly people each year (5M+ accidents, some).
I wanted to build a tool which would allow identifying the hazards to mitigate them, eg sharp corners etc.

This should help for places where vulnerable people come.

What it does

The user uploads photos, then a world model (we use Marble) turns them into a 3D space with a collision mesh.
Then in simulation "todlers" and "grannys" walk in the environment identifying the hazards.
The user is notified with what is dangerous..

How we built it

Using Devin, LLMs, and world models. The site is hosted on cloudflare (via chatgpt sites plugin)

Challenges we ran into

Mesh takes a long time to generate, so we used sample meshes initially.
Simulation works, but more precision is needed.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We identified real world application of world models where they can make a difference beyond games.
We built the whole system end to end.

What we learned

World models are extremely powerful, well beyond image or video generation.

What's next for HazardDetection

I am planning to publicly release.

projects.title: 360° world model clips for sports
projects.tagline: World Model powered video generation using sports clips. The future of sports highlights!
projects.description:
Inspiration: I was an F1 junior driver growing up, I love everything sports and I’m also obsessed with world models. When I saw what world labs (atlas) posted a couple weeks ago I had an idea for using it in sports and this is the closest thing I can get to that.

How it works: It ingests video data from YouTube, using transcript and crowd noise to auto source highlights for football, if anything else it allows for manual selection of highlights. It then allows for a freeze frame to be selected and runs it through H3 max to give the viewer a cool 360° view video playback before continuing the video onwards. Sound slowed down also to immerse the viewer.

How we built it: I was token maxxing on codex! Really though I created an HTML space to ingest video easily and used wispr flow to identify noise markers for highlights. Then set up an API call to H3 with a clever prompt to get the 360 perspective I wanted. I also firecrawled reactor (sorry) to get the design I wanted - UI is important!

Challenges we ran into: H3 is not thatttt good of a model in 4K, so it looks really cool but not to the level I’d like it to be.

Accomplishments that we're proud of: I’m proud to have something running in real time. It works, we can run it end to end in 1 minute. With more inference and better internet maybe I could get it down to 30 secs.

What we learned: that H3 max is not ready for production level viewing and inference just yet. Perhaps when world labs’ atlas is released that will be the answer here.

What's next for 360° world model clips for sports:

I had my YC interview just 2 weeks ago. They thought it was too ambitious for right now, waiting for inference to get to a place where this can run quickly enough that broadcast or socials viewers can really enjoy these clips right after they occur (near real time). I think World Labs Atlas will likely change that.
