projects.title: Hercules12labours
projects.tagline: I have always been intrested in classics and latin and ave taken them fo rgcse I always been interested in 12 hercules labours so i created game where you can experience it
projects.description:
Inspiration

I’ve always enjoyed Classics and Latin, which is why I chose them for GCSE. The stories, characters and places of the ancient world really interest me, and I wanted to combine that with my enjoyment of programming.

Hercules’s twelve labours felt perfect for a game because each one presents a different challenge, from facing the Nemean Lion to aiming at the Stymphalian Birds. I wanted players to experience these stories themselves, exploring landscapes inspired by their real settings. My aim was to share what I enjoy about Classics in a way that feels exciting and interactive.

What it does

Hercules12labours is a browser game where players take on all twelve labours in any order. Different challenges involve dodging monsters, jumping, aiming arrows, capturing creatures and solving environmental tasks. Completed labours are saved on the player’s device.

There is also a separate Stymphalian Birds archery game with a photographic lake setting. Players aim freely at moving bronze birds, with arrow drop, wind and draw strength affecting their shots. They can record their own gameplay.

An optional Reactor mode adds live AI rendering to the game.

How we built it

I used AI-assisted coding with React and TypeScript for the interface, Three.js for the original 3D adventure, and Canvas for the lighter photographic archery game.

I integrated Reactor X2 to transform live game frames while keeping movement, collisions and game rules in the local engine. The Reactor API key stays on the backend.

The landscapes combine research into the myths’ locations with generated imagery. They are historically informed interpretations, rather than exact archaeological reconstructions.

Challenges we ran into

The biggest challenge was balancing visual quality with responsive gameplay. Live AI video can introduce delay and change visual details between frames, which makes precise actions difficult.

I developed the lighter archery mode using a fixed photographic landscape and local physics, so aiming and shooting do not have to wait for AI-generated frames. Supporting Mac trackpad controls was another important part of making the game usable.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

I’m proud of bringing all twelve labours into one playable project, adding freedom to choose their order, and building an archery game with moving targets and projectile physics.

Integrating Reactor and adding gameplay recording also helped turn the idea into something that could be demonstrated.

What we learned

A beautiful generated image and a good real-time game are different challenges. Responsive controls, consistent scenery and clear objectives matter just as much as detailed graphics.

What's next for Hercules12labours

Next, I want to bring the photographic approach to more labours, improve creature animation and make the Reactor experience more consistent. I also want to strengthen the historical research behind each location and help players discover the myths through playing.

projects.title: Reinforcement Learning x World Model: Brain Surgery
projects.tagline: We use video LLMs as an agent to roam through World Models and receive real-time reward signals that guides LLM's next action to reach our goal.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Deep brain stimulation works — but only if the electrode lands in the right few millimetres of the subthalamic nucleus, and only if it never nicks a vessel on the way in. Surgeons build that intuition over hundreds of cases. Robots have no way to practise at all.

We wanted a world where a robot
could
practise: a brain you can fly a probe through, where stimulating the wrong nucleus visibly makes the patient worse, and where "did the tremor stop?" is a number, not an opinion. A world model in the real sense — an internal, functional model of cause and effect that an agent can act and plan inside — with a video model as the window into it.

What it does

A closed agentic loop for DBS electrode placement:

A 3D labelled brain.
A 64³ voxel volume with grey and white matter, STN, VIM, GPi, internal capsule, vessels, cerebellum and brainstem, jittered per episode seed. One hidden target coordinate.

A randomised surgery.
Each episode drops the probe at a random entry pose above the cortex; the agent has 120 steps of WASD + look +
stim
.

A real reward.
Distance shaping toward the target, +6 for therapeutic stimulation weighted by how close and which nucleus, −4 for capsular side effects (muscle contraction), −10 and instant death for a vessel haemorrhage, +20 for suppressing the tremor. Tremor starts at 1.00 and only falls when stimulation actually reaches the right tissue.

GLM-5.3-Flash as the surgeon.
Served on Modal, it reads the probe-eye render plus numeric telemetry each turn and returns JSON actions with its reasoning. Every prompt it was sent and every raw reply is visible in the UI.

LingBot-World 2 as the visuals.
The agent's exact keypresses are mirrored into a live LingBot-World 2 session (via Reactor), which repaints the run as a translucent colour-coded 3D brain scan, seeded from our own renderer.

A director agent.
A second GLM instance turns hidden simulator state into visible scene events — a vessel glinting on the left, tissue changing texture — injected into the world model's prompt, so the pixels tell the truth without leaking coordinates.

Free-roam mode.
The pilot sees
only
the generated world-model frames — no maps, no coordinates — while a hidden tracker scores it against the real anatomy. A pure world-model game with a real score.

How we built it

Three layers, deliberately separated:

Physics
— a deterministic NumPy voxel environment (
DBSEnv
) with a gym-style
step(action) → (pixels, state, reward, done)
. It owns anatomy, collisions, tremor dynamics, reward and termination. Always authoritative.

Rendering
— our own raymarcher: a probe-eye view, an orbiting whole-brain hologram with synthetic tractography fibres, and axial/coronal/sagittal slice maps with the probe and target marked.

Agents and generative view
— FastAPI + a single-screen telemetry UI; GLM-5.3-Flash on Modal for pilot and director; LingBot-World 2 over a live streaming session for the cinematic view, driven by seed image, prompt events and key events.

Challenges we ran into

Reasoning ate the answers.
GLM returned empty or truncated JSON until we discovered its reasoning tokens were consuming the entire output budget;
reasoning_effort: none
fixed it instantly.

A world model has no coordinates.
We wanted reward computed inside the generated world — impossible: it returns pixels, not state. The hidden-coordinate tracker was the honest answer, and it's what makes free-roam scoreable.

We tried to self-host LingBot-World 2.
The open 14B weights need 8 GPUs and the released path is offline-only (precomputed camera trajectories, no per-step action API). ~$30/hr and no realtime interface, versus the hosted realtime session — so we used the hosted one.

The director lied to the pilot.
It told the agent "vessel to the right" while the vessel was on the left; the agent strafed left and haemorrhaged. We gave it the vessel's real bearing.

The bottleneck wasn't the model.
The world model streams ~24 fps; our page showed ~1. Every render was also blocking the event loop, so
/status
took 1.4 s. Frames cached per step, encoding moved off-loop, keypresses coalesced, MJPEG stream instead of polling:
/status
now 1.5 ms.

Capacity.
Credits depleted, then 429s — so the UI degrades to the deterministic view and retries rather than dying.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The agent genuinely solves it: repeated end-to-end runs at +32 to +41 total reward, tremor 1.00 → 0.01, ~40 of 120 steps, on freshly randomised anatomy it has never seen.

Both failure modes are real and reachable — vessel haemorrhage terminates at −10, premature stimulation costs −4 for a capsular side effect.

Full transparency: the exact prompt, the model's raw reply, and the per-step reward are all on screen. No black box, no cherry-picking.

Diagnosing a navigation pathology from the logs: the agent burned ~60 steps spinning when the target was directly below it, because yaw error is meaningless at steep elevation. Scaling yaw error by bearing elevation fixed it.

The whole thing runs as a watchable game — the model plays, we don't touch the keyboard.

What we learned

"World model" and "video model" are not the same thing, and the difference is exactly where the reward lives. Generated video is a window; the functional model has to be something you can query for consequences.

Vision-language models are far better with a little numeric grounding than with pixels alone: the moment we added
aim_error_deg
and distance, the feedback loop stopped being vibes.

Reward shaping is where the surgery knowledge actually goes. Every clinical fact — the capsule causes muscle contraction, GPi is a weaker target than STN, a vessel is unrecoverable — is a term in the reward function.

In an agentic loop, honesty in the narration matters more than richness. One wrong spatial claim from the director killed the patient.

What's next for Reinforcement Learning Brain Surgical Simulation

Train a real policy.
GLM is a strong zero-shot pilot but a slow one; the environment runs thousands of headless episodes cheaply, so a small policy trained on this reward should beat it — and then the world model renders the trained agent's runs.

Latent planning.
With a self-hosted realtime world model we could snapshot its KV state and let the agent imagine K candidate trajectories before committing to one — the real promise of world models.

Ground the anatomy in real scans.
Swap the stylised voxel brain for segmented patient MRI/DTI so trajectories mean something clinically.

Sim-to-real.
Map the action space onto a surgical arm's joint space, add instrument compliance and tissue deformation, and validate on a phantom skull before anything else.

A learned tremor model.
Our tremor response is hand-written; fitting it to published DBS outcome data would make the reward clinically meaningful rather than plausible.

projects.title: Dream Island
projects.tagline: A tiny photo safari inside a live world model: wander a candy-coloured garden, wish for a little magic, and collect three postcards from a world that dreams as you explore.
projects.description:
Inspiration

What if exploring a world model felt like a tiny holiday? Dream Island turns curiosity into a playful photo safari.

What it does

Wander a candy-coloured garden, wish for stars, giant flowers or bubbles, and photograph three little wonders: a tiny friend, a dreamy view and a little magic. Label your discoveries, complete your album and download a souvenir. Original music and playful sounds accompany the visit.

How we built it

Built solo with TypeScript, React, Next.js, WebRTC, Canvas and Web Audio. Reactor's LingBot World 2 generates the visible world from an original starting image, movement commands and wish prompts. Server-side session tokens keep the API key off the client. Postcards capture actual received video frames, browser storage keeps the album, and Web Audio creates the music and effects.

Challenges and lessons

Capacity, latency and character drift affect the experience. We added short visits, clear connection states, visible input feedback and a recorded backup. Players label their own photos; there is no automatic image judging. Exact wishes, navigation and character consistency are not guaranteed.

Accomplishments

We completed live safari playthroughs and three-postcard albums. Bubbles visibly appeared after a Bubble party wish, and camera views changed after movement and turning. Generative exploration now has a simple goal and a keepsake.

What's next

More reliable availability, stronger visual continuity, more discovery challenges and persistent hosting.

Demo notes

The cover is the original AI-generated starting image; live scenery can evolve away from it. The live link is a temporary Cloudflare tunnel and requires the demo computer to stay online. Use the recorded playthrough if Reactor has no capacity. The published video is an earlier build; the current game adds clearer control highlights and input cues.

projects.title: PACT
projects.tagline: One flat. One app. PACT explains confusing letters in your language, splits bills fairly and keeps chores on track: the only flat app you'll ever need.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Moving into a shared flat, especially in a new country, comes with a pile of paperwork nobody explains: council tax letters, energy bills, tenancy forms. Around 686,000 international students study in the UK, and many face these documents in a second language. Money is already tight (76% of students worry about making ends meet), and in shared homes, 30% of people argue over bills. The help exists, but it's scattered, confusing and rarely in your language. We wanted to build the app we wish we'd had on move-in day.

What it does

Pact is one hub for your whole flat, with six tabs:
Docs, Bills, Chores, Roomates, Key Contacts, and Settings
.

Docs:
upload any letter or form and Pact summarises it in plain English, translates it into your language and sends key information straight to the bill tracker.

Read aloud:
summaries can be read out loud for accessibility, in your chosen language.

Bills:
split shared costs fairly between flatmates, allows for currency conversions for undertstanding, and allows for sending via WISE.

Chores:
assign tasks and keep everyone on track with reminders.

It fits Wise's "Max Ease" brief by removing friction from everyday shared living: confusing forms become plain answers, no arguing over money owed and newcomers don't need local knowledge.

How we built it

Frontend:
Next.js (React), Tailwind CSS and JavaScript, first scaffolded with Replit's AI Agent.

Backend:
Next.js API routes that send documents to the
Google Gemini 3.8 Flash Interactions API
for summarisation, translation and email drafting.

Accessibility:
the
ElevenLabs
text-to-speech API reads summaries aloud.

Email Knudge: We integrated the Resend API with a custom domain from GoDaddy to securely send the AI-drafted reminder emails directly to flatmates.

AI pair programming:
as non-coders, we used DeepSeek and Claude in VS Code to write our backend API routes, debug environment variables and fix JSON parsing errors. We managed our own API keys securely in environment variables.

Challenges we ran into

We ran out of Replit credits mid-hackathon.
Instead of stopping, we exported our code to GitHub, set up a local development environment in VS Code, and kept building.

Google deprecated the older Gemini models during the weekend
, so our API calls started failing. We pivoted to the brand-new Gemini 3.8 Flash Interactions API.

Debugging API errors (like the Gemini model rejection and ElevenLabs JSON failures) by reading error logs and fixing the logic step by step.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Going from zero coding experience to a working, accessible prototype in one weekend.

Integrating three live AI APIs (Gemini and ElevenLabs and ReSend) end to end.

Adapting to two major setbacks without giving up.

What we learned

How a web app is structured (frontend, backend API routes and external APIs), how environment variables keep API keys secret, how to use Git and GitHub, and how to debug by reading error messages. We also learned how to use AI tools responsibly and transparently as pair programmers.

What's next for Pact

Paying your share directly through Wise

Showing the original document side by side with the summary, so users can always check the AI's answer

Partnering with universities and letting agents to support new tenants

projects.title: lazyQ
projects.tagline: Scan. Join. Roam. Return.
projects.description:
Inspiration

While exploring London, we noticed how many people spent hours waiting outside popular restaurants, stores, and tourist attractions. Instead of enjoying their day, they were stuck standing in long queues. We thought, why should being in a queue mean wasting your time? That's how LazyQ was born: a smarter, simpler way to wait without actually standing in line.

What it does

LazyQ is a frictionless web app that tracks your live position in the queue and shows exactly how many people are ahead of you. Simply scan the on-site QR code and relax wherever you like instead of standing in line, with zero downloads and no sign-up required.

How we built it

We built LazyQ using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the frontend, with Python 3 powering the backend. We implemented rotating QR codes to let customers join queues instantly and used Server-Sent Events (SSE) to update queue positions in real time. We used JSON to store queue data, GitHub for team collaboration, and Render to deploy our application online with our custom domain, lazyq.vodka.

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges we faced was trying to secure the staff dashboard. I wanted to make sure that only authorized staff could manage the queue, but figuring out how to hide the authentication key and keep it secure was more complicated than I expected. I tried adding password protection, but it ended up causing issues with the dashboard and QR code functionality. After lots of troubleshooting, we decided to remove the new authentication system and return to our original working prototype.
It was frustrating but taught us an important lesson that sometimes keeping things simple is better than adding features that aren't fully ready. Another challenge was adapting our original idea. We initially wanted to integrate Arduino for our project as a physical button for the staff to click to call for the next person, but unfortunately hardware wasn't allowed, so we had to adapt quickly and change plans.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're proud that we turned a problem we see every day into a working web application in such a short time. We successfully connected our frontend and Python backend, implemented live queue updates and rotating QR codes, and deployed LazyQ online with our own domain. Most importantly, we're proud of our teamwork, communication, and ability to adapt quickly when things didn't go as planned. We created a simple, accessible solution that has the potential to make life easier for both customers and businesses.

What we learned

Throughout our project, we learned how to tackle a real-world problem in a minimalist, user-focused way. We realised the significance of not over-complicating our solution and adapting quickly in the face of issues. We learned the technical implications of turning an idea into a scalable product and the implementation of new tools.

What's next for lazyQ

We plan to integrate the Google Maps API to track real-time wait times for nearby venues and restaurants, and the Gemini API to create a chatbot that answers customer inquiries. We also want to strengthen security by improving staff authentication.

AI Usage & Transparency

We used
Claude Pro
to help write and improve our frontend code (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript) and
ChatGPT
Plus to help us with backend development and fixing bugs.
Our team was responsible for finding the problem, creating the LazyQ concept and coming up with a name, designing the UI, making technical decisions, integrating the application, and testing the prototype.
We carefully reviewed, modified, and adapted AI generated code and suggestions to fit our project's needs. AI helped us develop faster, but the creativity, decisions, and final product were driven by our team.

projects.title: JabMap
projects.tagline: A map for your travel jabs. JabMap offers personalised vaccine and health advice, live safety updates for your destination, and directs you to nearby clinics to get the jab. All in one place.
projects.description:
Inspiration

One of our team member's Zainab's recent personal experience with travel vaccines inspired JabMap! She is planning on taking her grandmother on a trip to Kenya and the process of researching the required vaccines, clinics, and health information when travelling to a specific region can be tedious, especially given her and her grandmother's varying needs and health conditions.

What it does

It bridges the gap between all the vaccination information out there and the user gathering and storing it in one place, thereby streamlining the process of getting the travel vaccines. The application provides the following features:

Personalisation:
JabMap allows the user to enter their upcoming travel details, existing health conditions, vaccine history, and link their NHS account. This enables the application to provide specific vaccine requirements alongside the generic recommendations.

Vaccine Information:
For a selected country/region, the recommended and/or required vaccines are displayed along with information on the reasons for getting it and what it protects against.

Live Safety Updates:
This feature uses AI to search for the latest outbreak and health updates of the user's destination, which alerts the user in case their travel dates overlap with an ongoing epidemic, for example.

Interactive Interface:
For each of the maps integrated into the application, the user has the liberty to navigate them however they like. The main world map colour-codes regions based on health risk, provides zoom-in facilitation upon clicking on a specific place, along with an automatic zoom-out once the user clicks anywhere else. The clinic map provides options to use the current or a manually input location, shows the nearby clinics pinned, and displays their information.

How we built it

We built the app using Claude code as an assistant to help us vibe code the infrastructure. 
We began with a simple web app with an interactive world map and search bar allowing you to find or click your destination, resulting in a summary of the government of which vaccines are recommended from official UK government travel and health advice sites. Below this a map widget with options for ‘Find Vaccines near you’. This started off using JavaScripts for each feature - for example the vaccine recommendation by country data, or the clinic lists, with another js file structuring the app and interactive portions, like the maps, and finally the html file pulling it altogether into a web app.

As we continued to develop this idea the structure remained relatively the same. We used a Gemini API for our app to give live news updates. This meant creating a python server with our API keys to facilitate this. The next development was improving the vaccine pharmacy/clinic search to enhance the ease and experience of the user. Instead of using a generic search on google for locations of vaccine clinics we used an NHS Service Search API to improve our clinic list. This allowed us to get our list of clinics from the NHS services list, and list them by location. Using a list from a search with Google Cloud console Places API we could create an overlapping list giving the user information with google reviews also. This allowed us to achieve a reliable, informative and user friendly  clinic / pharmacy search for users wanting to find out where to get their jabs done.

The next development was to improve our personalisation feature, allowing users to not only input their trip details and personal history but also demoing a connection to their NHS official UK routine vaccine records. We demoed this by using the open access NHS Immunisation sandbox which produces a sample record of a patient. For the purposes of our demo and looking to the future developments of the NHS Immunisation API we modified the sample to include more vaccine records. This feature demonstrates the possibility and use of connecting JapMap to the user’s personal official NHS records in case they have forgotten their UK vaccine history. It allows the app to give personalised advice for the user based on their history and official records.

The final improvements were mostly to the user interface ensuring maximum ease and enjoyment of use, particularly  to the interactive maps - world map for destinations’ recommended vaccines and the find a vaccine map. We also introduced travel insurance advice to go alongside the specific health and travel advice by destination.

Finally we successfully attached our web to the domain name :jabmap.health and made our web app ready for travellers looking for jabs!

Challenges we ran into

We ran into a few challenges throughout this process. The main challenges with the user interface were debugging the interactive maps and ensuring their accuracy. We improved the clinic map by changing from system which takes the inputted location / postcode and allows google to just guess a location and display a google maps widget, to using our own leaflet map from openstreetmaps with accurate locations using verified co-ordinates. For the world map we improved the user interface making it easier and more pleasing to use, introducing zoom features and ensuring the map is accurate and runs without bugs, as well as avoiding guessing regions.

We also ran into a challenge when overlapping the clinic search to use NHS Service Search information as well as Google Places info like google reviews. Due to naming discrepancies not every clinic each search pulled up can be reliably matched, so we made sure that only the ones which can be are displayed. The list is still comprehensive and users are of course able to click off links to google maps to find out more. The benefit of looking at clinics from the NHS list and being able to see google review ratings is retained,

Using the NHS Immunisation sandbox we did find that the capabilities and sample produced by this system was limited compared to what we were intending to demo. However we were able to demonstrate using the official NHS records using their sandbox and look forward to improving our capabilities to include more vaccines, as the NHS Immunisation API is improved, such as the three-in-one and MMR routine vaccines which are listed as ‘in development’ for the API to search from.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

As beginner hackers, we're particularly proud of our use of APIs in this project. We used the Gemini API for live updates and news on the health situation of the selected country/region. We also used the Google Cloud Console Places and the NHS service search API to create an overlapped list of vaccine clinics relevant to the user. 
Another achievement for our team was creating interactive maps to maximise ease for the user. 
Being able to demonstrate the connection to a user's official NHS records was also an important accomplishment for us. Looking to the future, this improves the personalisation feature of JabMap as well as demonstrating the potential for a stronger connection to the NHS. Overall, we've managed to compile all the health, vaccine, and location information into one place and personalised the entire experience, without introducing any unnecessary complications or navigation problems.

What we learned

We learnt how to utilise APIs to provide live updates and perform search requests for information from google and the NHS. 
We learnt how to debug interactive features, testing the user interface, noticing issues, finding the coded problem and improving the infrastructure. 
We learnt how to collaboratively code a web app using a git-hub repository.
Finally, we learnt how to use Claude Code as an effective and efficient vibe-coding assistant, to facilitate and implement our ideas and innovations.

projects.title: Local-ish
projects.tagline: Local-ish is an AI-powered travel companion that helps travellers check local prices through photos, voice or text, avoid overpaying, and make smarter spending decisions abroad.
projects.description:
In Bali, I suddenly felt rich. Five dollars became around eighty thousand Indonesian rupiah. I had all these banknotes in my hand without understanding what things were actually worth. 
A price could sound cheap in dollars and still be much higher than what locals usually paid. After being overcharged, I realised a currency converter couldn’t answer my real question: “Is this a fair price here?”

Travelling with friends added another challenge: remembering who paid and who owed whom, without making money an awkward part of the trip.

These experiences inspired Local-ish—a way to understand unfamiliar prices, track spending, and remember where money goes. Our one goal is removing the friction travellers face when making everyday financial decisions in unfamiliar places.

We built a web app with a TypeScript and Express backend, dividing our work between interface, data, and Voice & AI. Gemini interprets typed requests, while ElevenLabs handles transcription and spoken phrases. Users can review an expense, compare it with available reference prices, and save it to their money balance.

We learned that understanding a price requires context: “two teas for sixty” is different from “sixty each.” We also learned to use AI for interpretation and reference data for comparisons, rather than asking AI to invent a fair price. Voice input, API quotas, and connecting our separate parts were challenges, which we addressed through transcript review, fewer repeated requests, shared contracts, and automated tests.

This hackathon taught us that building a useful AI application isn't simply about integrating a chatbot. It's about making different technologies work together to solve a real problem. We gained practical experience with APIs, frontend and backend development, databases, AI integration, testing and team collaboration. We're especially proud of connecting our backend to TigerData, storing structured price references and combining price checking, budgeting and bargaining assistance within an interactive prototype.

We want Local-ish to become a smarter and more personalised travel-spending companion.
Our next steps include:
Budget-aware recommendations: Connecting the price checker with the traveller's remaining budget so it can evaluate both price fairness and affordability.
Photo-based price checking: Allowing travellers to photograph menus, taxi tariffs and price signs instead of typing everything manually.
Connected group accounts: Enabling friends to link their accounts and manage shared expenses more seamlessly.
More reliable price information: Expanding our database to additional destinations and improving the freshness and verification of our reference prices.
Our long-term vision is to make local price knowledge accessible to travellers everywhere, helping them make financial decisions with greater confidence.

projects.title: Squidwards.ink
projects.tagline: Find a seat, not a queue. A live crowd map for student study and food spots.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Coming from our own experiences as students, we know the frustration of walking across campus to a library floor or a cafe, only to find it completely full. With a one-hour break between lectures, we would spend half of it queuing, a quarter walking, and the last quarter rushing our food. If you are new to a university, or new to the city, you have no way of knowing in advance where it is quiet, where there are free plugs, or where the queue is out of the door. We wanted that question answered with a single tap, by the students who are already there. A live, crowdsourced map of campus spaces that tells you exactly where you can actually sit, study, or eat right now, without the guesswork.

What it does

Map with a Study / Food toggle.
Each space has a glow (traffic light system) that gets bigger and darker as it fills. Green = Quiet or Okay, amber = Busy, red = Packed, grey = no check-ins yet, faded = closed now. Interactive to show nearby student spaces, cafes and restaurants.
One-tap check-in.
Quiet, Okay, Busy or Packed. No account, no location stored. One check-in per space every 10 minutes per device.
Best time to go
and
next-hour prediction
(predict availability, every 30 / 60 min), built from check-in history. Until a space has enough check-ins it says so instead of guessing.
Weekly timetable import
(.ics or .csv) with gap-aware suggestions, smart filters.
Campus Digital Twin
. Interactive visualizationn of study spaces & occupancy across the campus.
Ask in plain English
, by typing or speaking: "somewhere quiet with plugs, open after 10pm". It shows what it understood as chips.
Where should I go?
Say how long you need a seat. It picks a space, keeps watching, and changes its pick when new check-ins arrive.

How we built it

We split the work by tool. In the initiation phase we used DeepSeek to develop and stress-test ideas. Gemini produced the figures that show why students need this. Claude and Codex built the first prototypes: three different UI designs, from which we kept the best features of each.  The final app is a single-page web app. The map uses MapLibre with CARTO / OpenStreetMap tiles. The spaces are the 64 real University of Leeds spaces from the open Leeds Spacefinder dataset (coordinates, facilities, noise levels, opening hours). Busyness comes from student check-ins, which can be shared through one small Netlify Function with Netlify Blobs. Typical times and 30/60-minute predictions are calculated from that check-in history. Read-aloud and voice input use the browser’s built-in speech APIs. We tested the check-in rules, the plain-English parser and the backend with automated checks.

Challenges we ran into

Initially, we wanted to make it for UCL. But UCL did not have any publicly available information about availability, nor historical data for social spaces/cafes/libraries, for the predictive availability. We tried UCL API github (had history endpoints), but could not access any historical data, they needed a UCL-affiliated token we couldn’t get. We tried BestTime.app but could not receive the suitable API Token to use. 
Most of the data we needed were hidden behind logins or files, and chasing it cost us much of the hackathon.
Hence, we looked at Imperial’s timetables were only visible to its own students, which we would then be able to imply the busy times on campus, or certain buildings. 
We also wanted to incorporate the side tracks like Presage (a camera for the timetable scanning, real time biometrics connected to your apple watch/fit bit to track heartbeat/stress so the software could suggest de-stress/quieter places), Incident.io (to include a "Where should I go?" agent that changes its recommendation when new reports arrive) and ElevenLabs (to ask by voice and hear the answer read back. To increase accessibility). However, due to lack of time, and a lot of time spent on trying to find the historical data and API Tokens, we were unable to incorporate them. Hence they would be future features.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We designed before we built, 3 times over. 3 different UI directions were created first (2 with claude, 1 with codex), then we combined the strongest ideas from each into one coherent interface (such as a heatmap using the traffic light system and a personalized timetable). It meant that the final design wasn’t “the first thing that worked”, it showed that it was the best pieces of 3 attempts.

Privacy By Design. No account, no login, no stored location. A check-in is a spot ID and a timestamp in the browser. Nothing Else.

Honest By Design. Every number on the map is either a real published data source for Leeds study and food spots, or a live student check-in. When a spot has no recent check-ins, the app would say so (“No recent check-ins”) instead of guessing. We would rather admit uncertainty than fake confidence.

What we learned

Publicly Available Data is Rare. There is no open, reliable feed of "how busy is this library right now" for campus spaces. The real asset isn't data, it's the crowd. That changed how we thought about the product: the users are the data source.

The first users need to see value before anyone has checked in. We learned that an empty map has to still be useful, so we leaned on typical hourly patterns and honest empty states until real check-ins arrive.

An app that admits "not enough data yet" earns more trust than a confident fake. We would rather show "No recent check-ins" than invent a colour. Trust compounds; fake data destroys it.

Check the data sources before designing the product. We started the other way round, we designed first, then went looking for data to fit the idea. 
Next time: verify the data exists, then design around it. This was the single biggest process lesson of the weekend.
Designing three UI directions and combining them was slower than picking one, but the final product felt more intentional than any single sketch.

What's next for Squidwardz

Student Discount. For cafes & restaurants to display if they have student discount.
Accessibility info. Report broken lifts and step-free routes, so students who need them can plan around outages.
Community notes. A bulletin board of short opinions about each café and study space.
Timetable-aware suggestions. Import a timetable and get recommendations for where to study or eat in each gap.
Study buddy and food partner matching. Opt-in matching for people with the same schedule.
Smart filters, by distance, availability, price and type of study space (plugs, adjustable tables etc.).
Presage (a camera for the timetable scanning, real time biometrics by your wearable API to track heartbeat/stress so the software could suggest de-stress/quieter places).
Incident.io (to include a "Where should I go?" agent that changes its recommendation when new reports arrive).
ElevenLabs (to ask by voice and hear the answer read back). To increase accessibility. Read aloud for spaces, the agent's pick and search replies.

projects.title: Pythagoras
projects.tagline: Imagine… that there is no elevator to have your pitch in because of a fire alarm. Where is the closest staircase? Pythagoras can help.
projects.description:
We were inspired to build this because whenever you do not know where a room is in UCL, you try to use Google Maps to get there, which almost always makes you leave the building, even though there may be a faster route internally. For me, it was the walk from the Physics Department to the Geology Department, which turns a 1 minute walk into a 4 minute one. Google Maps only knows the streets around a building, not the corridors, doors and staircases inside it, so it treats every building as a box you have to walk around rather than through.

Not to mention, the lift in the Physics building has been broken for months, and commuting to the lift on the other side of the building (if needed) would require an entirely different route, going around through the main quad instead of the back of the Physics building. For anyone who can’t use stairs, that isn’t a small detour. It changes their whole journey, and nothing tells them that before they set off. We wanted to build something that knows the inside of a building: which corridors connect, which doors your card will open, which lifts actually work, and when there simply is no step-free way through.

Throughout this project we learned that indoor navigation is really a network problem with a lot of real-world rules layered on top. A building can be described as a set of points (rooms, doors, corridor corners, stairs and lifts) joined by paths you can walk along. Finding a route is then a matter of finding the shortest path through that network, but “shortest” depends on who is walking. A visitor can’t get through card-controlled doors, a student can only use them before 6pm, and a wheelchair user can’t use any path that involves stairs. We also learned how much the quality of the map matters. A routing algorithm is only as good as the data underneath it, and checking that data by hand took far longer than writing the algorithm itself. Finally, we learned a lot about accessibility. It isn’t enough to offer a step-free option; the app also has to be honest when no step-free route exists, instead of quietly sending someone towards a staircase.

We built this project mostly using Python for the routing backend and a web app built with HTML, JavaScript and SVG files for the frontend. We started from the PDF floor plans of the Physics building and used Google’s AI to read them and turn each floor into a map of rooms, doors, corridors, stairs and lifts, each with a position. We then redrew all five floors as clean vector floor plans and lined them up with the AI’s map, so that routes from the backend land exactly on the right corridors on screen. The backend, built with Python and Jworks out the shortest walking route for each request, keeping only the paths that person is allowed to use based on their card type, the time of day and whether they need step-free access. If a step-free route isn’t possible, it says so clearly and tells the person to contact the building administration. On top of that, we added a way for students to report problems like leaks or broken doors and admin tools to close corridors for events, mark lifts as out of order, add rooms and facilities, and approve information suggested by students

Challenges we faced included turning the floor plans into something a computer could route on. The plans were flat images, not data, so we had to redraw them by hand and make sure the AI’s map lined up with them on every floor. This was harder than expected, because the AI’s coordinates were stretched differently on each floor. It was also difficult to verify the quality of the AI mapping, checking all the edges, adding accessibility features, and making connections between floors. The AI missed some rooms entirely, left others unnamed and joined some lifts to the rest of the floor only through the stairs. So we had to check the map floor by floor, give every room a sensible name, place the missing rooms using their positions on our floor plans, and link the stairs and lifts between floors ourselves.

We hope this project can be applied to larger scale buildings such as the whole of UCL, as well as other universities, and eventually other buildings, who can not only be inspired by our product and method, but hopefully in the future directly upload their floorplans into this software and be able to map out their building directly.

projects.title: SideQuest
projects.tagline: Less scrolling. More adventures. More SideQuests.
projects.description:
Two of our team members commute to and from university. This means that if they have large gaps in their timetables, they often end up in the same place, not knowing how to kill time for hours. Despite there being many events possibly happening at the time, it is hard to know which ones are best suited to their interests, how they are feeling on the day and how easy it is to get there and back on time for the next lecture. It also means that they have fewer opportunities to socialise and make friends unlike students living in accommodation, meaning they feel left out and feel less like they are part of a community.

Our project is an app that syncs events to timetables, showing you what events are happening during frees and how to get there with integrated links to google maps. You are able to filter out your mood, the type of activity you'd like, university, quiet or sociable spaces, as well as showing cross university events, allowing more opportunities to meet different people. The app involves accessibility options like text to speech or speech to text and the option to use AI to filter out events according to the prompt given, allowing ease and accessibility in navigating free time to be productive.

Using Claude Code as an AI coding tool, we built the base of the app, using instructions from Claude. The foundation of the app had a demo timetable, where if a gap was shown, you could find possible areas nearby to go to, such as cafes or libraries. However, this did not show many real society events and was a lot more general as there was few options on the filter originally. Also, it was not linked to google maps, so you could not see an actual map of where everything was on the website. We then continued to use Claude in order to figure out how to use APIs to add different features to the website, using API to add a maps feature. While this was happening, two of us built a spreadsheet of real society events and other opportunities happening around London across KCL, UCL and Imperial. We then added this data into the app, adding websites from each society to allow easy access to see exactly what each event is. We also added the option on the app for societies to add their events by uploading a poster of the event and AI can separate out the components and add this as a choice during suitable gaps. We then added more filters, such as events, cafes, study, activities, deals, price, university, social, quiet etc, as well as adding a speech feature using ElevenLabs so that you can speak to the app, and Gemini AI will filter events for you. We added another accessibility feature using API of text to speech so a voice will read out your options of socials - this can be turned on or off. We then realised that the app did not have a live location feature - it automatically assumes you are at your last lecture, where you might not be so we used Claude here to provide us a step by step on figuring out how to add live location, which the app can now use. After this, we realised that the app does not add the event selected to your calendar for the day, so we changed it so that it will do this too. After this, two of us added a domain from GoDaddy, after we sat and decided a name - notthelibraryagain.club, and built the powerpoint for the presentation. We then tried to understand the code and make sure that it could be used on a phone.

One of the biggest challenges was that all of us had zero to little coding experience. This meant that we were unsure where to start, so we used Claude Code as an AI tool to guide us through this and help make the foundation of the app and add different features. Although we were very confused at the start, which took up a lot of time, over time we started to figure it out more. The second challenge was that the API stopped working on day 2, and we couldnt figure out how to get it back. To get around this, two of us tried to work on it using different AI tools like Claude and this allowed us to add the API finally.

Accomplishments we are proud of include understanding how apps are built - this is completely new to us and a new experience that we are proud of trying. We also feel accomplished that we are now more confident in using AI to guide us through projects and navigate new technology.

We learnt how to utilise AI to help build code and add new features. We also learnt how apps are built and what programmes and software are used to build this. We learnt new terms such as API's and how to debug code although this was a big challenge. We also learnt how to work as a team and delegate roles accordingly to get everything we needed to do done on time.

For SideQuest, the next step would be to add new features such as a 'Notify your friends' feature where friends can be notified if you are going to an event, so that if they are free they can also come along. Incorporating TFL to the app would also be a next step as this is a large part of commuter's journeys as the app can tell you whether travel routes are delayed so that you can know if you will make it to lectures on time. Finally, we could expand SideQuest to more universities like in Greater London or the Midlands.

projects.title: BudgetBestie
projects.tagline: Don’t know how to plan your monthly budget plan? BudgetBestie creates a plan structured and tailored to your habits and behavioral traits!
projects.description:
Inspiration

Budgeting as students studying abroad was an issue we saw in ourselves and others. There are many apps that aren’t tailored to behavioural traits and are ineffective in helping us budget. We felt it was necessary to create a tool that is personalised to ensure a maintainable plan that aligns with your lifestyle and spending habits.

What it does

It is a visual web application that starts with a questionnaire covering your spending habits, including an International Personality Item Pool (IPIP)  that asks questions about your behavioral traits. Through this personality-informed method, this tool creates a weekly/monthly budget plan that is suitable for the user. Additionally, it can plan around your budget or suggest a budget for you, provide tips that will help maximise your savings, and provide you with 3 types of plans depending on your priorities (saver, balanced, or social budget).

How we built it

We discussed our ideas on ways to integrate a psychological aspect with the issue of budget planning, and created prompts that we put into Claude AI. To create the prompts, we used the following behavioural dimensions in order to curate an appropriate plan for the user: methodicalness +organisation, risk taking + fun seeking, and gregariousness + extraversion. Claude wrote the code necessary for creating the web application, which we then put into Visual Studio Code.

Challenges we ran into

We struggled to understand the code and how to run it in VS. Additionally, one of the commands in the code was incorrect, so we used Claude to understand what the issue was and how to fix it.  Finally, we used Claude to understand the basics of the code, as we don't have any prior coding experience.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud of integrating our studies into a field that we are not familiar with, and using it to create a web app that would help with an issue we faced when we first started studying in London.

What we learned

We learned the basics of coding, translating ideas into software, and how to use our studies to solve real life problems as international students.

What's next for BudgetBestie

This app is tailored for London university students, so we can include other countries and ensure that transportation, entertainment, groceries, etc are specific to the location. Furthermore, this web application is a budget planner, but an add-on function could be a budget tracker that would help determine if any changes to the original plan are needed.

projects.title: Docket
projects.tagline: A shared platform for provable record of a repair, where the law is applied in the open, and nothing that matters is decided by a machine.
projects.description:
Inspiration

In December 2020, Awaab Ishak died at the age of two. He had spent his whole life in a
one-bedroom social flat in Rochdale with mould his family reported repeatedly and nobody
fixed. The inquest found he died from prolonged exposure to mould.

The law changed in response. Section 42 of the Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023 inserted
section 10A into the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, "Awaab's Law", which puts time limits on
how long a social landlord may take to investigate and fix serious hazards. Phase 1 (damp and
mould, plus all emergencies) is in force. Phase 2 arrives on 30 November 2026.

So the legal machine exists. What doesn't exist is anything that makes it work in practice.
Ask a tenant what their landlord's deadline is and they won't know. Ask a landlord which of
their homes is nearest a breach and they'll open a spreadsheet. The facts that decide whether a
legal duty was met are scattered across a phone call, a photo in someone's camera roll, and a
paper certificate in a filing cabinet, so nothing can be proved by either side afterwards.

That gap is the product. Docket is a two-sided record of one repair, with the legal clock
visible to both people at once. Free for tenants; paid for by landlords, because "provable
compliance" is worth real money to a housing association that currently cannot prove anything
without a filing cabinet.

What it does

A tenant reports a problem in seconds - by voice, in any language, or by photo and text. Gemini
reads the report and extracts facts. A deterministic rules engine works out which legal duty
applies and when it is due. Both parties then see the same clock: the landlord's deadlines
(acknowledge, give access, investigate, fix) and the tenant's own duties (respond to an access
request, don't refuse reasonable works).

The workflow is an event log. If a deadline passes, Docket drafts a pre-action protocol letter
of claim and a PDF bundle of the evidence. Every piece of evidence and every case-log head is
fingerprinted and anchored on Solana, so the record cannot be quietly edited later, by either
party.
/verify
lets anyone check a file against the chain.

How we built it

Four layers, deliberately separated by how much we trust them.

1. An event-sourced case.
A case is an append-only log of facts and actions in
case_events
. Nothing is stored as "current state". All state is derived by replaying the
log, and every write goes through one function (
appendEvent
) that re-projects, diffs, and
stores the result in
case_revisions
. Each event is hash-chained to the one before it, so
rewriting history means recomputing every subsequent hash:

$$h_1 = H(\texttt{""} \mathbin| \mathrm{canonicalJSON}(e_1)), \qquad h_i = H(h_{i-1} \mathbin| \mathrm{canonicalJSON}(e_i))$$

where $H$ is SHA-256.

2. A pure, deterministic engine.

project(events, {now, law, landlordType})
takes the log
and returns the case state. No I/O, no model calls, no clock reads — "now" is passed in, which
is what makes the demo's time travel possible and the whole thing unit-testable. Inside it,
beliefs.ts
resolves facts from sources of differing reliability (an official record at 0.95, a
tenant report at 0.6); close disagreements become surfaced
conflicts
rather than averages,
and severity conflicts resolve safety-first.
rules.ts
turns facts plus law into obligations,
each carrying the facts it rests on, so
diff.ts
can explain
why
a conclusion appeared or
disappeared.

3. A careful AI boundary.
Gemini only ever
extracts facts
, and each extracted fact is
recorded as an assertion with a source (
ai_text
,
ai_vision
) and that source's reliability.
The model never decides a duty or a date. Deadlines come from
law.ts
, where every number
traces to a verified official source in
sources.ts
(legislation.gov.uk, gov.uk, and the
Justice pre-action protocol). Prompts are only changed against an eval harness: 14 real
reports across five languages, currently 14/14.

4. Integrations that make it feel like a product.
ElevenLabs runs the voice intake agent
(and Scribe for voice notes), with client-side tools so voice works on localhost with no tunnel.
Tiger Data holds the time-series side: hypertables for events and revisions, and a continuous
aggregate over simulated damp-sensor readings. Solana devnet receives a Merkle root over all
new evidence hashes and case-log heads as a memo, with pairs hashed in sorted order so a proof
is just a list of sibling hashes:

$$\mathrm{pair}(a,b) = H\big(\min(a,b) \mathbin| \max(a,b)\big)$$

Challenges we ran into

Being legally honest was harder than being clever.
Our first version called every deadline a
"legal deadline". It wasn't true. Awaab's Law sets fixed periods, and the pre-action protocol
sets 20 working days, but section 11 of the 1985 Act imposes a duty to repair
within a
reasonable time
and names no number at all. We rebuilt the vocabulary: only fixed periods in
law are "legal deadlines"; Docket's own estimates are "targets", labelled differently on screen.
The landlord's "missed deadlines" counter counts only the real ones. This matters more than it
sounds, a product that overstates the law is worse than no product, and we would rather be
correct in front of a judge than impressive.

The law moves, so the engine had to.
Awaab's Law Phase 2 is laid but not yet in force, and
its real start date is 30 November 2026. We model commencement dates as data, so
/demo
can
advance the clock and a heating case visibly gains statutory deadlines. It also means we can
show a judge the caveats honestly: Phase 2 is subject to Parliamentary approval, and we say so.

Models are bad at numbers, so we don't let them near numbers.
Free-tier Gemini is limited to
five requests per minute per model, which shaped the architecture as much as it shaped the
budget:
generateStructured
retries and then falls back through a chain of models, and the
intake eval is paced so a full run takes about three minutes. The harder problem was trust. A
model that reads "the boiler is broken" and returns a deadline is a model that will eventually
invent one. So extraction and judgement are separate layers, and only the deterministic one is
allowed to have an opinion.

Explaining a changed mind.
Our favourite demo moment came from a bug fix. When a contractor
records a leak into the subfloor, the appliance duty is dropped and the section 11 repair duty
appears. That's correct and completely confusing unless you say why. Every conclusion now
carries the facts it rests on, and the revision feed reads like a person explaining themselves:
"the appliance is no longer the landlord's to fix, because
whether the landlord supplied the
appliance
changed to no."

Working days are not arithmetic.
"10 working days" excludes weekends, Christmas Day, Good
Friday and bank holidays, and the deadline ends at the end of a day in Europe/London, which is
not the same length on the two days a year the clocks change. We built it on the GOV.UK bank
holiday feed and asserted the 2025–2027 dates match exactly.

Rediscovering the edge of a framework we'd just adopted.
Next.js 16's Cache Components
refuses to prerender a route that reads the request, and a session read is a request read. Our
sign-in guard therefore had to either stream and bounce the browser after the fact, or opt the
segment out of instant navigation so it blocks on the server and returns a real redirect. We
took the block, and found out that the honest cost of a server-side check is a slower navigation.

What we learned

That the interesting engineering in a legal product is not the AI. It is deciding what the
system is allowed to claim. Two rules did more for the quality of this build than any model
choice:
one deterministic core

projects.title: AMI
projects.tagline: My by womxn, for womxn
projects.description:
Inspiration

We wanted to create a website to make it easy to navigate safely. So we created ‘AMI’ (French for ‘friend’) to help women and non-binary people walk around while helping to keep them safe. Walking alone, especially at night, can be a daunting experience and for many women and non-binary people requiring people to think about many factors. We wanted to simplify this process and have everything you need in one place, including safe routes to take, an agent who you can call anytime, and a supportive network of other women and non-binary people.

What it does

Our project allows people to see nearby events and register. The safest routes to navigate around using streetlights, open shops, and other users ratings. Each user can rate a route they have taken and identify any safety aspects they want to highlight. We also set up an AI agent who you can call to make it seem like you’re not alone. On user profiles you can add your interests and emergency contacts. Our buddy system allows verified tier 2 users to match with other users of similar interests so they can chat and also go to events together. To access tier 2, the user will have to go to one event where they can get verified as a trusted user. This is just to block out anyone pretending to be someone else from direct messages and meeting up with other users outside organised events. Additionally tier 2 users ratings of routes are valued higher as we know they are more trustworthy.

How we built it

The main AI tools we used were GitHub co pilot and gemini through antigravity, we came together as a group and drafted up a detailed plan so we can make specific and well defined prompts to our ai agents.

We created a GitHub repository to ensure everyone in the team could contribute their local work and access any new updates easily no matter time and location.

The main languages of the product are; Typescript for the backend and apis, and html and css for the frontend/ui. PostgreSQL was used to design the database which will manage user information, event locations, ai call features etc.

Challenges we ran into

We ran into trouble accessing a working map because we used the google map open API first and tried to draw paths on top of it for our website We overcame this by switching to open streetmap.

We had a lot of issues with running out of credits for free trials so we continuously switched which laptop was doing each thing to max out our usage.

Integrating our ElevenLabs AI agent successfully.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Our main struggle was working on how to seamlessly integrate our eleven labs agent “Adam” - when the call button would work, the voice response would stop and vice verse. But the moment everything worked together in tandem with the ai voice we were especially proud.

We were also proud of managing to complete so much in so little time regardless of half the team not having computer science/tech background, fortunately with the help of ai and our creative minds we managed to build a full working web application from scratch.

What we learned

Some of us had previously had some prejudice against ai due to their effects on the planet and young minds but whilst working on this project and also during the wise panel talk with their employees we managed to see that ai is beneficial in multiple ways when used wisely.

We also learnt how to work well in a team with members from different backgrounds, degrees and universities whilst successfully communicating with each other and asking for help when needed.

What's next for AMI

Our next goal is to integrate the Presage camera tracking into the video call because we had challenges incorporating with the ElevenLabs model. This would measure the user’s breathing rate with the camera and if it is greater than or equal to 30, it would be flagged suggesting user is stressed, anxious or in an unsafe situation. Therefore, we also wanted to enhance the Presage model so that if a sudden phone movement is detected, such as if the phone is dropped, it would cause the AI agent to call the police in case of emergency.

projects.title: FlatMate
projects.tagline: Your rental sidekick that's got your back: the AI companion that reads your lease, tracks your bills, and stays with you all the way to move-out day.
projects.description:
Project Story

About the project

Inspiration

Renting property in the UK is notoriously stressful. From deciphering dense 30-page tenancy agreements written in legal jargon to tracking confusing utility bills, navigating energy ratings (EPC), and trying to hold landlords accountable to the Housing Act or the Renters' Rights Act, tenants are often left completely on their own.

We were inspired to build FlatMate because we wanted to bridge the gap between initial lease-signing and the final day of the tenancy. Too many renters miss critical clauses regarding guest policies, illegal financing, or unfair restrictions simply because agreements are designed to be incomprehensible. We wanted to create an AI-powered buddy that doesn't just read the lease upfront, but stays with you throughout the entire life of your tenancy.

What It Does

FlatMate is an end-to-end tenancy companion application designed to support renters at every stage of their renting journey:

Lease Demystifier:
Uploads and analyzes tenancy agreement PDFs, instantly flagging crucial need-to-knows, hidden restrictions, and potential legal contradictions against UK legislation (such as housing acts).

Automated Landlord Communication:
Automatically generates formal draft emails to landlords regarding any legal discrepancies or issues found within the agreement.

Ongoing Tenancy Buddy:
Acts as an interactive chatbot helper from move-in day onwards, assisting with maintenance issues, tracking bills based on regional estimates, and handling meter readings.

Move-In Bookkeeping & Calendar Management:
Features photo upload capabilities for move-in condition tracking and a smart calendar that coordinates bill payments and calculates notice periods (such as 2-month termination notice tracking).

How We Built It

We designed FlatMate with a robust modern tech stack tailored for flexibility, document processing, and AI intelligence:

AI & LLMs:
Powered by the Gemini API to handle complex multimodal document analysis (processing lease agreements and move-in photos) and power the conversational chatbot buddy.

Backend & Deployment:
Built to scale and deployed seamlessly using Vultr.

Data & Architecture:
Utilizes Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) coupled with a dedicated database of UK housing legislature to ensure all advice and flags remain strictly grounded in current legal frameworks.

Challenges We Faced

Complex Legal Parsing:
Ensuring the AI could accurately distinguish between standard tenancy clauses and actual legal contradictions or illegal financing terms required fine-tuning prompts and establishing strict guardrails against UK housing law.

Multimodal Inputs:
Balancing the processing of text-heavy PDF agreements alongside image uploads for property condition tracking required careful optimization of our LLM pipeline.

Feature Scope:
Keeping the app focused on an end-to-end journey—from initial agreement review to ongoing bills and final move-out notices—meant carefully prioritizing core features for our hackathon MVP.

What We Learned

We gained a deep understanding of UK tenant rights, housing acts, and the complexities of building localized, legally-grounded RAG applications. We also learned how to effectively structure an AI assistant that transitions smoothly from a document parser into an active, day-to-day lifestyle companion for renters.

projects.title: FairTime
projects.tagline: Your calendar knows when you're free, FairTime knows what's fair: an extension that minimizes inconvenience and recommends the fairest meeting time directly inside your calendar.
projects.description:
Inspiration

The topic of Max Ease joined with Wise's product pillars of speed, convenience, and transparency led us to rethink group scheduling from the ground up. We realised that scheduling shouldn't require hidden personal sacrifices and so we built FairTime to move away from slow, awkward negotiations and hidden compromises toward an automated, transparent, and mathematically fair experience.

What it does

FairTime is like Grammarly but for fair meeting scheduling. Rather than merely identifying blank calendar slots, it calculates the personal inconvenience of meeting times for each attendee, balances sacrifices across the team, and suggests the fairest option with complete mathematical transparency. It acts as an ambient extension that overlays your active workflow from your current digital calendar (such as Google calendar or Outlook). Rather than forcing groups to switch to a third party polling site or dashboard, FairTime sits along your existing tools as an extension that can be used as required when scheduling meetings.

How we built it

Under the hood, FairTime operates as a fully deterministic system rather than relying on blackbox AI. Our engine takes in authorized calendar free vs busy data, automatically filtering out protected windows and existing commitments such as rest times and assignment deadlines. It then evaluates feasible slots in 5 minute increments, scoring penalty costs based on distance from each attendee’s preferred working hours. To ensure no single person bears the brunt of the compromise, FairTime runs a minimax optimization algorithm to minimize the worst case individual burden across the group. Finally, an ACID-compliant time series ledger on Tiger Data PostgreSQL looks at each user's historical inconvenience, ensuring past sacrifices are remembered and team members who took late calls previously are automatically protected in future sessions. The frontend delivers this seamlessly via an ambient Manifest V3 browser extension embedded directly inside Google Calendar and Outlook, paired with a Next.js web application for account and group settings.

Challenges we ran into

With tour entire team coming from non-CS backgrounds, coordinating multi-branch Git merges, configuring relational schemas in Tiger Data (PostgreSQL), and structuring browser extension messaging under the deadline was intense and stressful. To bridge this gap, we used generative AI tools like GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT as interactive pair-programmers to help us navigate unfamiliar syntax, debug complex problems, and scaffold our Tiger Data PostgreSQL schemas. Every line of generated code was manually reviewed, integrated, and validated by our team.
Because we worked in parallel across distinct components - the browser extension UI, calendar ingestion, minimax scoring engine, and Tiger Data PostgreSQL database - linking everyone’s individual modules into a unified, seamless pipeline was a significant engineering hurdle. Enforcing strict API data contracts and standardizing UTC ISO timestamps early on proved essential to prevent integration breaking bugs during the final assembly. 
Ultimately, we found that the most effective solution was the most simple - open, constant communication and regularly syncing on what each person was tackling and how we were approaching it proved to be the most useful tool.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We translated Wise's core product pillars (speed, convenience, and transparency) into a direct solution for an everyday problem that we ourselves face and then successfully engineered a browser extension that allows users to request, inspect, and confirm meetings without  manual availability entry. Which we did within the tight time limit and working with completely new technical territory.

What we learned

-When our code broke while linking the modules together, the solution didn't come from writing more code. It came from active team communication stopping to walk through what each person was building and agreeing on strict API contracts before merging.
-As first time builders, we learned how to use generative AI responsibly. We used tools like ChatGPT as an interactive tutor to explain unfamiliar syntax and query structures, while keeping ownership of our architecture.
-Solving an issue we live through weekly gave us clarity under pressure. Beyond rapidly expanding our technical abilities, collaborating on FairTime accelerated our personal growth as it sharpened our communication, collaborative problem solving, and presentation skills.

What's next for FairTime

Looking ahead, we plan on scaling FairTime from focusing on students to distributed enterprises. If FairTime reclaims just 35 minutes per person of wasted scheduling coordination time per week, a 10 person team can reclaim roughly 300 hours of wasted time each year. This translates to approximately £15,000 in saved time annually. Not only does FairTime prevent worker burnout (by scheduling fair meeting times), it also boosts team satisfaction which further boosts productivity.
