projects.title: Phase Zero
projects.tagline: Clinical trials without the friction. We streamline applications for clinical trials on both the academic and patient side, and let patients track their medications with ease.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Joining a clinical trial is a pile of paperwork before any care happens. You search a registry built for researchers, then read dense eligibility text, then enter the same medical details into one form after another. If you’re on medication, you also have to look out for prerequisites of doses taken. Many people give up before they even reach a coordinator.

Wise’s Max Ease theme asks us to remove friction from a complicated process and make it accessible. We chose this one because the people who most need to understand a medical form are often the least able to spare the effort. What if you fill in your details once, and every step after that is done for you?

What it does

PhaseZero is one patient profile that connects three things people normally do in separate places:

Fill in once. A three-step profile (about you, your conditions, your location) is reused everywhere. There is no re-typing.

Scan
instead of type. Photograph a prescription. Gemini reads the medicine, strength, dose and how often.

A schedule that
builds itself
. A confirmed prescription becomes a weekly blister-pack calendar. Tap a dose to mark it taken, and tap again to undo. Each type of medicine (tablet, inhaler, injection, cream) gets its own icon and animation.

Trials in plain English
. We find recruiting studies on a free API from ClinicalTrials.gov and break each study’s criteria into short statements. For each one we show whether it appears to apply to you: yes, no, or unknown. We list the questions to ask the study team. We never say whether you are eligible.

A
daily diary
. Log how you feel with a note. Presage tracks your breathing rate and heart rate to monitor your vitals.

How we built it

Frontend
: Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind.
Backend
: Python FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2, Alembic migrations, and Pydantic validation on every request.
Database
: Postgres hosted on Tiger Data. It stores profiles, medications, dose events, check-ins and bookmarks.
Gemini
: read prescription photos into a strict JSON schema, and explain trial criteria in plain language.
ClinicalTrials.gov API v2
: live search for recruiting studies, with a local cache of real records as a fallback.
Auth
: signed, HTTP-only session cookies. Our sign-in is a clearly labelled demo mode; magic-link email isn’t set up yet.

Challenges we ran into

Not trusting the model. Early on, Gemini’s output couldn’t be used as-is. Some schema keywords were rejected, and a label with no clock times invites a made-up “9am” after the time has already passed, making it impossible to take the dose. We integrated the calendar more strongly made the model return only what’s printed.

Eligibility is a safety line. A friendly “you qualify!” would be wrong and risky. We built it so the model assesses individual criteria, the app works out the overall status with plain rules, and every quote is checked against the original text. We always strive to put the highest ranking applications on there.

Four people, one database. We split ownership by file and kept one migration history. The frontend was built ahead of the backend, so contracts drifted until we tested the real flow end to end.

Time is messy. Daylight saving changes, “today” versus the patient’s timezone, and what counts as a missed dose all took careful decisions.

A bug that only appeared end to end. Running the full flow against a real database showed that some bad input caused a server error instead of a clear message

Accomplishments that we're proud of (robust data handling)

We never invent medical details. Gemini’s output is validated: only real HH:MM times survive, frequency must be one of a fixed list, and a missing dose or duration is shown as “we couldn’t read this” so you fill it in.

Trial explanations are checked. Every explained criterion is verified against the study’s own text, the overall status comes from rules rather than the model, and names and emails are kept out of the AI prompt (covered by a test).

Your data is only yours.

Schedules behave. They are timezone- and daylight-saving-aware (tested). Doses already past when you scan are skipped, overdue doses become “missed” by themselves, and the week runs Monday to Sunday.

Honest numbers. Adherence is always “marked taken”, never verified. There are no invented match percentages. Logging a dose early updates the dashboard immediately.

Privacy by design. No camera video is stored, secrets live in environment variables, and every error uses one consistent format.

What we learned

Friction removal is mostly about what you leave out. Every field we pre-filled was one the person no longer had to read, type or remember.

AI helps most when it’s boxed in. Structured output, validation and human confirmation made Gemini useful instead of risky.
In healthcare, the wording is part of safety.

“Possible match” and “needs more info” are different promises from “eligible”.
Integration tests catch what unit tests miss, as the error-handling bug showed.

AI Transparency

In the product: Gemini reads prescription photos and explains trial criteria, and ElevenLabs creates the voice audio.
Claude (Anthropic) helped generate the repo scaffold, and the tests. The backend and frontend was researched thoroughly and built from scratch with Claude assisting debugging.

projects.title: Wise Piggy: A Budget Trip Planner
projects.tagline: A group trip planner where nobody has to say their budget out loud and splits the trip costs automatically with Wise.
projects.description:
Wise Piggy: Group Budget Trip Planner

Tagline:
Transparent costs, private budgets.

Track:
Wise: Max Ease

Side challenges:
ElevenLabs, MLH Best Use of Gemini API, MLH Best Use of Snowflake API, Vultr, GoDaddy

Inspiration

We've all experienced how complicated planning a group trip can get before anyone has even booked anything. One person suggests a weekend away, someone else is trying to save money, and another person ends up coordinating everyone's schedules. Sooner or later, the conversation turns to budgets, and not everyone feels comfortable sharing how much they can afford.

Planning gets even trickier when friends live in different countries. Flights cost different amounts depending on where everyone is travelling from, people use different currencies, and receipts get lost in group chats. We wanted to make travelling with friends about enjoying the trip, not having to explain your personal finances.

What it does

Everyone enters three budgets privately, using their own currency: a budget for flights, their share of group expenses, and a daily allowance for food and extras. They also enter the dates they're available. Nobody else can see their individual budgets.

The server uses everyone's information to create a shortlist of destinations that
fit everyone's budget
. A destination only makes the list if the flights from each person's airport, their share of accommodation, and their estimated daily food costs all fit within their individual budgets. The group's overall spending limit is calculated on the server and never shared with other members.

Each destination also shows how much previous groups have typically spent there per day. Everyone can vote anonymously, so the group sees the results without knowing who voted for which option. If no destinations fit, everyone receives the same neutral message, without revealing whose budget is limiting the options.

Once the trip begins, you can take a photo of a receipt and Gemini will read its individual items. You then select who had what, and the bill is split according to what each person actually ordered.

You can also record expenses using your voice. For example, you could say, "I paid 42 euros for dinner, Amara had the pasta for twelve." ElevenLabs converts the recording into text, and Gemini turns it into a draft expense for you to review. Once you confirm, ElevenLabs reads back something like, "Saved €42 for Dinner. Amara owes you €12."

Expenses can be shared or personal and can use any currency, with live exchange rates from Wise. Everyone can privately track their spending against their own daily budget.

At the end of the trip, the app calculates who owes whom and finds a way to settle everything with as few payments as possible. Each amount is converted into the payer's home currency, with a link to Wise to make the payment.

How we built it

Frontend:
React.

Backend:
Node.js, Express and PostgreSQL. All the core financial logic, including date overlaps, the hidden spending ceiling, destination feasibility, expense splitting, settlement and daily budget tracking, is handled by deterministic code. We wrote 75 unit tests for it.

Wise API:
Used for exchange rates. Each expense records the rate, its source and the time it was retrieved. Any fallback rates are clearly labelled.

SerpApi (Google Flights):
Provides live flight prices from each member's own airport. We cache results and manage searches carefully to stay within the monthly limit.

Gemini API:
Handles receipt scanning and spoken expense descriptions using structured JSON output. A lighter fallback model takes over when the main model is busy. Our code handles currency amounts in minor units rather than leaving that work to the model.

ElevenLabs:
Scribe v2 handles speech-to-text, while Eleven v4 Turbo reads out spoken confirmations.

Snowflake:
Stores anonymised analytics and powers a Streamlit dashboard showing figures such as how much previous groups spent per day. When available, Cortex generates the "why this trip fits the group requirements" explanations.

Privacy was a key consideration throughout the build. AI models never receive anyone's budget. Gemini only receives receipt images, transcripts and member names, while Cortex receives destination tags, the number of nights and the month.

Challenges we ran into

Keeping budgets private without making the app less useful.
We made sure every response contains only explicitly approved fields. If a live flight price rules out a destination, the group isn't told whose flight caused the issue.

Splitting receipts fairly.
Item prices don't always add up neatly to the receipt total because of tax, tips and discounts. We distribute the total proportionally based on each person's items, using integer minor units and largest-remainder rounding to make sure the final shares always add up correctly.

Handling different currencies.
Google Flights doesn't support NGN, so searches for those users run in EUR and are converted using Wise exchange rates. We also had to account for currencies that don't use decimal subdivisions.

Working around API limits during a 24-hour build.
Gemini sometimes returned "high demand" errors, so we added a fallback model. SerpApi's free plan only allows 250 searches per month, which meant caching prices and keeping some searches in reserve. Snowflake Cortex wasn't available on trial accounts, so we added a template-based fallback for destination explanations.

Merging two people's work at 3 a.m.
Both the Gemini and voice branch and the main branch had changes to the expenses code. Bringing everything together meant carefully resolving conflicts and checking that the features still worked.

Finding out the Gemini "free credits" weren't actually available.
We activated the Google student offer expecting the monthly Google Cloud credits associated with Google AI subscriptions. After digging through the documentation, we realised the free student plan was Google AI Plus. The credits ($10 per month, not £10) were only included with Google AI Pro and Ultra.

Creating an API key in AI Studio was straightforward, but the paid tier required a minimum prepaid top-up. Even Pro users were reporting a known synchronisation issue between developer credits and the newer prepayment system. The relevant information was spread across Google One help pages, Developer Program FAQs, AI Studio billing documentation and forum discussions, with each source explaining only part of the situation.

How we solved it:
Instead of getting stuck on billing, we built the project using the free tier of the Gemini API. We used gemini-3.8-flash as our main model and lighter Flash-Lite models for simpler tasks. We also designed the app around the free-tier rate limits, allowing the project to run at no cost.

Getting voice recording lengths right for ElevenLabs.
Recordings needed to be long enough to capture a complete sentence, such as "Amara had the pasta for twelve", but short enough to transcribe quickly and stay within our credits. We settled on recordings that automatically stop after 30 seconds.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Helping a group go from having no plan to choosing a destination without anyone needing to disclose their budget.

Building receipt scanning that splits costs by item, alongside voice entry that understands descriptions like "Amara had the pasta" and confirms the saved expense aloud.

Making it possible to settle expenses across GBP, NGN and EUR without anyone having to calculate exchange rates manually.

Making sure every fallback is labelled with its source, so the app stays transparent when a service is unavailable.

What we learned

Privacy needs to be built into the data the server returns, not just the information hidden in the interface.

AI is most useful for handling messy inputs and making interactions feel natural. Financial calculations are better handled by deterministic, tested code.

Structured output and a strict schema made Gemini

projects.title: Eyes Wise Open
projects.tagline: Work hard. Blink more. Work better.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Around 30% of the UK struggles with dry eye disease, and it is especially prevalent amongst office workers or people who spend a lot of their time looking at screens. A lot of people also don't know about it, or that they might be facing it as well! Amongst this demographic was us: STEM university students. Two of us have struggled with dry eyes. It is seriously exacerbated by the reduction in blinking that happens when we work on our computers all day and causes headaches, exhaustion, and burnout. And having to take breaks every 10-20 minutes when we were very busy was a challenge! So, we built Eyes Wise Open to make us blink more so that we can take fewer breaks and feel better and healthier.

What it does

Eyes Wise Open tracks the user's blinks to calculate their blinking rate. It can be used for a few minutes every day to track how blinking rate changes over time (so the progression of dry eyes over a month or year) or for a single longer session. In a single extended session, notifications will pop up over reasonable intervals to let the user know if their blinking rate is too low and if they need to blink more. Eyes Wise open also tracks whether a blink is incomplete (another symptom of dry eyes) and informs the user of this.

Individuals can also use Eyes Wise Open to view graphs of the change in their blinking rate over all of their sessions and compare it to the healthy levels (based on reviewed scientific papers and surveys) or compare a single one of their sessions to an average healthy level. Companies can use Eyes Wise Open to look at the dry eye progression of their employees (with their consent) and get suggestions on what future steps might look like.

How we built it

We shared the tasks and ideas between us and built the product with Claude Code in VS Code. Rebecca and Manavi are beginner developers, and this is their first hackathon. Shahida has more experience, so she guided them through the stages of a hackathon: scoping the idea, getting one working loop first, deploying early, then adding extras. Feedback from a Wise mentor changed our direction, from a break reminder to a one-time company eye health check.

The check.
The front end is React, Vite and TypeScript. MediaPipe Face Landmarker runs in the browser, with its model files hosted by us, and counts blinks and flags partial ones. Each person calibrates first, and the app warns about low light or a lost face instead of guessing. Video is never recorded or uploaded. Only anonymous numbers leave the browser.

The employer side.
People can choose to share an anonymous result. A small Express server stores these, and a manager view at /manager shows the team picture. A rule-based team agent (plain code, no model) gives its call on the team, its confidence and a recommended action for the priority the employer picks. It updates when new responses come in, when the priority changes, or when the employer corrects an assumption, and it shows what changed and why.

Evidence.
Our reference blink ranges come from the American Academy of Ophthalmology and published studies, and we flag where published figures differ.

Sponsor tools

Gemini API (gemini-3.5-flash-lite):
writes the short result summary and an opt-in trend explanation from anonymous numbers only. Each is labelled as written by Gemini or by a template.

Vultr:
hosts the live site at eyeswiseopen.health, behind Caddy for HTTPS, with a GitHub Actions workflow that redeploys on every push.

incident.io (Adaptable Agents):
the team agent summary / suggestions.

AI use.
Claude Code (Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5) wrote the first drafts of the code and ran builds. Google AI Studio only created the Gemini key. Every task is logged in AI_DISCLOSURE.md. [Add one sentence on what you changed or decided yourselves.]

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges we had was narrowing down the design of our exact product. Our focus remained on dry eyes throughout, but we contemplated building the product to automate the entirety of the DSE compliance process to make it more effective and actually look after employee health year round. However, the many components of DSE processes range from posture to fire safety and training required many features, and we ended up losing our focus in the haze. We lost track of who our product was intended for and how exactly it would work. If asked to describe our product in a single sentence, we wouldn't be able to. However, after discussions with Wise mentors and others around, we realised that our automation would not be a very effective solution unless built in collaboration with the specific company and decided to focus on the major issue of dry eyes specifically. Fortunately, we had enough time to build a much more coherent product that specialises on dry eyes and produces more comprehensive, understandable, and usable results!

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're very proud of all the extensions we have integrated into the product. Eyes Wise Open uses Google Gemini API to produce simple explanations to help the user understand the product. We're very happy with it because while Eyes Wise Open can definitely be used by companies to help improve worker productivity and health, the Gemini-based explanations can help a user sort through all the overwhelming information that comes with learning about any health-related issue. The explanations do not provide any medical advice, making them safer, and can help the individual user (maybe a university student, like us!) understand their specific results.

Another extension we're very happy with is the Google product we used for our blink tracker, because it gives very accurate blink count rates and incomplete blink rate percentages. The product we used was MediaPipe Tasks Vision (FaceLandmarker), and we're happy with how seamlessly and bug-free it has been integrated into our product (per our testing!).

What we learned

We learnt to focus on one use case rather than scope. We changed our project trajectory mid-hakathon to focus on the dry eye issue rather than automating the DSE assements, this meant that our product will be suited for a wider audience from companies, individual workers seeking to imporove their eye health to university students. We also learnt to accomodate for edge cases such as poor lighting, users switching to websites mid-session or being in a call.

What's next for Eyes Wise Open

There are many opportunities to extend our work such as providing more personalised helath tips by incooperating local weather data (pollen for allergies) and travel plans such as flights. We also hope to help companies automate DSE check such as doing realtime posture and screen distance checks. Another feature we hope to add is a personalised chat bot that helps provide holistic, year-round eye care and also educational material on general eye health (such as complete vs incomplete blink, eye hygiene, how to manage stress and fatigue).

projects.title: SavourIt
projects.tagline: Turn your Groceries into Meals, not Waste. An AI powered smart fridge that tracks food freshness, prioritises ingredients before they expire and suggests personalised recepies to reduce food wastage.
projects.description:
Inspiration

When I moved to university and started living away from home for the first time, I suddenly had to figure out what to eat every single day. Between lectures, assignments, part-time jobs and grocery shopping, cooking for myself was a bigger challenge than I expected.

I've often bought vegetables with plans to cook something healthy, only to find them spoiled at the back of the fridge a week later. And as a student on a budget, throwing away food also means throwing away money.

That's how the idea for SavourIt started. I wanted to make one small part of independent student life easier:
figuring out what to cook with the food I already have, before it goes to waste.

What it does

SavourIt is a smart pantry that helps students keep track of groceries and decide what to cook.

Scan:
Take a picture of a grocery item and let Gemini identify it.

Track:
Keep your groceries, quantities and expiry dates in one place.

Cook:
Get recipe suggestions based on what's actually in your fridge, your dietary preferences and how much time you have.

Save:
Prioritise ingredients nearing expiry instead of letting them go to waste.

The goal is simple: less time wondering what to eat and less food ending up in the bin.

How we built it

We built SavourIt using
HTML, CSS and JavaScript
for the frontend and
Python with FastAPI
for the backend.

We integrated
Google Gemini
for grocery image recognition and AI-powered recipe generation, and
TigerData (PostgreSQL)
to store and retrieve pantry inventory.

The interesting part was connecting everything together, so that recipe suggestions aren't just random AI-generated meals but are based on the ingredients users actually have.

We also prepared a Docker-based deployment setup for Vultr.

Challenges we ran into

With two team members coming from non-CS backgrounds, one of our first challenges was figuring out how to bring our different skills together and learn unfamiliar technologies quickly.

On the technical side, getting all the pieces to communicate properly was harder than expected. At one point, our recipe feature was showing hardcoded suggestions instead of using groceries stored in TigerData. Tracking down and fixing that took more debugging than we expected!

We also ran into Gemini API reliability issues and had to handle failed requests without breaking the cooking experience.

And of course, building everything in 24 hours meant constantly deciding what to prioritise and what to leave for future integration.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're proud that we managed to turn a problem we personally relate to into a functioning prototype. We connected a real database, built an AI-assisted grocery scanning flow and made meal suggestions work with actual pantry data and cooking-time constraints.

We built something we'd genuinely want to use ourselves.

What we learned

We learned how to break a big idea into smaller tasks, debug problems together and make decisions under a tight deadline. We also realised that getting an AI model to generate an answer is relatively simple and quick but making sure the data flows correctly, handling errors and creating an interface that's easy to use are just as important.

Working with Gemini, TigerData and FastAPI also gave us a much better understanding of how different services come together in a full-stack application.

One of our biggest takeaways was that
a simple idea, executed well, can be more valuable than lots of complicated features.

What's next for SavourIt

Technically, we'd love to integrate ElevenLabs for a voice-powered cooking assistant that guides users through recipes hands-free, and deploy SavourIt to the cloud using Vultr so anyone can access it.

We also plan to add expiry notifications and a dashboard showing how much food and money users have saved.

Ultimately, we want SavourIt to make eating well, saving money and reducing food waste a natural part of student life.

projects.title: Wise LifeSwitch
projects.tagline: When you move abroad, you carry two things that don't fit in a suitcase: your payments and your people. LifeSwitch carries both for you.
projects.description:
Moving abroad is complicated enough. Managing money & family across borders shouldn't be.

When you move abroad, you carry two things that don't fit in a suitcase: your payments and your people. LifeSwitch carries both for you.

Inspiration

We have friends who are international students, and one of our teammates made the move from India to London. We saw how offer letters, tenancy agreements and fee invoices arrive together, each hiding different amounts, currencies and deadlines creates a friction. We were inspired to fix it!

The stress doesn't stop with the student. Families back home often help manage large payments without being familiar with the destination country's banking system or payment instructions.

The problem is real. In a
2021 Flywire survey
of 1,010 students, 72% said tuition payments were a significant source of stress, and 28% cited unclear processes from their institution.

We were also struck by a
Mastercard feature produced with the Financial Times
, which described parents having to pay a £60,000 tuition bill from their savings, using instructions in a language they did not speak.

This led us to one insight:
paying for a move abroad is both a financial challenge and a family challenge, but these are usually handled separately.

We built Wise LifeSwitch to bring them together.

What is Wise LifeSwitch?

LifeSwitch is a mobile-first & web platform that helps international students organise relocation payments, understand unfamiliar paperwork and keep their families informed.

Instead of switching between documents, calendars, banking apps and family chats, students can manage their move through one connected journey.

What you can do

1. Organise your move
Set up where you're moving from and to, and why, then view upcoming payments and deadlines on a single roadmap.

2. Turn paperwork into a payment plan
Upload an offer letter, tenancy agreement or invoice. Gemini extracts payment details such as the payee, amount, currency, due date and reference, alongside the original sentence for verification. You review the results before using them.

3. Understand what you're paying for
Get plain-language explanations of unfamiliar terms such as CAS, guarantor, IBAN and sort code, with multilingual support.

4. Prepare payments more safely
LifeSwitch prepares a guided payment journey around Wise. Scam Shield applies rules to flag suspicious messages, including requests to use new bank details. Payments in the current demo are mocked; no real Wise transfers are sent.

5. Keep family in the loop
The LifeSwitch Circle gives families a private space for chat, milestones such as "Landed in London" and city-level location sharing. Sharing is optional and can be paused.

6. Share everyday costs
Group Split turns receipt information into suggested shares, helping groups work out who owes what. The demo uses Stripe test mode for its payment flow.

7. Support someone you care about
The Care Card supports a daily spending limit and alerts for gambling, large cash withdrawals and doorstep sales, set up together with the cardholder, with every change visible to them.

8. Never miss a deadline
Get reminders before every due date, with one tap to the payment.

LifeSwitch also includes multilingual interfaces and voice support to make the experience more accessible.

See it in action

Meet Tara, moving from Chennai to London to study Computer Science.

She starts by setting up her move and uploading her tuition invoice. LifeSwitch extracts the payment details and shows where they came from. She checks the information, reviews her roadmap and prepares the tuition deposit.

Later, a message asks her to send the deposit to new bank details. Scam Shield flags the suspicious request for review. Once Tara has verified the payment information, she can proceed through the demo payment flow. Her family can follow her milestones in the Circle without needing to manage every step themselves.

The goal is simple: help students stay in control of their money without leaving their families out of the journey.

How we built it

Frontend:
Next.js and TypeScript, with a responsive, mobile-first interface.

Document and message analysis:
Gemini returns structured information from documents, receipts and suspicious messages.

Data storage:
Postgres, using Tiger Data for Circle and Group Split data.

Payments:
Wise transfers are mocked behind a dedicated payment service. Stripe test mode supports the Group Split demo.

Voice:
ElevenLabs supports multilingual voice functionality.

Safety:
Scam Shield and Care Card checks use explicit rules, making their warnings easier to explain.

We designed the main experience around one connected flow:

Document → Roadmap → Payment → Family Circle

Every extracted payment detail can be checked against its source, and the demo does not automatically send money.

How we used AI

Gemini powers document, receipt and message analysis inside the product. Users review extracted information before acting on it.

We used Claude and Claude Code to explore designs and generate the framework for our application from our mock-ups and instructions. Team members directed changes, integrated features, tested flows and made implementation decisions.

Our AI usage disclosure is available in
AI_USAGE.md
.

Challenges we faced

Bringing separate problems into one product.
We had to narrow several ideas into one coherent journey connecting relocation paperwork, payments and family communication.

Collaborating across branches.
We divided ownership by user flow, developed features on separate branches and integrated them into the main application.

Building for trust.
Financial mistakes and unnecessary family monitoring were concerns from the beginning. We used source references, payment confirmation and optional sharing to keep users in control.

Working with different experience levels.
Clear feature ownership helped the team contribute and gave each member a part of the product to demonstrate.

What we learnt

A useful financial product needs more than automation. It needs to make information understandable, show users where important details came from and let them decide what happens next.

We also learnt how to combine different skills, integrate AI into a working application and collaborate under hackathon time constraints.

What's next?

Our next step is to integrate the Wise API for real transfers, subject to the necessary access and safeguards. We also want to explore Wise eSIM integration, broader multilingual voice guidance and support for relocating professionals and expats. Making sure its accessible for everyone at MAX EASE.

projects.title: PayProoof
projects.tagline: Before you make a payment, know how much it will actually cost.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Scams are becoming more common these days, with so many suspicious messages and fake payment requests going around, it's not always easy to tell what's real and what's a scam. For international students and travellers, the friction of transferring money is high, but the anxiety of getting scammed or losing money to hidden exchange rate markups is even higher.

Wise’s mission is all about removing friction and bringing transparency to money. We were inspired to build PayProoof which is a tool to check whether the transaction is a scam or compares rate from different banks within a few seconds. You just need to paste the message or upload the screenshot, and PayProoof will provide clear and instant answer.

What it does

PayProoof is a friction removal tool that checks a payment before you make it. Users can send a message, upload picture and compare currency exchange rates by inserting the values.

The app has four core modes:

Scam Check: Flags high-pressure language, fake landlord requests, and "bank details changed" scams using AI.

Rate Check: Calculates exactly how much money you lose when a provider offers a bad exchange rate.

Convert: Calculates live mid-market conversions.

Auto: Detects what the user is asking for automatically.

How we built it

We built PayProoof as a lightweight, responsive web app:

Frontend: Vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript for fast loading, with CSS variables for theme switching and font scaling.

Backend & AI: An LLM connected through a secure backend for OCR and natural language understanding.

APIs: Frankfurter API to fetch European Central Bank reference exchange rates.

Security: A backend proxy keeps our AI API keys hidden from users.

Challenges we ran into

-AI Hallucinations: Since AI isn't always reliable with numbers, we use it to extract structured JSON data, while JavaScript fetches exchange rates and handles calculations for accurate results.
-API Failures: We built a fallback system using regex-based local. Analyse to detect common scam phrases and currencies when the AI API is unavailable.
-Accessibility: We used CSS clip-path to create distinct shapes and textures for Safe, Caution and Danger alerts, making them easier to recognize without relying on colour alone.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

-Verdict Cards: We designed receipt-style result cards to make financial information easier to read and understand.
-Fallback System: Our app can still handle currency conversions and basic scam checks even when the AI API is unavailable.
-Accessibility: We added text-to-speech and high-contrast mode to make our website easier for everyone to use.

What we learned

We learned that building reliable AI products means knowing when to use AI and when to rely on traditional code. AI helps us understand user input, while code ensures accurate calculations and reliable results.

Accessibility is a design constraint, we make sure that our website is easy for everyone to use, including people with visual impairments.

We realized that making financial services easier isn't just about saving time. More importantly, it's about helping users feel safe and confident when managing their money.

What's next for PayProoof

Browser Extension: Develop a Chrome/Safari extension that automatically scans websites, such as rental listings, and flags potential scams before users interact with them.

Wise API Integration: Integrate the Wise API to let users make transfers directly through our app after checking exchange rates, with secure payment authorization.

Community Scam Reporting: Build a crowdsourced database where users can report suspicious phone numbers and bank accounts to help others avoid scams.

projects.title: Streetwise
projects.tagline: Streetwise links your trip plan, your savings jar, and the price in front of you, so one photo tells you not just what something costs, but whether you can afford it.
projects.description:
Inspiration

This summer, we took our first trip without our parents: a girls’ trip to Greece. We were thrilled, and completely unprepared financially. With no idea how to budget, we built a spreadsheet of predicted costs and tried to track our savings in our heads. Without a concrete plan, we kept dipping into our savings whenever a restaurant or souvenir shop caught our eye. Even a spontaneous museum visit meant checking our bank balances on patchy signals, which made the holiday more stressful than it needed to be.
When we read the brief, “make it easy to do more, in more places, with less effort,” that spreadsheet was the first thing we thought of. Wise’s travel hub already offers live exchange rates and holiday advice, but nothing helps travellers get to the trip financially. Banking apps have introduced “pots” for general saving, so we asked: what if Wise had a pot that knew what your holiday would actually cost, so you can enjoy the trip without worrying about it?

What it does

Streetwise turns “I want to go on holiday” into a savings plan you can actually follow.
Start your plan. Choose to create your own budget or get a Wise-recommended budget based on your trip, e.g. 4 days in Lisbon for 2 people, filtered by price range.
Build it out. Add the expenses you already know about: flights, accommodation, activities.
Save automatically. Streetwise generates a weekly savings commitment and sends it to a Wise Jar, so the money is set aside before you travel.

How we built it

We built Streetwise as a web app using HTML, styled to match Wise’s design language to blend seamlessly. We “vibe coded” with Claude: we described features in plain English and iterated on what it generated.
Our work: the problem research, the user flow and wireframes, all feature decisions, testing, and the Wise-style design direction.
AI-assisted: code generation and refinement of each prototype.
Every iteration of the app is in our GitHub, with notes explaining why each feature changed.

Challenges we ran into

We spent longer than planned on ideation, so we had to choose: code it ourselves and ship something unfinished, or vibe code and ship something that matched our vision. We chose the latter, then learned to write sharper prompts to get the results we wanted.
Our bigger challenge was scope. We wanted an “on trip” feature that lets you log spending and adjusts your remaining daily budget. After feedback from the Wise sponsors, we realised the plan was trying to do too much, so we cut it back to do one thing well. We felt that having too many features on an extension can be overwhelming and offputting for users, so focused on simplicity and functionality. We made cutbacks and focused on one main issue, budgeting in advance.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We found a real gap in Wise’s travel hub, based on our own holiday experiences and matched Wise’s look so feel so Streetwise feels native. Through acting on sponsor feedback by simplifying the app we changed “travel style” to “price range” to remove confusion and decreased the number of functions to ensure easy navigation and a seamless flow. We went from zero to prototype and learnt to prompt effectively and iterate quickly whilst combining our three different skill sets into one cohesive project. We managed to use GitHub effortlessly and run into no issues whilst using it.

What we learned

Two of us come from life science backgrounds with little coding experience, so this weekend was a steep climb. Under Manya’s guidance (she studies computer science), we learned how to use GitHub, including pull requests and publishing to a repository, and how to write and refine prompts to steer Claude toward what we wanted. The biggest lesson: good prompting is really good product thinking. The clearer we were about the user’s problem, the better the output.

What's next for Streetwise

Our next steps are live adjustment  by introducing an “on trip” mode. This allows users to log spending during the trip and watch your daily budget update automatically. We would also like to introduce a deeper Wise Jar integration by connecting savings plans directly to jars so contributions are automatic as well as smarter recommendations to include more destinations, trip lengths, price ranges and currencies.
We deliberately saved the live feature for later. Our sponsor feedback was to pick one thing and do it well, so we focused on the planner.

projects.title: IdkUp2U
projects.tagline: A little time together goes a long wayFind a time for whoever's in.Keep your calendar personal, compare availability with any friends, and make a plan together.
projects.description:
Inspiration

IdkUp2U was inspired by a group of King's students in their respective final years, but their final years differ because some of them did a placement year! As a result, planning any hangouts is extremely difficult with their differing schedules. We wanted to make it easy to find a time when everyone was free, which is why we created this very useful web application.

What it does

Our project is made up of several components, which will be explained below:

1) Your Calendar

A view just for you! You can import an existing .ics file, and add 'busy' periods of time for that week. Easy to keep up to date, so hangout times are as accurate as possible.

2) Group Availability

A view for you AND your friends! A weekly view showing everyone's availability with a number (i.e. how many of you are free on that day/time). You can toggle each person on/off if you don't want to see their availability.

3) Propose A Hangout

A section to create a hangout proposal. After selecting the friends you want to invite, let Gemini API take care of the rest! It will suggest a time and a place to meet. Then, after submitting, the RSVP gets sent straight to your friends. Your friends are able to add input to Gemini, stating the issues they have with the time/place, and Gemini will intelligently adapt to their needs, changing anything that needs to be changed.

4) Group Invitations

A section where you can see proposals that have already been sent, and you can RSVP yes/no and give suggestions to the AI on what to change. It will then regenerate the location/time for you to review.

How we built it

We built IdkUp2U in one day as a team of three, using TypeScript and Next.js so that the frontend and backend shared a single codebase. Before writing any features, we agreed on the shared data shapes (users, busy blocks, proposals, beliefs and agent steps), so each of us could work in parallel. The frontend, built with Tailwind CSS, started on mock data and typed fixtures and was swapped over to the real backend later. We used Gemini API: it uses function calling to pick tools such as free-slot lookup, RSVP history and belief updates, then returns structured JSON that the UI displays. We kept the date and free-slot maths in plain code, so Gemini handles only the messy human input, how much to trust each calendar, and explaining its changes. Calendar data, RSVP events and every belief revision are stored in Tiger Data, a time-series Postgres database, and the app is deployed with Vultr.

Challenges we ran into

We ran into an issue with SSL certificate verification when connecting our Next.js backend to Tiger Data’s PostgreSQL database. Despite following the documentation, testing different connection configurations, and restarting the database service, we continued receiving a SELF_SIGNED_CERT_IN_CHAIN error. Due to the time constraints of the hackathon, we temporarily disabled certificate verification to unblock development but we recognise that a trusted certificate would be needed for a secure production deployment in the future. Relying on the Gemini API during a one-day hackathon meant living with limits we couldn’t control. At peak times the API was overloaded and returned “model busy” errors, which stalled the agent loop in the middle of a run. We also ran out of free-tier tokens and credits while testing, so we had to switch to a different model partway through the build.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

In a single day, we built an AI agent that does more than schedule: it states what it assumed, notices when new evidence proves it wrong, and explains how it changed its mind. We’re proud that this revision is visible. As three students building a tool for a problem we’ve all had in first term, we got the frontend, agent and backend working together by agreeing on a shared contract early.

What we learned

We learned that the hard part of building an agent is not the API call but deciding where it adds real value. Working in parallel taught us to agree on data shapes before writing features, to build the UI against mock data so nobody is blocked, and to commit often.

What's next for IdkUp2U

We would want to add login functionality - unfortunately we didn't have the time to implement it fully, and had to rely on seeded data. Longer term, we’d weather suggestions so that outdoor activities aren't suggested when its forecast to rain for example, so IdkUp2U can help new students not only find a time to meet but also decide what to do.

projects.title: Almanac
projects.tagline: Too much to do? Almanac schedules tasks around your calendar and preferences, adding new ones as you finish and rescheduling unfinished tasks so nothing gets forgotten.
projects.description:
Inspiration

What it does

Almanac
does not just store tasks, it schedules your every day life.

While our team was discussing problems that we face as students, one common aspect came to mind: organisation. We all have very chaotic calendars; if we do not complete a task, we have to reschedule it, and it piles up alongside new assignments. We also have to manually plan, rearrange and categorise tasks via colour codes, which can be very overwhelming.

Our solution is Almanac: a resource where you can connect your Google calendar and a to-do list (Task Manager) to the website. For the latter, users submit their personal preferences: a name for a task, a time-frame and options to reschedule it. When a task is completed, Almanac schedules the next priority. If a task is not completed, it is automatically rescheduled.

We built our software by having the front-end using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, which provided the presentation for our user interface. At the back-end, we have the Python Flask framework.

Initial Ideation

As a group, we brainstormed ideas based on issues many university students like us face on a regular basis. We considered the possible problems a student may face due to the difficulty of factors such as planning their assignments, mealtimes, and meeting friends with similar interests. Eventually, we decided to create a calendar that connects to a student’s Google Calendar, permits a student to add their own tasks to it, and orders said tasks based on priority, length, and time frame. We chose this idea as it reduces the time, stress, and effort required by students to schedule their time efficiently. We also believed it was the solution that appeared most simple and relatable to the greatest number of students: this makes it easy to use, giving students an air of familiarity despite using a new app altogether.

Challenges we ran into

Over the course of the IKU Women in Stem hackathon, we faced numerous challenges that took hours for us to solve. A few examples of these included setting up the server, configuring the Google API to work correctly, and dealing with numerous domain crashes.

Accomplishments that we are proud of

Building a working web application
Creating a registration system that stores all key inputs and outputs
Creating a working demo ready prototype

Skills we learnt

We learnt as a team *
3 key skills: *
Time management, Patience and Resilience. To structure our time we spent our first hour planning an hour by hour itinerary. This ensured that we all stuck to our goals but stayed on time. As well as that we added buffers. We included clear checkpoints with measurable goals to get a sense of achievement and decomposed our problem into manageable chunks.

We learnt patience when we were all getting tired and slow from staying up for the whole hackathon and to discuss with each other our ideas best.

We learnt resilience when we made mistakes to bounce back from them and also to ask our team mates.

Wise track

Almanac removes the stress out of planning by navigating our busy everyday lives. Our solution purposefully looks as similar as possible to everyday calendars and todo lists to ensure that it is fully able to meet the requirements. In later developments we want to make our software even more accessible by having an inbuilt read out loud button instead of if the user wishes to use on they have to download one externally.

Tiger Data track

When a user registers on our web page, their information is saved in Tiger Data. We created a hashing algorithm for user ID: when they log in, we can easily query the database for their information. We decided to use Tiger Data because it can store our data without deletion if we were to store it locally, for example on a local JSON file.

Beginner hackers track

This hackathon project enhanced our critical thinking skills, as we had to consider our target audience (university students), put ourselves in their shoes and analyse which one of our ideas would benefit university students the most: an easily understandable solution to a common issue. We also improved our knowledge of programming by learning how to utilise GitHub to collaborate with others, as well as programming a website targeted towards the rest of the student body. This also improved our debugging and problem-solving skills, as we ran into many obstacles along the way, such as figuring out how to get the Google API to work properly, as well as domain crashes occurring at the last minute. While designing the website, we considered easily memorisable features and aesthetics, in order to make the experience of documenting tasks and going through a calendar as quick and stress-free as possible.

Best domain name track

We researched words with correlations to terms such as “schedule” and “calendar”, considering the importance of etymology and significant meaning behind the domain name, as well as ensuring it is easy to memorise and pronounce by as many students as possible. We eventually decided on “Almanac”, a term derived from Spanish, Portuguese and Arabic, and defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as “a book published every year that includes information for that year such as important days, times of the sun rising and going down, or changes in the moon”. With the decline of physical documentation of events, school notes and other important information, we wanted our domain name to pay homage to a type of book used since archaic eras, and preserve this. Our website is called “www.almanac.luxe” as the art of scheduling one’s time efficiently is elegant and classy, and in a way luxurious.

What's next for Almanac

Our next steps would be to implement the following features:
Add a voice feature with daily summaries
Algorithm to anticipate schedule issues
Syncing schedules with multiple other users of the website, so as to be able to arrange and co-ordinate events such as group projects and meetups with friends.

projects.title: AreaMD
projects.tagline: Because where you live is part of your health.
projects.description:
Inspiration

A GP has minutes. In that time they ask about symptoms, history and lifestyle. They almost never see the air you breathe on your commute, the damp in your flat, or how different your last neighbourhood was from your current one. It isn't that nobody cares. The data is public, but it sits across a dozen sites in formats no one has time to decode mid-appointment.

We asked: what if the environment showed up in the consultation as naturally as blood pressure does?

What it does

AreaMD turns a London postcode into a one-page environmental briefing for the doctor. 
Take Susan, our fictional patient: 34, asthma since childhood, a non-smoker who lives in Marylebone and works near Luton Airport. Her symptoms have been worse for six weeks, and she says they feel worse on workdays. Her history can't answer whether her home or workplace area deserves a closer look, however, AreaMD can.

The doctor enters where the patient lives and works, and AreaMD shows both places side by side with:

Air quality
from the London Air Quality Network

Water observations
from the Environment Agency Water Quality Archive

Flood context
from the Planning Data platform

A short plain-language summary
of the key points

Data limitations
, so the doctor knows what the readings can and can't say, for example that they come from nearby monitoring sites, not exact addresses

Local news sources and source details

Every card names its source. The report is observed area context for clinical review- It does not diagnose, and it describes the area, not the patient's personal exposure.

How we built it

Written in Python, running on a Flask server and using Tiger Data to store doctor and patient details.

Fetched data about various environmental factors using government data sources and other reliable sources e.g. London Air Quality Network.

Transformed the data into a structured format, to generate a risk profile from.

The evidence collected is passed to the Gemini API to generate a summary both from the structured data from the water, air and planning datasets, but also from a free news API and Google RSS feeds if environmental articles relevant to the patient's home or work are found.

Challenges we ran into

Validating data from the various data sources, making sure they reliably return relevant information for the reports was time consuming.

Limited data for certain environment factors.

We initially intended to have the Gemini API search for relevant news in the area but ran into a block as we were using the free tier which does not allow this. Worked around this by using a free news API to fetch relevant articles for a patient.

The API used for news did not reliably return articles, therefore we connected a Google RSS feed to fetch articles. We had to be careful to make sure that only relevant, reliable articles were used to generate the summary as using the more general RSS feed meant that any article could potentially be used regardless of the quality or reputation of the source.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Integrating multiple different sources to create a report, using guardrails to make sure that only relevant information is used and Gemini does not attempt to diagnose or make any comment on the patient's health.

A working report that shows a patient's home and workplace side by side, with the source of every card shown

Turning separate public datasets into plain language a GP can read in seconds

A design that keeps the doctor in control: area context for review, not a diagnosis

First ever hackathon, built in 24 hours

What we learned

Validating data is most of the work because fetching public data was the easy part. Making sure each source reliably returned something relevant for a given postcode took far longer.

Some environmental factors have little data, readings come from nearby monitors, and flood coverage varies by area, so showing those limits in our tool and being honest about what it can't tell us creates more trust than hiding them.

We learned that useful health tech comes from restraint: a few relevant signals, plain explanations and visible limitations work best.

What's next for AreaMD

More environmental factors:
building age, green space, so the report covers more of what GPs ask about.

More clinical focus areas.
consider the patient's health conditions to look more specifically for news and factors that may affect them, e.g. for an asthma patient, looking more deeply for particular evidence of smog, pollution, construction work.

Testing with real GPs.
We believe this could save time and improve history-taking, but we haven't shown it yet. Ideally we would integrate our tool with the current NHS tools, so patient details can be imported and don't need to be entered multiple times in an appointment.

projects.title: Ding
projects.tagline: Ding is designed by women, for women, to be the best safe route planner. Getting you from location A to location B
projects.description:
Our Inspiration:

Last year 4,593 VAWG offences were recorded across the transport network, only around 3% resulted in a charge or summons, while around 58% of cases identified no suspect. [Source: Written evidence submitted to the Police and Crime Committee by British Transport Police.] Unfortunately, this is also only the recorded number of offences. From our own personal experiences as women, safety when travelling is something we always have to take into consideration. Whether we are travelling back from a night out or going home after a late lecture, it's not ideal when Google Maps identifies the best or quickest route and it includes walking through a dark alleyway. As students we also frequently have to weigh up the cost, time and safety every single time you travel which takes up time.

What it does:

Our project is an app that calculates the safest route from location A to location B where our target audience is women. There will be 2 main categories: safety and travel time. The user can enter in safe areas which will be stored on Vultr and as local storage. Although we are not able to include every single one, we have considered several factors to determine the safest route. By weighing these factors, sourcing the public data and combining these factors we get a safety ranking of different possible routes. The user can then choose which route to take, avoiding any pubs or clubs indicated by a tiny flashing light on the map. As of right now, we are focusing on London only and walking routes for the hackathon.

How we built it:

We developed
Ding
, a walking safety navigation app by first designing an intuitive user interface and implementing user authentication. We integrated mapping and routing APIs, including Google Maps, Google Routes and OpenRouteService to generate walking routes between locations. We then built a database to store safety-related features, their weightings and route information. Using this data, we developed a scoring algorithm to evaluate routes based on safety factors such as crime, street lighting and nearby open businesses. Our rerouting algorithm identifies sections that fall below a minimum safety threshold and generates alternative routes to avoid them. Finally, we implemented route comparison, colour-coded safety ratings, live navigation and rerouting functionality to help users choose routes that balance safety and journey time.

The challenges we ran into:

One of our biggest challenges was developing a way to quantify walking safety as it's subjective and depends on several different factors. We also had to integrate multiple APIs, manage incomplete or inconsistent location data and balance route safety against journey time. [Designing an algorithm that could identify lower-scoring sections and generate alternative routes without creating excessively long detours was particularly challenging.]

Accomplishments that we're proud of:

Ding addresses an extremely common problem that women face, particularly when walking alone. A key achievement was developing a transparent, data-driven safety scoring system that considers crime, street lighting and nearby open businesses. We're also proud of our approach to rerouting which prioritises avoiding potentially concerning sections.

What we learned

This project taught us how to integrate mapping APIs, work with geospatial data and develop algorithms that balance multiple competing factors. [We gained experience with databases, user authentication and route optimisation while learning how important it is to account for missing data and the limitations of safety predictions.]

What's next for Ding!

Our next step is to develop Ding into a fully functional mobile app that also takes into account public transport and expand our coverage beyond London. We also hope to improve our safety scoring model using more comprehensive data and user feedback, introduce real-time safety updates and further develop personalised routing based on individual preferences. Ultimately, we want to make travelling feel safer and easy to access.

projects.title: Tripezium
projects.tagline: Twenty tabs and no idea what it costs? Tripezium turns your saved TikToks into a day-by-day itinerary, costed in local and home currency, and re-plans by chat when holidays or plans change.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Planning a trip usually means twenty open tabs, a camera roll full of TikTok screenshots, and no real idea what any of it will cost, especially when you're spending in a different currency. While planning a trip to Japan, we found ourselves struggling to research each and every place we come across on TikTok, co-ordinating travel, cost, and timings. We wanted a planner that would catch this, fix it, and ensure places are open and public holidays are accounted for before we left. Reducing friction in holiday planning is our priority.

Foreign currency is also where most people first meet hidden fees and confusing conversions, which is why we built the project around money as well as itineraries.

What it does

Tripezium turns the places you've saved online into a costed, multi-currency itinerary, and adapts when plans change.

Plan:
tell us the countries, cities and dates for each stop, then pick interests that make sense for that destination and season.

Import:
paste TikTok links or upload screenshots, and we extract the places automatically.

Itinerary:
get a day-by-day, mapped plan with every stop costed in local currency and in your home currency, plus a budget per day and per city and a running trip total.

Holiday-aware:
public holidays are checked for every country on your route. If a must-see lands on a closure day, the agent weighs the trade-off, moves or replaces it, and explains why. Kyoto on 1 January becomes a first shrine visit (hatsumōde) at Fushimi Inari.

Edit by chatting:
"cheaper dinner in Osaka", "swap day 2 and 3" or "we're arriving a day late". The agent re-plans everything that's affected (other days, budget, closures) and explains what changed.

Money prompts:
"load your card" reminders tell you roughly how much to convert and when, and overspend alerts suggest cheaper swaps.

How we built it

Back end:
Python with FastAPI and Pydantic, deployed on a Vultr Ubuntu VM with Caddy for HTTPS, at
api.tripezium.club
.

Database:
Tiger Data (PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB). Trips, places and suggested stops are relational tables, each itinerary is stored as one JSONB document, and exchange rates go into an
fx_rates
hypertable. It's also our cache for holidays, video imports and geocoding, so demo content survives redeploys.

Gemini:
generates itineraries as structured JSON against a fixed schema, reads videos, screenshots and captions to extract places (multimodal), and handles chat edits and re-planning.

Code, not the model, does the maths:
Gemini only estimates local costs per person. Currency conversion and every total are calculated in code with exact decimals, using Frankfurter (ECB) exchange rates with a hardcoded fallback.

Data sources:
Nager.Date for public holidays, Open-Meteo for forecasts and historical climate, Google Places for weekly opening hours, and Nominatim for geocoding.

Voice:
ElevenLabs speech-to-text and text-to-speech.

Map:
Leaflet with OpenStreetMap.

Challenges we ran into

Making an LLM's output reliable.
Itineraries are only useful if every item can be rendered, edited and costed, so we validate every response (exact trip dates, real place IDs, 24-hour times, ISO currency codes) and retry once with the problems listed.

Closures.
Holidays are only part of the story. After generation, a deterministic pass checks each stop against the holiday list and real opening hours, and anything risky goes back for a revision. When we can't be sure, the app says "check hours before going" rather than presenting a guess as fact.

Untrusted input.
Captions and imported text can contain instructions, so we pass them to Gemini in a clearly delimited block it's told never to obey, with delimiter text stripped first.

No TikTok API for saved folders.
Collections can't be read, so import works from pasted links (via oEmbed captions and thumbnails) and screenshots.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Solving a real problem we ran into ourselves, the difficulty of planning travels abroad.

A budget you can trust, because the AI estimates and our code does the arithmetic.

An agent that changes its priorities, not just individual items. When the user says "cut the budget by £200" or "we're arriving a day late", it drops conclusions that no longer hold and re-plans what depends on them.

A fully deployed system with fallbacks for rates, models and opening hours.

What we learned

Treating LLM output as structured data, validated by code, is what makes it usable in a real product.

Keep the model for judgement and creativity, and use deterministic code for anything that has to be exact, like money and dates.

Being honest about uncertainty, "check hours before going" builds more trust than confident but wrong answers.

What's next for Tripezium

Use the phone's location and time instead of the simulated trip clock.

Live opening-hours and closure checks with search grounding.

Real prices where available, instead of AI estimates.

More import sources, such as Instagram.

Shared trips with cost splitting and booking links.

A "Trips" feature inside Wise that tells you how much to convert and when, driving card spend and currency conversions.

projects.title: HerPath
projects.tagline: Healthcare shouldn't feel like a maze. Our main goal is educating women about their reproductive health and connecting them to professionals and spaces to support them.
projects.description:
What inspired us:

Many woman around the world struggle with reproductive health issues, such as PCOS and endometriosis. Especially, due to the stigma around menstruation and problems related to it, many woman do not feel comfortable speaking about or are told that it is "normal" and "just their hormones".  We wanted to build a warm and welcoming space to help these woman, with all of sorts of queries they may that they feel uncomfortable speaking about. HerPath is our website, which delivers information on everything to do with reproductive health for a woman and is place for them to find information for the treatments and on going research for these health issues to. However, our main goal and aim is to reduce the time it takes for woman to get professional and clinical help from someone. The NHS and GPs are already working overtime dealing with so many people at once that woman's struggling with menstruation problems gets overlooked or not prioritised enough, which is unfair to those having to deal with such unbearable pain and bleeding that they can continue with their normal routines. Meanwhile, private hospitals are not accessible for everyone and the costs sometimes cause the person not prioritise their own health. This is where 'HerPath' comes in: we want to build a platform that forms this connection between woman and practising gynaecologists, clinicians, pharmacists, who can provide medical advice and researchers and care navigators, who can help discuss and guide their concerns in the best direction or to the best clinician available. We plan to build our revenue through consultation commissions, employer partnerships, university partnerships, pharmacy and healthcare partnerships. We will also introduce a feature to locate the nearest pharmacy or public restroom that can provide free sanitary pads and tampon to woman in the are, who may need it. There will also be an option to text/voice note to the professional you're speaking too and there will be a multilingual services on our website so that woman all across the world in their respective regions.

What we learned:

We learnt how to implement APIs using Gemini API. We also learnt about how revenues work and the importance of critical thinking to evaluate our work properly, by questioning what is missing or what could go wrong with something and how we could correct it or implement a new idea to fix it. As 2 out of 3 members of our team are from none-computing backgrounds, we learnt the value of clear communication to understand the different technical aspects that are required to build a website such as using accurate AI prompts and frameworks like 'Streamlit' and APIs.

How we built our project and the challenges we faced:

We built the projects using Python, Streamlit, Gemini API and Claude for the techincal side, and Canva and ChatGPT for the design side. The main page provides the educational content, which was produced by ChatGPT, but double-checked line by line and cross-referenced with the NHS and other medical websites for accuracy.

Then the main service of the website, which is offer contact to specialised professionals is made up of the Professional Sign Up and Find a Professional pages. The professional sign up page was set up with a secret SQLite database to protect private information and contains a verification process to make sure that there's no misuse of the service.

The other service that our website provides is a map tab, where users can search for places that provide period products for free near them. Our demo only includes, a small area around KCL, which would be expanded, and there is a filtering tab for users to specify their needs and a Gemini API smart search tab for  filters to be applied according to the user's request.

One of the challenges we faced is formatting the website design from Canva to the actual website. It included all of the educational content and a sample pages of how our professional page set up will look like. We tried implement our design to the website it was cropping our information and due to the time constraints we were no able to accommodate everything in.

Our goal is similar to that of Wise, as we want to make managing money more transparent, accessible, and simpler to everyone.

This pushes us to think about the financial challenges that are faced by students and young adults, more specifically budgeting, splitting bills, managing shared expenses. We want to create something that brings those features together in one platform. That's how PennyWise works, a financial tool to help you spend smarter.

What it does

PennyWise is a financial management tool designed to help young adults to take charge of managing their money without juggling between apps. PennyWise has incorporated these features:

Budget tracker: record expenses, organize spendings, and understanding where your money goes 
Deals/rewards: discover discounts and cash back opportunities
Trip/goals: encourage users to plan and save ahead towards exciting experiences such as holidays 
Shared home: help organise shared household expenses such as rent, utility bills, and groceries 
Money owed: easier to keep track of money borrowed between friends

How we built it

We started by brainstorming ideas as a team, discussing the financial challenges faced as a young adult. We then narrowed down ideas to the features that would be the most useful and achievable in the hackathon's timeframe.

We began building our website via VS Code, where we generated and developed the initial code and website structure. Throughout the development process, we use GitHub Copilot to help us with coding and navigating the technical aspects of building the website. We use HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to build the interactive website.

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges we faced was that none of us had much experience in building a website or using AI tools to assist with coding. At the beginning, we were unsure of where to start or what the workflow would look like.

Learning how to navigate VS code and GitHub Copilot was a challenge itself but we quickly realised that we still needed to understand how different parts of the website worked together. However, we managed to approach this challenge as a team through trials and errors as well as researching solutions.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The accomplishment that we are proud of is that we managed to turn an idea into a functioning and interactive website with such limited prior experience. Another achievement was learning how to navigate VS code and GitHub copilot. Most importantly, we are proud of how we worked as a team, troubleshooting, researching, and tackling new challenges.

What we learned

We learned how to use AI tools to help us build a website with limited coding experience. We discovered that AI is at most useful when paired with human creativity and curiosity as well as teamwork. This experience has taught us that to persist through a challenge, we can turn ideas into reality.

What's next for PennyWise

Our next step is to turn PennyWise from a prototype into a fully functioning platform. Ultimately, we want to incorporate PennyWise into an everyday financial tool that helps everyone navigate their finances.

Inspiration

After brainstorming, we came up with The Hub, a web application for students that collates information from different sources together whether that be course information, assignment deadlines or society events into one platform to support students getting a comprehensive and simplified view of their university life and commitments.

From our first year, we typically found that we would have to search different platforms and webpages for different pieces of information. For example, EIE at Imperial uses Teams, Canvas, Panopto and Edstem to upload lecture recordings, submit courseworks/project work and discuss with coursemates. On top of that, society information was kept largely separate, with Instagram being the most reliable source to get any updates about events going on. This was not only very overwhelming, but it also felt that we would essentially play an endless game of catch up with something always being missed until the last minute. This is why we wanted to create an application that enables students to easily access and navigate through to identify any clashes in committments and the essentials they need to do well in their course.

What it does

The Hub is a student-focused web application designed to bring together all the information students usually have to track across different platforms in one place. It helps students view their course modules and assessment details, keep up with assignments and deadlines, explore society events and updates, and see everything in a single calendar so they can spot clashes and manage their commitments more easily. In short, it gives students a clearer, simpler overview of their academic and extracurricular life, reducing the stress of switching between multiple apps and websites.

How we built it

I (Irede) am currently working on a website that was built with Go so I thought it would be good to build the frontend using this language as it allows templates to be created and reused across multiple pages - which is a convenient way to avoid code duplication. Afterwards it was multiple prompting session between me and GitHub copilot to refine the styling (CSS), add different functionality (Javascript) and overall refinement. Zara was meanwhile working on the backend in Python to set up our database of fake users and then integrating the python and javascript functionality together to get a working website.

Challenges we ran into

Time and scale of what we wanted to achieve. It was a lot of work to complete between two people.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

I think we did manage to do and learn a lot over the past 24 hours. We were also very resilient until the end.

What we learned

a) No more working in the final hour of anything
b) Go is a pretty convenient language

What's next for The Hub

Mainly tweaking little things that we couldn't get to work in the hackathon - like implementing the Google API and then scaling it up to contain more universities and more courses.

projects.title: tempo
projects.tagline: app made for helping dyslexic people learn online
projects.description:
Inspiration

We wanted to build something that actually helps real people, not just a cool demo that gets forgotten after the hackathon. Reading online is genuinely hard for people with dyslexia and ADHD — dense walls of text, no pacing, no breathing room — and none of us felt like existing tools actually solved that well. So we picked that as our problem and just went for it.

What it does

Tempo is a Chrome extension that calms down any webpage and reveals text one sentence at a time instead of throwing a full wall of text at you. You read at your own pace and never lose your place. It also comes with dyslexia-focused accessibility features like adjustable fonts, spacing, and overlays so reading feels as comfortable as possible.

How we built it

We built it as a Chrome extension using JavaScript, HTML/CSS, and the Chrome Extension APIs, all inside the 12-hour window. We split up fast — Parth, Vihaan and Saad handled research, ideation and the script/pitch, while I focused on actually building the extension. No sleep, way too much caffeine, and a whiteboard covered in half-legible ideas by hour 3.

Challenges we ran into

Honestly the biggest headache was just getting the extension's permissions and API access working properly — we burned a good chunk of time fighting with an API key that kept failing silently with no useful error message, which in a 12-hour hackathon feels like losing an hour you'll never get back. On top of that, agreeing on scope as a team was its own challenge — we had way more ideas than hours, so a lot of the day was just ruthlessly cutting features so we'd actually have something working by the deadline.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Winning LeafHacks '26 outright, for one. But honestly just as proud that we went from a blank page to a working Chrome extension in 12 hours that does something real, not just a shiny prototype. We also worked properly as a team under pressure — nobody panicked, everyone just found their lane and got on with it, which made the whole day a lot smoother than it could've been.

What we learned

We learned how much a clear division of labour matters when time is that tight — the moment we stopped overlapping and just trusted each other's lane, we moved twice as fast. Also learned not to underestimate how much time "small" integration issues (like auth/API stuff) can eat into a hackathon timeline, so next time we'll stress-test that stuff earlier instead of assuming it'll just work.

What's next for Tempo

At the end of the day, the plan was simple: don't let this die as a one-off hackathon project. We wanted to keep building on it and actually turn it into something people could use for real.
