projects.title: Unravel
projects.tagline: One in five students opens a PDF and can't start. Not because it's hard, but because there's no entry point. Unravel lives on the page and pulls one thread at a time. Just understanding.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Open a dense PDF when you have ADHD and you don't hit "this is hard" — you hit a wall. Your brain won't even start. There's no first step, just a slab of text and that stuck feeling before you've begun. Tools like NotebookLM or ChatGPT don't fix this; they make you leave the page, copy, paste, screenshot, switch apps — and a distractible brain only has to slip once to give up. We wanted something that lives on the page you're already reading and pulls the tangle apart one thread at a time. Hence the name, and the ball-of-yarn logo.

What it does

Highlight any text on any page and a concept map opens in a side panel using progressive disclosure — you see only the core idea first, then tap to reveal one layer at a time, so you're never shown a wall of text again. It also works on PDFs and diagrams: since Chrome blocks extensions from its PDF viewer, we screenshot the tab and send the pixels to Gemini's vision, which is what lets it read the actual files students revise from. There's a coach chat that already has the whole page as context (no pasting), 30-second micro-quests with XP and confetti to make it stick, and an interactive sandbox where Gemini pulls the variables out of a formula so you can drag sliders and watch the graph move. Plus streaks, a dashboard, dyslexia-friendly font, reduced-motion, and light/dark.

How I built it

A Chrome extension built with WXT, React, TypeScript and Tailwind. A content script handles the highlight button, a background service worker talks to Gemini and manages state, and a side panel renders the map, quests, sandbox and coach. We use Gemini 2.5 Flash five different ways — text-to-concept-tree, vision-to-concept-tree, chat, quiz generation, and formula extraction — all with structured JSON output so responses are always parseable. Formulas are evaluated safely with mathjs, charts with Recharts.

Challenges I ran into

Chrome's PDF viewer sandbox was the big one — no extension can read text inside it, so we flipped the whole approach and used Gemini's multimodal vision instead. Getting the side panel to open reliably from an in-page click was fiddly because of Chrome's user-gesture rules, and we had to disable Gemini's "thinking" mode to get responses fast enough to feel instant.

Accomplishments that I'm proud of

What I learned

That accessibility isn't a feature you add at the end — for this audience it's the entire product. And that Gemini's vision was the unlock: it turned "we can't touch PDFs" into our single biggest advantage.

What's next for Unravel

Spaced repetition that resurfaces quests you struggled with, shareable maps for study groups, and teacher/SEN dashboards.

projects.title: Clarity
projects.tagline: Documents through a new lens.
projects.description:
What it does

Clarity is a web app that takes in documents (.pdf, .docx, .txt or pasted text) and Anki decks (.apkg) and converts them to make them more dyslexia friendly.
It offers two conversion pathways:
    Partial Transformation — keeps your words and changes typography, layout & formatting: increased letter/word/line spacing, left-align only, short line lengths (~66 characters) and a cream, low-glare background with dark navy text (WCAG-compliant contrast).
    Full Transformation — everything in the partial transformation, plus a rewritten clear content structure (active voice, consistent short sentences, inverted-pyramid ordering and scannable headings) using the Gemini API.
Documents can be read in an accessible in-browser reader or downloaded as a reformatted PDF. Anki decks are rebuilt as a new .apkg with dyslexia-friendly card styling.

How we built it

Frontend: Next.js (App Router, TypeScript)
Backend: Python + FastAPI
PDF extraction & generation: PyMuPDF
Anki processing: zipfile + sqlite3 (reading), genanki (rebuilding)
AI rewriting: google-genai (Gemini API)
Deployment: Vercel

Challenges we ran into

Getting the Anki libraries to run and converting out output into an anki file.
Uploads were crashing the web app, until we realised vercel has a 4.5mb cap.

projects.title: QuizzVerse
projects.tagline: AI-powered quiz platform: generate smart quizzes from any topic or document, compete in real-time multiplayer rooms, and master your mistakes with AI flashcards.
projects.description:
Inspiration

QuizzVerse was born from a simple frustration: studying is boring, and existing quiz tools are either static PDFs, behind paywalls, or require manual question writing.

As students, we've all experienced the same pain — spending hours making flashcards, searching for practice questions, or studying alone without any feedback. Traditional learning feels passive. You read, you memorize, but you never truly engage.

The idea hit during exam season. We were drowning in notes, PDFs, and textbooks, wishing there was a way to turn all that content into something interactive — something that felt less like cramming and more like a game. What if you could upload any document and instantly get a quiz? What if you could challenge your friends in real-time, turning study sessions into friendly competition? What if an AI could explain why you got something wrong?

That's when we discovered Groq Cloud's blazing-fast LLM inference. The possibility of generating high-quality, personalized quiz content in seconds — not minutes — was a game-changer. We realized we could build something that combines AI, gamification, and collaboration into one seamless experience.

QuizzVerse is the result: an AI-powered quiz platform where you can generate smart quizzes from any topic or document, play solo or compete in real-time multiplayer rooms, review your mistakes with AI-powered flashcards, and earn achievements along the way. It's studying reimagined — active, social, and actually fun

What it does

QuizzVerse is an all-in-one AI-powered learning platform that turns passive studying into an active, social, and rewarding experience.

Here's what you can do:

🧠 AI Quiz Generation — Pick from 24 topics (Science, Math, History, Programming, Mythology, Robotics, etc.) or type any custom topic. The AI generates a complete quiz with MCQ, True/False, and Fill-in-the-Blank questions in seconds. You control difficulty, question count, and timer.

📄 Document-Powered Quizzes — Upload a PDF, DOCX, or TXT file — lecture notes, research papers, or textbook chapters. The AI reads the content and creates a quiz tailored to your material. No manual question writing needed.

🎮 Real-Time Multiplayer Rooms — Create a room with a topic or document, share the 6-character code or QR invite, and challenge friends in live quiz battles. Each player progresses at their own pace with AI-scored answers, speed bonuses, streak tracking, and a live leaderboard. Optional video chat via LiveKit.

🤖 AI QuizzBot Chat — An AI tutor that answers questions, explains concepts, generates practice questions, and summarizes topics. Supports file upload (PDF, images, audio), voice recording with Whisper transcription, and markdown-formatted responses.

📚 Smart Flashcards & Review — Every wrong answer is automatically saved as a flashcard. Review them on the dedicated Review page with filters for difficulty and status. Flip to reveal the correct answer, explanation, and your original wrong answer — turning mistakes into learning opportunities.

🏆 Achievements & Gamification — 14 unlockable badges (First Steps, Perfect Score, Legend, etc.) with real-time popup celebrations, confetti animations, and sound effects. Progress bars show how close you are to the next milestone.

📊 Dashboard & Analytics — Track total quizzes, quizzes played, total score, and average score at a glance. Quick actions to generate quizzes, upload documents, or create rooms. Recent quizzes list with difficulty badges and delete options.

How we built it

QuizzVerse is built on a modern full-stack architecture designed for speed, scalability, and real-time interactivity.

Frontend — Next.js 16 + Tailwind CSS 4
The frontend uses Next.js 16 (App Router) with React 19 and TypeScript 5. The UI follows a custom dark-purple design system defined entirely in Tailwind CSS v4's @theme inline — glassmorphic cards, gradient text, glowing shadows, and 14 custom animations (float, shimmer, confetti, pulse-glow, etc.). Every component is mobile-responsive with touch-friendly targets.

Key frontend libraries:

Supabase JS for auth session management
Lucide React for all icons
qrcode.react for QR invite generation
react-markdown + remark-gfm for rich AI chat responses
LiveKit (@livekit/components-react + livekit-client) for video rooms
Backend — FastAPI + WebSockets
The Python backend uses FastAPI with 9 modular route files under /api/ — auth, users, quizzes, documents, rooms, chat, flashcards, achievements, and LiveKit. Each endpoint is auto-documented via Swagger at /docs.

WebSocket multiplayer is handled by a custom RoomManager class that maintains in-memory state per room — active connections, question progression, scores, streaks, and hints. Each player progresses independently through questions. The manager broadcasts real-time leaderboard updates and syncs via REST polling fallbacks for environments that don't support persistent WebSockets (e.g., Vercel serverless).

AI — Groq Cloud
All AI features use Groq Cloud with the openai/gpt-oss-120b model for ultra-fast inference:

Quiz generation — Prompt-engineered to output valid JSON with MCQ, True/False, and Fill-in-the-Blank questions. Response parsed into structured quiz + question records.
AI hints — Per-question subtle hints that avoid revealing the answer.
Title generation — Pre-generates short quiz titles before full generation to avoid Vercel 10s timeout.
Audio transcription — whisper-large-v3 via Groq for voice recording in chat.
QuizzBot — Conversational AI tutor with profile-aware context and markdown responses.

Challenges we ran into

Real-time multiplayer on a serverless budget
Vercel serverless functions don't support persistent WebSocket connections. But multiplayer rooms need real-time communication — scoring, leaderboard updates, question progression. We couldn't just give up on serverless deployment.

Solution: We built a dual-mode architecture. A custom WebSocket RoomManager handles real-time gameplay locally, managing per-player state — current question index, scores, streaks, hints used, and answer tracking — all in-memory for zero latency. On Vercel, a REST polling fallback syncs player lists and detects quiz activation every 3 seconds. The frontend seamlessly switches between modes without the user noticing.

Individual question pacing in multiplayer
In most quiz platforms, the host controls progression — everyone sees the same question at the same time. We wanted each player to answer at their own speed, but this meant the server had to track independent state for every connected player simultaneously.

Solution: The RoomManager maintains a dictionary per room mapping each user to their current question index, current question ID, hint usage count, and answer status. When a player sends next_question, the server fetches their next question on-demand, caching full question data lazily. Players who finish early see a "You're Done!" screen while others continue. The players_done set tracks completion, and only when all connected players finish does the server broadcast quiz_end. This required careful state synchronization across 7 parallel dictionaries and a race-condition-free disconnect handler.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Real multiplayer, real-time, real fun. Two players on different continents, different speeds, different questions — but the same room, same leaderboard, same competitive energy. We built a custom WebSocket protocol with 14 message types, per-player state tracking across 7 synchronized dictionaries, and a REST polling fallback that makes it work even on Vercel serverless. Players feel the tension of a live quiz without the complexity of a dedicated game server.

A design system that hits above its weight class. Every pixel of QuizzVerse — the glassmorphic cards, the floating particle animations, the gradient text that shifts, the breathing timer at 5 seconds, the confetti burst when you unlock a badge — was built from scratch with Tailwind CSS v4.

The Idea: A platform that imports any standard lecture video or textbook chapter and chops it into ultra-short, engaging "reels" or interactive stories.

Have captions

How it works: Instead of passively watching a long video, the student encounters a quick 60-second clip, followed by a sudden "micro-challenge" (a rapid-fire quiz, a slider to predict an outcome, or a fill-in-the-blank meme). Answering correctly unlocks the next segment.

Gemini api usage:

Automated Text Chunking: When a user uploads a long lecture transcript or textbook chapter, the API acts like an assistant editor. It scans the text and intelligently cuts it into logical, chronological "micro-lessons" so the user isn't overwhelmed.

Content Rewriting: It changes the tone of the boring text. In our prompt, we told it to use an "energetic tone" to make the content feel closer to a social media script rather than a dry academic definition.

Instant Quiz Generation: It reads the text, extracts the most critical concept from each chunk, and engineers a 4-option multiple-choice question on the spot, complete with realistic wrong answers.

Daily learning streak with XP and badges

projects.title: Adapt
projects.tagline: Advanced Dyslexia Adhd Personal Tutor
projects.description:
Inspiration

Ask most students how they revise and they'll tell you the same thing: they read it again. And again. The research is brutal about this — Karpicke, Butler & Roediger (2009) found
84% of students re-read to study, but only 11% ever test themselves
— and re-reading is one of the
least
effective things you can do.

Now stack the deck.
1 in 10 people in the UK are dyslexic
. Over
549,000 people in England are waiting
right now
for an ADHD assessment
, and only about 1 in 9 people with ADHD have a diagnosis on record. For them, a standard wall of homework text isn't just boring — it's a wall.

We wanted to build one thing that fixes both problems at once: reshape the material to how a student's mind actually works, and then get them off the least effective study method and onto the most effective one —
teaching
.

What it does

Adapt
is a Gemini-powered study companion built on one idea:
you don't read it again — you teach it once.

Pick your profile
— Dyslexia-friendly, ADHD Focus, or Classic. One choice re-themes the entire app: fonts (Lexend / OpenDyslexic), colour, contrast, spacing, pacing —
and
how the AI talks to you.

Reader
— paste any dense text and Gemini re-chunks it into short, plain, self-contained pieces, keeping
100% of the facts
, with adjustable emphasis and high-contrast options.

Explain
— get the same idea as an analogy, a story, or step-by-step. (Modes, not "learning styles" — we're careful about the science.)

Teach it Back

(the headline)
— you teach
Gem
, a curious AI classmate who knows
nothing
. Gem never lectures; it asks one specific question at a time. When you're done, a strict, schema-enforced gap analysis gives you an
understanding score
, what you nailed, the
exact gaps you missed
(with a hint in Gem's voice), follow-up questions, and a cleaner rewrite.

The magic trick: teach Gem photosynthesis but never say
chlorophyll
, and Adapt finds precisely that gap — the thing you didn't know you'd left out. Re-reading would never have caught it. Teaching did, in about ten seconds.

How we built it

Frontend:
a fast, dependency-free single-page app (vanilla JS + a hand-built design system), profile-driven theming via CSS variables, animated SVG score ring, Web-Speech-free voice.

Backend:
a tiny zero-dependency Node proxy. The Gemini key lives
server-side only
— it never touches the browser.

Gemini:

gemini-3.5-flash
with
strict
responseSchema
structured JSON
on every route — the gap analysis is a schema, not a prompt we beg for text from. The Teach-it-Back engine is a
two-phase design
: Phase 1 keeps "Gem" in character as a confused peer; Phase 2 is a rigorous analyzer that grades honestly against the source.

Voice:
we record audio and transcribe it
through Gemini
(see Challenges) → text → the teach-back pipeline.

Demo-safety:
a circuit breaker + per-route cached fallbacks mean the app
never shows an error on stage
, even if the wifi or API dies — and it self-heals to live the moment the connection returns.

The engineering story is the profile object:
one
structure drives the interface
and
the model's prompt. That's the part that makes Adapt an engineered product, not a prompt box.

Challenges we ran into

A Gemini project stuck at zero quota.
Our first key returned
429
even when completely idle — the project's per-minute quota was a hard
0
. We learned the hard way that
rate limits are per-project, not per-key
, spun up a fresh billed project, and it came alive.

Voice kept breaking on the venue network.
The browser's Web Speech API needs Google's speech servers, which VPNs and filtered networks block — it kept throwing "network unreachable." So we
ripped it out and rebuilt voice as record → Gemini audio transcription
, using the same key that aives any network.

"Dead" buttons that weren't dead.
Real-click testing (headless Chrome, actual mouse events) caught bugs our first synthetic tests hid — a Send tap during an in-flight turn was silently dropped. We made every busy state visible.

Staying on the right side of the science.
We deliberately don't call emphasis "Bionic Reading" (a trademark with no proven benefit), we frame explanation
modes
not "learning styles" (contested), and we're honest that dyslexia-font evidence is mixed — so we offer the
choice
rather than

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The
"you teach the AI" inversion
— a genuinely different framing that demos with a

A live gap-finder that surfaces the
exact
concept you skipped, backed by structured JSON — not a vague "add more detail."

An app that is
demo-proof
: it works on localhost, on a phone via QR, and even fully

Accessibility treated as engineering: WCAG-minded focus states, reduced-motion, 48px targets, one profile object doing real work.

What we learned

Teaching is one of the most evidence-backed ways to learn.
Fiorella & Mayer (2013) found actually teaching produces a delayed-test effect of
d
= 0.56 versus
d
= 0.22 for merely preparing to teach — more than double. Vanderbilt & Stanford have shown the same "teachable agent" effect sinc the idea; we built the tool that lets any student do it alone, at 2am.

Structured output changes everything.
Forcing Gemini to fill a schema turned "an AI that talks about your answer" into "an AI that reliably returns a score, gaps, and a next question" you can build a UI on.

Build for the demo, not just the ideal.
Fallbacks, circuit breakers, and real-click testing were what actually made it survive contact with a hackathon network.

What's next for Adapt

Dyscalculia support
— a genuinely under-served gap (~6% of people), visualising quantities and breaking arithmetic into concrete steps.

Live voice tutoring
with the Gemini Live API for real-time back-and-forth.

Spell-it-back
and handwriting input for younger learners.

Honest roadmap note: full
sign-language
generation is still an open research problehan fake it.

Two notes for the Devpost form:

"Built with" is usually a separate tags field on Devpost — put these there: gemini, google-gemini-api, node.js, javascript, css, html, web-audio-api, claude.

Keep the AI-credit line somewhere (MLH requires it): "Built during LeafHacks '26 with C; Gemini is the reasoning engine, the accessibility engineering is ours."

projects.title: RedPen - AI Maths Marking
projects.tagline: Draw your maths working by hand - our AI reads it like a teacher, turns the exact wrong line red, and writes the correction in matching red-pen handwriting.
projects.description:
Inspiration

A-level maths is brutally unforgiving in one specific way: it's not that students don't know the method, it's that they lose marks on
one
line - a dropped negative sign, a forgotten constant of integration, a chain rule they skipped - and by the time a teacher's red pen finds it, days have passed and the moment to learn from it is gone. We wanted to give students that red pen back immediately, on the actual page they wrote on, not a generic "wrong answer" message in a box.

RedPen - AI Maths Marking
:
Draw your maths working by hand - our AI reads it like a teacher, turns the exact wrong line red, and writes the correction in matching red-pen handwriting, instantly.

What it does

A student opens a question - say,
differentiate
$y = 3x^2 + 5x$ - rendered properly with KaTeX, and works it out by hand on a grid whiteboard: pen, eraser, colours, undo, exactly like paper. When they hit
Mark my answer
, their handwriting is sent to Gemini, which reads the working line by line like a real examiner. Instead of drawing a box around a mistake, we recolour the
exact stroke
the student wrote  their own ink turns red - and the correction appears right there in a handwriting-style font, positioned like a teacher's actual annotation. Hovering the red line explains why, in plain English, in a side panel. Every attempt autosaves and reloads, so a full history of past questions - solved, marked, and annotated

How we built it

Frontend
: React + Vite, with
react-konva
driving the whiteboard canvas (grid background, freehand pen strokes, stroke-level eraser), KaTeX for question rendering, and a settings panel for light/dark mode and swapping the Gemini model (Flash-Lite vs Flash vs Pro) between speed and accuracy.

Backend
: FastAPI, receiving the canvas export as a base64 image plus question context, and calling Gemini with a strict JSON response schema — error regions as normalized bounding boxes, completion text with position and font-size hints, plus a short summary.

The core trick
: rather than overlaying Gemini's bounding boxes as decoration, we match each returned box against the student's actual stroke coordinates (in the same normalized space) and recolour the matching
Line
shapes directly, turning feedback into something that looks hand-marked instead of computer-generated.

Persistence
: without time to stand up a full Supabase pipeline, we built a lightweight Vite dev-server middleware that writes each whiteboard's strokes, PNG snapshot, and marking result to disk — enough to demo real save/reload behaviour end-to-end.

Challenges we ran into

Two people building the whiteboard and the marking pipeline in parallel meant real merge conflicts — including one where a teammate's commit accidentally deleted the
save()
method while adding the "Mark my answer" flow, silently breaking autosave on every question navigation. We also hit a nasty stale-closure bug where a successful marking result wasn't actually being persisted because React state hadn't re-rendered yet when we tried to save it; a version mismatch between
katex
and
react-katex
that made maths render as garbled internal macro code instead of typeset symbols; and a
ResizeObserver
feedback loop where a scrollbar toggling on and off fought with our responsive canvas scaling and made the
entire page visibly shake
.

projects.title: Study Net
projects.tagline: To help people, 6 formers / college students specifically of all neurodivergent backgrounds to revise and study efficiently through personalised materials and communities to help motivate & support.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Many neurodivergent students struggle to study, revise, and learn using traditional methods that are designed for the majority of learners. Existing study tools are often generic and fail to provide the personalization needed for different learning styles.

This project is also deeply personal to our team. Two of us have parents who are neurodivergent, so we understand how challenging education can be without the right support. We wanted to create a platform that helps the next generation of neurodivergent students reach their full potential without facing the same barriers—especially in college, where grades and academic performance have a significant impact on future opportunities.

What it does

Study Net is a personalized study platform designed to support students from all neurodivergent backgrounds. It helps users discover learning techniques that work best for them while providing a supportive learning environment.

Key features include:

Personalized revision and study advice

Resource library with accessible learning materials

Study groups to encourage collaboration and peer support

User accounts with customizable profiles

Adjustable settings for a personalized experience

How we built it

We began by following the Waterfall development methodology. First, we gathered requirements and researched the needs of neurodivergent learners before designing the structure of our application.

As a team, we created algorithms and two flowchart diagrams to map out the user journey and application logic. Brainstorming played a huge role in shaping our final product, and we continuously refined our ideas throughout development.

We used AI-assisted ("vibe") coding with Gemini AI to develop the web application. We regularly wrote detailed prompts, tested new features, critiqued the results, and improved the application through multiple iterations. Finally, we carried out beta testing by using the application as real users would, identifying bugs, usability issues, and opportunities for improvement.

Challenges we ran into

Our original flowchart had several gaps, and after reviewing it with Gemini AI, we realised our project scope was too broad. We redesigned the flowchart to create a more focused and achievable product.

Early in development, we accidentally built the project on a platform that required payment to export the source code. Near the end of the hackathon, we discovered this limitation and had to manually transfer the code into GitHub, which cost valuable time.

Although these challenges were frustrating, they helped us improve our teamwork, planning, and problem-solving skills.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We collaborated exceptionally well as a team, combining our individual strengths and supporting one another throughout the hackathon.

We successfully applied computational thinking principles, particularly decomposition and abstraction, to break down complex problems into manageable tasks.

We significantly improved our coding skills and gained valuable experience using AI-assisted development tools.

Despite travel disruptions caused by Pride Festival events, we successfully completed a fully functional web application within the 12-hour hackathon.

What we learned

Always research your development platform before starting a hackathon. Choosing the wrong platform can create unnecessary obstacles later in the project.

The Waterfall methodology worked well for this hackathon because it helped us define clear requirements, organise our time effectively, and stay focused throughout development.

Iterative testing and continuous feedback greatly improved the quality and usability of our application.

What's next for Study Net

Our next goal is to expand Study Net by partnering with schools, colleges, and local communities so more neurodivergent students can benefit from personalized learning support. We also plan to continue developing the platform by adding new accessibility features, improving AI-driven recommendations, widening the broad of the study group by making a discord or WhatsApp community and using user feedback to make the experience even more effective and inclusive.

projects.title: Peckish
projects.tagline: Teach Peckish until the idea pecks.
projects.description:
Inspiration

We built
Peckish
because revision often feels passive: students read notes, highlight them, and hope the knowledge sticks. We wanted to flip that around. Instead of asking students to simply consume information, Peckish asks them to
teach it back
.

How We Built It

We built Peckish with
Django
, using server-rendered templates, SQLite, vanilla JavaScript, and custom CSS.

Gemini is used to generate study notes, split content into concepts, create revision resources, and evaluate student explanations. The app stores sessions, teaching attempts, fossils, XP, learning profiles, and generated resources in the database.

Challenges We Faced

One challenge was making AI feedback feel helpful without simply giving the answer away. Peckish needed to act like a curious learner, not a strict examiner, so we tuned the feedback to include what the student got right, what was missing, and a gentle next question.

Another challenge was making fossil cards useful rather than discouraging. We wanted mistakes to feel like learning artifacts, not failures.

We also spent time improving the UI: making flashcards interactive, fixing mind map spacing, replacing irrelevant images with connected idea boxes, and making progress feel rewarding with XP and level animations.

projects.title: Kyneta
projects.tagline: Gamified learning
projects.description:
Inspiration
Revision for UK STEM GCSEs is broken—students are trapped in rote memorization and past-paper grinding. Inspired by competitive rating platforms like Chess.com, I built Kyneta. It gamifies revision by cloaking strict exam criteria inside abstract, cyberpunk-style logic puzzles, keeping the tediousness of standard study completely invisible until the round is over.

What it does
The Contest Loop: Users race against a 2-hour timer in a brutalist "Cyber-Moss" interface, solving abstract logic puzzles generated on the fly.

The Hidden Learning Engine: While tracking energy costs or token counts across nodes, users are secretly executing GCSE Mathematics or Science curriculum tasks.

The Post-Sprint De-Masking: The final dashboard lifts the curtain, mapping completed puzzles back to their exact specification modules (e.g., EDX-M-02: Sine and Cosine Rules) to reveal what they mastered.

How we built it
Frontend: Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS styled with a sharp, high-contrast monospace layout.

AI Core Architecture: Powered by Google Gemini 2.5 Pro using a Blueprint-Driven Generation Architecture mapped to Bloom's Taxonomy. It forces the LLM to convert specific syllabus registry data into complex logic puzzles.

State & Auth: Integrated Clerk to handle persistent user profiles and Elo ratings serverlessly via publicMetadata, avoiding heavy database setups.

Challenges we ran into
Attempting to feed massive 100+ page specification PDFs straight into the model on every click via Vertex AI created massive cloud infrastructure and latency bottlenecks. We quickly pivoted by pre-parsing the specifications into highly optimized, string-based exam criteria blocks. This compressed our prompt payloads by 99% and slashed generation times down to an immediate 2 seconds flat.

Accomplishments that we're proud of
Zero-Lag UX: Achieving high-speed, dynamic AI puzzle generation that feels like a native terminal application.

Targeted Cognitive Prompts: Ensuring the AI reliably outputs rigorous, analytical scenarios matching strict GCSE constraints rather than simple trivia.

Uncompromising Aesthetics: Crafting a cohesive, dark-mode brutalist design that breaks the mold of boring, corporate EdTech tools.

What we learned
We mastered constraint-driven AI prompting—learning that an LLM must be tightly grounded with structural criteria to act as an accurate academic examiner. We also gained practical experience optimizing large token payloads and handling serverless user histories through metadata injection.

What's next for Kyneta
Gemini File API Ingestion: Swapping to the standard Google generative-ai SDK serverless file manager so schools can upload any raw PDF to instantly spin up custom topic queues.

Live Matchmaking: Implementing WebSockets to support head-to-head competitive sprints between students nationwide.

Dynamic Elo Scaling: Automatically scaling the mathematical complexity and compound constraints of the prompts as a user's skill rating increases.

projects.title: PRISM.
projects.tagline: An adaptive learning engine, designed to build durable memory through retrieval practice.
projects.description:
Project Story

Modern educational platforms tend to measure whether a student gets an answer right or wrong, but they rarely understand why. We wanted to create something that adapts to the learner rather than expecting every learner to adapt to the platform.

Project PRISM was built around the idea that education should reflect how cognitive science shows people actually learn. Instead of acting as another AI question generator, we wanted to build the foundations of an adaptive learning system that identifies misconceptions, adjusts the presentation of content, and supports accessibility from the start.

Our proof of concept focuses on Sixth Form students, but the architecture is designed so it could eventually support learners of all ages and abilities.

⸻

Inspiration

Our inspiration came from several areas of research.

We explored cognitive psychology, memory science, adaptive learning systems, knowledge tracing, accessibility research and psychometrics. Research into the spacing effect, retrieval practice, cognitive load theory, metacognitive calibration, Item Response Theory, Knowledge Graphs and modern adaptive learning algorithms showed us that many existing educational platforms still rely heavily on static question banks and simple percentage scores.

We wanted to combine these ideas into a single platform that continually asks:

“What is the student struggling with?”

rather than

“Did they get this question right?”

This shift in thinking became the foundation of Project PRISM.

⸻

What it does

Project PRISM is an AI assisted adaptive learning platform that analyses much more than a student’s final answer.

Our proof of concept records correctness, confidence and concept information before using Gemini to provide personalised feedback and identify likely misconceptions.

Rather than moving through questions in a fixed order, the platform models concepts as connected knowledge. If a learner struggles with an advanced topic, the system can recommend revisiting prerequisite concepts instead of simply repeating similar questions.

Accessibility is also integrated directly into the interface. Rather than treating accessibility as an afterthought, the UI can adapt its typography, spacing and presentation style to better support different learners while maintaining a clean, distraction free experience.

Although the current prototype demonstrates these ideas on a smaller scale, the architecture is designed to expand into a fully adaptive learning platform.

⸻

How we built it

The frontend was built using modern web technologies with an emphasis on clarity, accessibility and responsive design.

The backend manages user interactions, question data and communication with the Gemini API.

We structured educational content around concepts rather than isolated questions, allowing the platform to reason about relationships between topics instead of treating every question independently.

Gemini is not simply used to mark answers. Instead, it acts as an educational reasoning engine, generating personalised feedback and suggesting appropriate next steps based on the student’s performance.

Throughout development we continually referred back to educational research to justify design decisions, ensuring that each feature had a cognitive or pedagogical rationale rather than existing simply because it was technically possible.

⸻

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges was balancing ambition with the limited timeframe of a hackathon.

Many of the cognitive models we researched, including Deep Knowledge Tracing, adaptive spaced repetition algorithms and psychometric models such as Item Response Theory, would normally require large datasets collected over weeks or months before producing meaningful results. As a result, we had to simplify these ideas into a proof of concept while preserving the overall architecture.

Another challenge was preventing AI from becoming the entire product. Rather than relying on Gemini to simply generate questions, we focused on using it as an educational reasoning engine that could explain misconceptions and personalise learning pathways.

We also spent considerable time simplifying complex educational research into an interface that remained intuitive and accessible without overwhelming users.

⸻

Accomplishments we’re proud of

We’re particularly proud that the project is driven by educational research rather than trends.

Instead of building another AI chatbot for education, we combined ideas from cognitive science, memory research, adaptive learning, accessibility and knowledge modelling into a coherent proof of concept.

From a technical perspective, we successfully integrated AI into a structured workflow rather than allowing it to make arbitrary decisions. The platform separates educational content, learner state and AI reasoning, making it scalable and maintainable.

We’re also proud that accessibility was considered throughout the design process instead of being added afterwards. Features such as adaptable layouts, clearer typography and personalised presentation demonstrate how educational software can be more inclusive without compromising usability.

Finally, despite the limited development time, we’ve built a strong foundation for a system that could eventually support adaptive revision, personalised feedback, intelligent prerequisite detection, knowledge graphs, confidence calibration and scientifically informed learning pathways. Our goal was not simply to build another revision website, but to demonstrate a different way educational software could work.

projects.title: Fire shield
projects.tagline: Fire Shield is a real-time firefighter safety platform that helps incident commanders reduce exposure to hazardous conditions and operational risks.
projects.description:
Fire Shield: Protecting Those Who Protect Us

Every time firefighters respond to an emergency, they face not only immediate dangers from flames and structural hazards but also long-term exposure to harmful environmental conditions. Fire Shield is an intelligent decision-support platform designed to reduce firefighter exposure to hazardous environments and mitigate operational risks in real time.

By combining geospatial intelligence, exposure history, personnel data, and incident information into a single operational view, Fire Shield helps command staff make safer deployment decisions and identify when firefighters should be moved out of danger zones before exposure becomes critical.

Built using geospatial analytics and simulation-based operational data, Fire Shield provides actionable insights that improve situational awareness and support smarter resource allocation during emergency response. Our goal is simple: give decision-makers the tools they need to better protect firefighters in the field.

What we're most proud of is that Fire Shield is already fully operational and demonstrates how technology can directly improve firefighter safety. Through this project, we learned that data-driven decision support can play a critical role in reducing risk and protecting first responders.

What's next? We plan to integrate live sensor feeds, real-time environmental monitoring, predictive risk modeling, and department-wide exposure tracking to create a comprehensive firefighter safety ecosystem that proactively identifies risks before they become threats.

projects.title: Pharos
projects.tagline: Pharos tells NHS pharmacists which patients need medication review before a climate event kills them. Live UKHSA alerts. Real prescribing data. Zero guesswork. The tool Thompson 2024 said didnt exist.
projects.description:
Inspiration

A 2024 BMJ Public Health paper by UKHSA and LSHTM researchers studied
430,682 deaths in England and wrote: "We are unaware of any guidance
for clinicians or patients which addresses this need."

The need: knowing which patients are going to end up in hospital during
a heatwave because of the drugs they are on, and doing something before
that happens.

I checked the NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service's medication review tool
list in February 2026. Everything there covers falls, frailty,
polypharmacy. Nothing is triggered by weather. Not for heat. Not for
cold. Not for air quality.

129 people died from heat in London in June 2025. Those deaths
concentrate in patients on antipsychotics, anticholinergics, diuretics,
and ACE inhibitors, in Tower Hamlets, Newham, Hackney. PCNs that had
no tool to know they were the highest-priority practices that week.

Pharos is the tool that paper said didn't exist.

What it does

Two things, for two different users.

For PCN pharmacists: a dashboard.

When a UKHSA Heat-Health Alert fires, Pharos ranks every London PCN by
medication-driven excess hospitalisation risk. The score fuses six open
datasets: NHS prescribing volumes from OpenPrescribing, practice-to-LSOA
patient distribution from NHS Digital, LSOA heat exposure from Friends
of the Earth, England IMD 2025, Gasparrini/LSHTM DLNM spatial mortality
coefficients, and the ONS National Statistics Postcode Lookup.

For each PCN you see the drug breakdown by class with published relative
risk ranges and DOI citations, estimated patient counts per cohort, an
AI-generated outreach brief, a FHIR R4 export, and nearest cooling
centres. The dashboard converts population stats into a prioritised SMR
action queue. That is the exact workflow NHS England's Network Contract
DES mandates but provides no tool to execute.

For patients: a WhatsApp agent.

Text any medication name to the Pharos number. A LangGraph stateful
agent retrieves guidance from a Qdrant hybrid RAG index built over five
NHS clinical PDFs using Anthropic's contextual retrieval technique,
which cuts retrieval failure rate by 67% versus standard chunking. It
calls live tool functions: current UKHSA alert level, drug class heat
risk with published RR, nearest GP surgery, nearest cooling space. It
responds in under three seconds.

When a patient on furosemide texts "I've been vomiting since this
morning," the agent applies NHS Sick Day Rules immediately and tells
them to contact their GP before their next dose. That is the feature
most likely to prevent an actual AKI hospitalisation. It escalates to
999 instantly on emergency language. It sends proactive alerts to
registered users when the alert level changes. It responds in the
user's language: Bengali, Somali, Romanian. The highest-risk PCNs in
Tower Hamlets and Newham have large non-English-speaking populations
and this matters.

How we built it

Pipeline.
DuckDB ETL joining OpenPrescribing JSON exports, NHS
patients-by-LSOA (1.16M rows), NSPL postcode lookup (2.7M rows), IMD
2025 (33,755 LSOAs), and FoE heat vulnerability (32,844 LSOAs) via the
ONS LSOA 2011 to 2021 exact-fit crosswalk. Each practice gets a
population-weighted LSOA score rather than a single postcode score.
A practice in Whitechapel serving patients across six LSOAs gets a
weighted average of those LSOAs' heat exposure, not just the score for
its front door's postcode.

Risk engine.
PAF-based excess hospitalisation scoring using
published RR values from five peer-reviewed studies (Layton 2020, Chen
2025, Hospers 2024, Nordon 2007, Thompson 2024). Modified by the
Gasparrini DLNM PC1 spatial vulnerability component, the same
framework LSHTM used operationally during the June 2025 heatwave.
Output: 6,092 practice scores and 1,297 PCN scores with drug breakdown
JSON carrying low/mid/high confidence intervals per drug class.

RAG.
Docling parses five NHS PDFs. Chonkie chunks with a markdown
recipe. Kimi K2.6 generates 50 to 100 token contextual prefixes per
chunk using Anthropic's contextual retrieval technique. Chunks stored
in Qdrant Cloud hybrid collection: dense via bge-small-en-v1.5, sparse
via BM25. Cross-encoder reranking via bge-reranker-base.

Backend.
FastAPI on GCP Cloud Run europe-west2. APScheduler polls
UKHSA every 15 minutes. PostgreSQL on Neon.

Agent.
LangGraph StateGraph with AsyncPostgresSaver checkpoint
persistence keyed by phone number. Four tool functions. Kimi K2.6
primary, Groq Llama 3.3 70B as fallback.

Frontend.
React 18, Deck.gl, MapLibre with CARTO dark-matter
basemap (no API key needed). TanStack Query. Tailwind.

Challenges we ran into

The Gasparrini DLNM coefficients are in R's binary RDS format.
Converting them without losing the uncertainty structure meant
understanding the meta-analytical framework before touching the pipeline.

The NHS patients-by-LSOA publication switched from 2011 to 2021 LSOA
codes in January 2026. The Gasparrini model uses 2011 codes. Missing
the ONS 2011 to 2021 exact-fit crosswalk would have caused a 15 to 20%
silent join failure with no errors, just missing risk scores.

Additive PAF overstates joint risk when patients are on multiple drug
classes simultaneously. We flag this in the methodology panel and frame
the estimate as a conservative upper bound.

The Twilio sandbox requires every recipient to send a join code first.
We onboard judges at check-in Saturday morning so the 24-hour session
window is open by demo time Sunday.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The retrospective validation worked. The risk model flagged Tower
Hamlets, Hackney, Newham, and Barking as highest-risk before we looked
at syndromic surveillance data. The UKHSA NSSP Week 21 2026 report
confirmed elevated NHS 111 heat call volumes in those boroughs during
the May amber alert.

The drug breakdown chart is the first place a PCN pharmacist can see:
"11.15% of my patients are on ACE inhibitors and ARBs, RR 1.3 to 1.9,
estimated 3,831 patients," with a DOI on hover and a one-click
outreach draft.

The WhatsApp sick day rules response is the first automated clinical
prompt for the AKI prevention pathway in the context of heat events.
It works in under three seconds, cites NICE NG5, and does not require
the patient to call anyone first.

What we learned

The gap between "a paper says no tool exists" and "we built the tool"
is surprisingly small when the underlying data is already open and
structured. OpenPrescribing, NHS Digital, ONS, UKHSA, and the
Gasparrini group published everything needed. The barrier was not data
access. It was someone connecting the pieces.

Equity cannot be added at the end. The red-tier PCNs are in Tower
Hamlets and Newham because deprivation, heat exposure, and medication
burden concentrate in the same postcodes. Keeping the IMD score
separate and labelled in the UI rather than folding it into the
clinical math was the right call both methodologically and ethically.

What's next for Pharos

Air quality.
The LAQN API gives real-time DAQI by London borough.
OpenPrescribing already publishes the SABA/ICS ratio as an NHS quality
measure. On a high-DAQI day, Pharos surfaces the practices with the
highest uncontrolled asthma burden. Same pipeline, same channels,
different signal.

Cold weather.
The UKHSA Cold Health Alert runs on the same
four-tier system from November to March. Beta-blockers, NSAIDs, and
thyroid medications carry elevated cold-weather cardiovascular risk.
The cold module activates automatically when the Cold Health Alert
fires.

Year-round.
Heat in summer. Pollen and air quality spring to
autumn. Cold in winter. Every month, the same vulnerable patients,
the same medications. Pharos is not a heatwave tool.

EHR integration.
The FHIR R4 endpoint is live. Next step is SMART
on FHIR so the SMR action queue appears inside EMIS and SystmOne
directly rather than as a separate dashboard.

CHAPI.
System's Climate Health API targets a 2027 public launch
with a Clinical Decision Support category. Pharos fits that layer.

GitHu

projects.title: HeatGuard
projects.tagline: Real-time adaptive heat safety decisions for outdoor crews in the Gulf State region.
projects.description:
Inspiration

Every Gulf state protects outdoor labourers with a fixed-calendar midday work ban: Saudi Arabia 12:00 to 15:00, the UAE 12:30 to 15:00, Qatar 10:00 to 15:30, each running roughly mid-June to mid-September. A calendar cannot sense weather, and it gets this wrong in both directions. Replaying the committed Dubai weather archive, we found extreme heat arriving a full month before the 2025 UAE ban began. The season peak hit 46.5°C, with 12 unprotected danger hours on a single focus day in mid-May. The same archive shows 1,237 danger hours across the season that the ban never covers at all, simply because they fall outside its fixed window.

It is also unprovable in either direction. A contractor who did deliver water, rest, and shade on a dangerous day outside the ban window has no way to demonstrate that to an inspector, a lender, or a court. The intervention that actually works, the ILO and La Isla Network water-rest-shade protocol shown to cut acute kidney injury by roughly 94%, does not fail on the science. It fails on responsiveness and verifiability. We wanted to build the tool that closes both gaps at once.

What it does

HeatGuard is an adaptive, WBGT-driven work-rest-hydration scheduler that replaces the calendar with a live physiological read of the site. Every hour, for every site, it outputs exactly one signal: WORK, REST IN SHADE, DRINK NOW, or STOP. Each signal comes with a work/rest minute split, a hydration target in cups per hour, and a plain-language reason a supervisor can act on without interpreting any weather data themselves.

Under the hood, three layers run for every decision, and the most conservative one wins:

Screening. Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature is estimated via the Liljegren algorithm, or taken directly from a supervisor's own meter reading when one is available, then checked against ACGIH TLV/AL step tables using exact lookup rather than interpolation, so the numbers match what an inspector already recognizes.
Acclimatization. A NIOSH-based ramp holds newly arrived, unacclimatized workers to roughly 3°C stricter thresholds than veterans in identical conditions, since the first days on site carry the highest risk.
Physiology. The ISO 7933 predicted-heat-strain model computes sweat loss, water requirement, and maximum safe continuous exposure.

Every decision is written to a SHA-256 hash-chained audit record that is append-only, tamper-evident, and exportable per site and season, so a contractor can finally prove what a calendar ban never could. A supervisor dashboard layers a live signal, a WBGT gauge, an adaptive-versus-calendar timeline, an acclimatization tracker, and season-level impact and ROI figures on top of the same engine. A Gradient Boosting model trained on synthetic physiological profiles adds an advisory personal-risk overlay, flagging individually vulnerable workers for extra shade rest, without ever being allowed to override the regulatory signal underneath it. A fully local, citation-first retrieval system also lets a supervisor or auditor ask questions against the actual GCC regulatory text, such as UAE Ministerial Resolution No. 44, and get back an answer traceable to a real clause instead of a hallucinated summary.

How we built it

The core is a single deterministic Python engine. Given the same inputs, it always produces the same signal. Five different surfaces sit on top of it: a FastAPI backend, a Vite and React dashboard, a CLI, a Streamlit validation app, and a set of Jupyter notebooks used to validate the science against published tables. The engine uses pythermalcomfort for the Liljegren outdoor WBGT estimate, implements the ACGIH TLV/AL screening tables and ISO 7933 PHS hydration model directly against the standards text, and layers a NIOSH acclimatization ramp on top. Weather data comes from live Gulf meteorology feeds plus ERA5 reanalysis data for historical replay and testing.

The ML personal-risk layer is a scikit-learn Gradient Boosting model trained offline on synthetic physiological profiles covering age, weight, and comorbidities against WBGT. It is deliberately kept outside the regulatory decision path and covered by a non-interference test, so it can flag risk without ever being able to change a signal. The policy assistant is a fully local TF-IDF retrieval system indexed over the actual GCC legal text, chosen specifically so answers stay traceable to a real citation rather than a generative model's best guess.

We built the whole thing in a single 24-hour sprint, using Claude Code for the core build, OpenCode for review, and Cursor for additional iteration, going from a blank repo to a working engine, API, and dashboard in one day.

Challenges we ran into

The hardest problem was that there is essentially no open-source outcome data for heat-related occupational illness in the Gulf specifically. The epidemiology we could ground the model in, including AKI incidence and the La Isla intervention effect size, comes from transferred international studies rather than the region we are actually targeting. We had to be explicit in the product about which numbers are directly measured and which are transferred assumptions, instead of blurring the two together.

The physics side had its own challenge. ISO 7933's predicted-heat-strain model is a genuinely complex standard, and getting WBGT estimation, the acclimatization ramp, and the PHS hydration model to agree with each other, and with the published step tables an inspector would actually check against, took real care. We made an early architectural decision that the most conservative of the three limits always wins, specifically so a looser layer could never accidentally override a stricter one.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud that four people who had not built together before turned into a working team inside 24 hours. More specifically, we are proud that what came out of that sprint was not a demo hardcoded to one scenario. It is one deterministic engine, validated against the published ACGIH and ISO tables, feeding five real interfaces including a production FastAPI service and a live React dashboard. It placed third in the Health in Climate AI hackathon and earned us a fast track into an accelerator, which tells us the judges saw the same thing we did: this is closer to a real product than a hackathon prototype.

What we learned

We learned how much of building trustworthy AI for safety decisions is an architecture problem rather than a model problem. The discipline of always taking the most conservative of three independent limits, and of keeping the ML personalization layer strictly advisory and non-interfering with the regulatory signal, mattered more to the credibility of the system than any single algorithm choice. We also learned a great deal, quickly, about building with Claude Code and OpenCode in tandem, going from idea to a working prototype with real government standards embedded correctly in under a day.

What's next for HeatGuard

The immediate next step is to pitch our project to accelerators. That's where the prototype becomes pilot-capable. Our roadmap is already scoped for it: a real trust boundary so the platform can safely hold a customer's data, a durable and independently verifiable compliance ledger in place of today's in-memory reconstruction, a 72-hour forecast across all seven registered sites instead of two days on four, and a standards engine separated out into its own auditable package. None of that touches the underlying science. It's the work that turns a hackathon build into something a contractor can actually run.

Longer term, two directions.

Geographic: the Gulf's fixed-calendar ban is not a Gulf-specific failure, it's a pattern. California's Central Valley, the US Southwest, Southern Europe, and South and Southeast Asia protect outdoor labour with similarly blunt or nonexistent rules. Swap in the local standards tables and the engine generalises directly.

Hazard scop

projects.title: Prisma
projects.tagline: Women's health x major climate factors x microclimate factors cross risk assessment and resilience tool
projects.description:
Inspiration

Climate change is no longer just an environmental issue—it is a public health challenge that disproportionately affects vulnerable populations, particularly women across different stages of life. Existing health risk assessments rarely combine climate hazards, social determinants of health, and sex-specific biological factors into a single, personalised experience. We wanted to bridge that gap by creating
Prisma
, an AI-powered platform that transforms complex climate-health data into actionable insights while making the assessment engaging through the metaphor of growing a plant.

What it does

Prisma is an AI-powered web and mobile application that delivers personalised climate and health risk assessments. Users complete a guided questionnaire where each completed section helps a virtual plant grow—from a seed to a flourishing plant—symbolising resilience and wellbeing.

The platform securely collects demographic, environmental, lifestyle and health information, then combines it with climate hazards such as heatwaves, flooding and drought, alongside local environmental conditions and social determinants of health. Prisma generates a personalised risk profile, monitoring recommendations, preventative actions, emergency guidance and location-aware notifications. Privacy is embedded through secure data handling and GDPR-compliant design.

How we built it

We designed Prisma using a user-centred approach that combines AI with evidence-based climate and public health research. Our framework integrates climate risk data, environmental indicators, women's health research, and social determinants of health into a single assessment engine.

The application follows a plant-growth journey to simplify data collection, while the AI analyses multiple risk factors—including biological sex, reproductive life stage, ethnicity, environmental exposure, housing, lifestyle and local climate—to generate personalised recommendations. The platform is designed to support both web and mobile experiences with notification capabilities for changing climate conditions.

Challenges we ran into

One of our biggest challenges was balancing scientific accuracy with an intuitive user experience. Climate-health relationships are highly interconnected, requiring us to combine environmental hazards, health research and social factors without overwhelming users.

Another challenge was ensuring the platform remained inclusive by accounting for different life stages, demographic backgrounds and environmental contexts while maintaining strict privacy and data protection standards. Translating complex policy and research into simple, actionable recommendations also required careful design.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're proud of creating a solution that brings together climate science, public health and AI into a single personalised platform. Rather than focusing only on environmental risks, Prisma recognises that health outcomes are shaped by biological, social and environmental factors simultaneously.

The plant-growth experience transforms a traditional questionnaire into an engaging journey, encouraging users to complete assessments while visualising their progress. We're also proud that privacy, accessibility and inclusivity were considered from the beginning rather than added later.

What we learned

Building Prisma reinforced the importance of interdisciplinary thinking. Effective climate adaptation requires collaboration between healthcare, environmental science, technology and policy.

We also learned that personalised communication is essential. Presenting complex health and climate information in an engaging, visual and easy-to-understand format can significantly improve user engagement and awareness. Finally, we recognised the critical need for sex-disaggregated health research and equitable AI systems that better represent diverse populations.

What's next for Prisma

Our next step is to integrate real-time environmental and health datasets, including weather alerts, flood monitoring and air quality data, to provide dynamic risk assessments. We also plan to incorporate wearable device integration, longitudinal health tracking and predictive AI models that adapt recommendations as conditions change.

Future versions will support healthcare providers, researchers and local authorities with anonymised population-level insights while maintaining individual privacy. Ultimately, Prisma aims to become a trusted climate-health companion that empowers individuals, supports preventative healthcare and strengthens community resilience in a changing climate.

projects.title: climatecare-sentinel
projects.tagline: ClimateCare Sentinel — A climate-health intelligence platform that uses open environmental data to monitor risks, forecast health impacts, and support proactive decision-making
projects.description:
ClimateCare Sentinel

Inspiration

Climate change is increasingly affecting public health across the world. Extreme heat, poor air quality, floods, and environmental stressors can lead to rising hospital admissions, respiratory illnesses, heat-related conditions, and increased strain on healthcare systems.

We wanted to create a solution that helps communities, healthcare providers, and decision-makers understand these risks before they become emergencies. ClimateCare Sentinel was developed to transform complex climate and environmental data into actionable health intelligence.

What it does

ClimateCare Sentinel is a climate-health analytics platform that monitors environmental conditions and identifies potential health risks in real time.

The platform provides:

Climate Health Risk Monitoring

Air Quality Analysis

Heat Risk Assessment

Hospital Load Forecasting

Interactive Risk Mapping

Health Risk Trend Analysis

Emergency Alert Visualization

Impact Assessment Dashboard

By combining multiple data sources into a single dashboard, users can better understand how climate conditions may affect public health and healthcare capacity.

How we built it

We built ClimateCare Sentinel as a modern web application focused on usability, performance, and data visualization.

Frontend

React.js

Tailwind CSS

Framer Motion

Recharts

Leaflet.js

Architecture

Component-based design

Responsive dashboard layout

Real-time data processing

Interactive visualizations

Data Sources

Open weather datasets

Air quality datasets

Public environmental datasets

Climate risk indicators

The platform converts raw environmental information into meaningful insights through custom risk analysis and forecasting models.

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges was translating large amounts of environmental data into information that is useful and understandable for users.

Another challenge was designing a dashboard that could present maps, forecasts, alerts, and analytics without overwhelming the user.

Balancing performance, visualization quality, and responsiveness required careful optimization throughout development.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Developed a complete climate-health intelligence dashboard.

Created an interactive risk mapping system.

Implemented hospital load forecasting visualizations.

Built comprehensive health risk monitoring tools.

Designed a scalable and modern user experience.

What we learned

This project highlighted the strong relationship between climate conditions and public health outcomes. We learned how data visualization, predictive analytics, and environmental intelligence can help organizations make more informed decisions.

We also gained valuable experience in designing systems that communicate complex information in a clear and actionable way.

What's next for ClimateCare Sentinel

Future improvements include:

Expanded forecasting models

Additional climate indicators

Regional disease risk monitoring

Mobile notifications and alerts

Advanced healthcare resource planning

Support for multiple cities and regions

Our long-term goal is to help communities become more resilient to climate-related health challenges through accessible and data-driven decision support tools.
